Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro arrives at St Paul ACK church in Engineer Town for the service on September 20, 2026. [James Munyeki, Standard]

There was drama at St Paul ACK church in Engineer Town during service on Sunday after Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro clashed with Kinangop MP Zachary Kwenya Thuku over an alleged threatening message.

Thuku, who is allied to the Kenya Kwanza government led by President William Ruto, is said to have warned Nyoro against attending the service.

"Yesterday, I received a message from the MP for Kinangop, Kwenya Thuku, warning me not to attend the church service. If I am lying, let him come here and read the message he sent me," Nyoro said.

He challenged the Kinangop MP to read the message aloud to the congregation.

"If anything happens to me today, Kenyans will judge whoever will be responsible," said Nyoro.

The Kiharu MP challenged Thuku to face him at a public rally at Engineer Trading Centre.

When he rose to speak, the Kinangop MP said he would not address the matter in church.

Instead, he said this was a political issue that the leaders would resolve.

"Let us solve this matter amicably. We are all brothers in this political journey," he said amid cheers from the congregation.

Recently, Nyoro added his voice to the growing political realignment in Mt Kenya, openly acknowledging the political tightrope he now walks as he distances himself from his former allies in the ruling party.

In a candid interview, he admitted that his previous close ties with President William Ruto and the Kenya Kwanza administration have left him vulnerable to suspicion from both sides of the political divide but insisted his decision to abandon the ruling party, United Democratic Alliance (UDA) was deliberate, difficult, and necessary.

World.title: Ruto leaves for New York ahead of UN General Assembly
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Ruto leaves for New York ahead of 81st UN General Assembly. [PCS]

President William Ruto has departed for New York, United States, to attend the 81st United Nations General Assembly.

Ruto is expected to push Kenya’s investment agenda and advocate for increased financing for Africa.

According to a statement from State House, Ruto will use the global gathering to seek partnerships in energy, infrastructure, manufacturing, health, agriculture and technology.

He will also advance Kenya’s agenda on artificial intelligence and Africa’s participation in the global digital economy.

Ruto is expected to co-chair roundtables hosted by the Africa Finance Corporation (AFC) and Global Africa Business Initiative (GABI), alongside industrialist Aliko Dangote.

A key focus will be the planned Sh2.2 trillion East Africa Refinery in Lamu, which the government says will have a capacity of 700,000 barrels per day and create more than 60,000 jobs. The project is scheduled to break ground on September 30, 2026.

On artificial intelligence, Ruto and Finland President Alexander Stubb will co-lead the AI Middle Powers Initiative, which seeks to enable countries to pool computing resources, data and talent to build AI capabilities.

Kenya will also advance the Africa Development Bank-backed AI 10 billion initiative, which aims to mobilise up to 10 billion dollars by 2035 for investment in Africa’s artificial intelligence sector.

The President is further expected to sign a global declaration and roadmap on child online AI safety alongside leaders from Spain, the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia.

He will also launch an Africa Resilience Compact that will use artificial intelligence, satellite earth observation and predictive technologies to strengthen preparedness for El Niño and other climate shocks.

During his address to the UN General Assembly, Ruto is expected to champion an Africa-financing-Africa approach, calling for reforms and international guarantees to unlock more African capital for infrastructure and enterprise.

Ruto will also highlight Kenya’s National Infrastructure Fund, which the government says is designed to mobilise up to 40 billion dollars without adding to public debt.

On the sidelines of the General Assembly, the President is expected to hold meetings with heads of state and government, multilateral institutions and global corporations to discuss trade, investment and diplomatic cooperation.

He will also engage Kenyans living in the United States as the government advances a Diaspora Investment Platform intended to channel diaspora capital into productive investment in Kenya.

World.title: Inside Parliament's probe into secondary school fees and capitation
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Pangani Girls School Chief Principal Dr Millicent Odhiambo before the National Assembly Public Investments Committee on Governance and Education. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

Parliament’s scrutiny of the Auditor-General’s report on public secondary schools has exposed inconsistencies in capitation funding, student enrolment figures and the National Education Management Information System (NEMIS).

The National Assembly Public Investments Committee on Governance and Education has raised concerns over the impact of funding shortfalls on school operations and called for discussions with Ministry of Education officials to address the challenges.

The committee is also exploring whether the secondary school fee structure should be reviewed amid concerns that current capitation is insufficient to meet rising operational costs.

Chaired by Luanda MP Dick Maungu, the committee raised the concerns after the Auditor-General’s report showed that several national schools (C1) had sought additional fees from parents above the approved Sh53,000 annual amount, citing rising costs and inflation.

MPs also questioned disparities between capitation disbursements and the actual number of students in schools, which principals said had contributed to underfunding.

For the first time, administrators of national schools appeared before a parliamentary committee to respond to audit queries, with several saying discrepancies between NEMIS figures and actual school records had affected the amount of capitation they received.

Chief principals from Alliance High School, Alliance Girls, Bishop Gatimu Ngandu Girls, Limuru Girls, Mang’u High, Kenya High School, Pangani Girls and Kabare Girls, among others, said they had experienced difficulties validating learner data on NEMIS.

They said capitation received by their schools did not cover all students, with principals reporting that they receive less than the Sh22,244 expected per learner annually. The amount, they said, averages about Sh15,000.

Schools defend additional fees

During the committee’s examination of Alliance High School’s audit report, the Auditor-General flagged the irregular increase in school fees, including Sh17.6 million collected from parents.

“The school charged fees of Sh68,554 whereas the fees as per the Ministry’s guideline is Sh53,554 and the school thus raised fees by Sh15,000 per student annually contrary to Regulation 44 of Basic Education Regulation 2015, which states that no public school or institution shall issue alternative fee structure other than that approved by the Cabinet Secretary,” the auditor read. ‎Alliance High School's Principal David Kamau before the National Assembly Public Investments Committee on Governance and Education. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

Alliance High School Chief Principal David Kamau admitted that the school had sought alternative funding but said the initiative came from parents.

He said the approved Sh53,000 fee was insufficient to sustain the school’s budget amid rising costs and expectations of maintaining the institution’s standards.

“We have a certain lifestyle we have to maintain and that is why parents came in – in fact it was their idea – and asked us to maintain that. They came in and suggested they can do a budget support so that we maintain the same standards. For us, to acquire the results, we have to do a lot of activities to make sure we give a holistic education associated with the school over the years,” he explained.

“Parents approve that at an Annual General Meeting and we write to the Ministry but that letter of authority has never been granted. We have followed the process to the letter in terms of seeking approval for extra levies from parents,” he added.

The audit also flagged fee arrears in almost all the schools, with Alliance High School reporting arrears amounting to Sh36 million.

Kenya High School Chief Principal Rev Edith Koech was also required to respond to an audit query over unapproved fees under the parents’ association support programme, through which parents were charged Sh25,000 above the set amount per student without approval from the county education board.

Koech said the school had written to the Ministry seeking approval and, although it did not expressly receive authorisation at the time, it had since obtained it.

She said additional funds were approved during annual general meetings, where two budgets were presented — one based on Ministry guidelines and another reflecting what parents felt should be covered.

“Kenya High has its standards, for instance we have tea three times a day and they eat githeri once, they will burn the school if we change,” Koech explained.

Kiminini MP Kakai Bisau said the issue of additional levies had emerged in many schools, with principals arguing that the funds were necessary for students’ wellbeing.

“Looks like this issue is conflicting the law yet public participation is conducted among parents of respective schools. This is something we need guidance on and embedded in policy,” he said.

Other MPs questioned what happens to students from poor backgrounds who cannot afford the additional charges.

Lungalunga MP Chiforomondo Munga said principals had been entrusted with following the law, which states that public schools should not issue alternative fee structures without approval.

“I was a parent of Alliance but all said and done, you have done contrary to the law because approvals must come from the CS and I can assure you there is nobody who will approve that because they know they will be breaking the law and will be held accountable,” he said.

He said the situation presented a dilemma because schools were expected to maintain certain standards while operating within existing regulations.

Embakasi West MP Mark Mwenje said the issue of additional fees had existed for years, noting that he had paid about Sh40,000 while he was an Alliance High School student about two decades ago.

“We just need to sit down with the Ministry because it is becoming obvious that this money is no longer sufficient but we need to inform the principal that whenever such things are happening, there should be concurrence of the Principal Secretary but when we meet with the CS that issue should come out because we can no longer bury our heads in the sand,” Mwenje said.

Igembe Central MP Daniel Karitho described the issue as a “tricky” one, given rising inflation and the need to comply with the law.

“We cannot allow parents from any institution to just sit down and agree because there are those who are voiceless. This is an issue that needs to be discussed even in the House on the fees structure and if there is something that needs to be done, even on the basic regulation so that we can have a level,” Karitho said.

Alliance principal, however, maintained that the school’s process was transparent, with parents being provided with budget documents during annual general meetings and informed why additional funds were required.

“We tell the parents that is their decision to make and if they want to stick to the Sh53,000 but what we can offer as a school will reduce. I can assure we are conscious of the needy and we do not send anyone away because of the fees, either for statutory or additional,” he explained.

Kenya High echoed similar sentiments, saying additional contributions were based on public participation among parents and that no child was sent home over fees. The school also has endowment funds, it said.

NEMIS discrepancies

In another case, MPs questioned how Limuru Girls High School received an additional Sh785,946 in capitation after discrepancies emerged between its student enrolment records and figures captured in NEMIS.

The committee noted variances in Limuru Girls’ records and those of other national schools for the financial years 2020/2021 to 2024/2025.

The Auditor-General’s report for the year ended June 2024 showed that NEMIS recorded 2,099 students at the school in September 2023, 2,300 in January 2024 and 2,354 in May 2024.

However, records presented by the school showed enrolment of 2,062 students in September 2023 and 2,253 students in both January and May 2024.

The difference resulted in Sh785,946 in excess funding, raising concerns over whether the variance affected service delivery in other schools that did not receive capitation and made it difficult to confirm value for money.

Limuru Girls Chief Principal Susan Kariuki acknowledged the discrepancies but attributed them to differences between physical enrolment records and learner information captured in NEMIS.

“The difference arose from variations between the school’s physical enrolment records and the learner information captured in NEMIS at the respective reporting periods. The school did not intentionally provide inflated enrolment figures,” Kariuki said.

“So, because you are given more money, where do you take it?” Maungu posed.

Kariuki, however, said the school had not received the full amount of capitation due per learner and therefore did not consider itself overfunded in the ordinary sense. She said the Government was expected to provide Sh22,244 per learner but the school had been receiving about Sh15,000.

Narok Woman Representative Rebecca Tonkei questioned how Limuru Girls received higher funding for learners who were not captured in NEMIS, noting that other schools appearing before the committee had complained of underfunding caused by incomplete NEMIS records.

Maungu questioned the reliability of NEMIS, saying a system used to determine public funding should be predictable, consistent and dependable.

“This is not a good system. A good system should be predictable, consistent and dependable. But this system gives some people less and others more, sometimes the data is missing,” Maungu noted.

Starehe Girls raises fresh questions

Starehe Girls presented a different case that the committee said contained several grey areas after it emerged that 70 per cent of the school’s 776 learners are fully sponsored while the remaining 30 per cent are self-sponsored.

The school explained that all learners receive about Sh16,000 in Government capitation. For the 70 per cent, their upkeep is sourced through the board of trustees, while self-sponsored learners cover their own costs.

“Being a C1 school, by law it should pay Sh53,000. Instead, some are paying Sh150,000 meaning Sh96,000 extra to take care of the vulnerable. On this other side, you are saying they have a sponsor who take care...are you seeing the kind of confusion because they are already sponsored?” posed Maungu.

Despite the school’s unique funding arrangement, the committee said Starehe Girls remained a public institution and should therefore be audited.

The committee noted that not all financial years had been covered in the audit, unlike other C1 schools, and directed the institution to present all relevant documents for review.

Meanwhile, Mang’u High School surprised the committee when its administration said the school also faced challenges posed by snakes and hyenas that sometimes invade the institution.

World.title: Ruto faults Uhuru for undermining his government
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto join traditional dancers in Homa Bay on September 17, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has renewed his public criticism of former President Uhuru Kenyatta, accusing his predecessor of undermining the government and urging him to withdraw from active political mobilisation.

Ruto said he had supported Uhuru throughout their political partnership and expected reciprocal support when he sought the presidency.

“I stood by you through four elections; I stood by you, helped you, took care of you, and worked for you.”

Ruto claimed the two had discussed an arrangement in which each would serve as president for ten years. He accused Uhuru of failing to honour that understanding, saying:

“When the time came for you to help me, after you said ‘ten years for you, ten years for me,’ not even for a single day did you support me.”

Ruto also appealed to Uhuru to respect the position of former President and withdraw from political activities that he said were aimed at destabilising his administration.

“A former president! Surely, my brother, you are lowering the dignity of the office of the former president. You are a retired president respect your office, go and relax. Let us plan for this country of ours, Kenya,” Ruto said.

Ruto made the remarks on Thursday, September 17, 2026, in Sindo, Homa Bay County, as he concluded a four-day development tour of Nyanza.

The tour covered Kisumu, Siaya, Migori and Homa Bay and focused largely on roads, markets, housing, water and other development projects. The Star+1

The latest confrontation adds another chapter to the complicated political relationship between the two leaders.

Ruto served as Uhuru's deputy from 2013 to 2022, after the two politicians formed a political alliance that won the 2013 and 2017 presidential elections.

Contemporary accounts describe their original arrangement as involving support for Kenyatta for two terms, followed by support for Ruto's presidential ambitions. The Washington Post

The President nevertheless acknowledged Uhuru's democratic right to oppose his government but urged the former president to respect the office he once held.

“You are running schemes to sabotage the government. You are a retired president respect your office, go and relax. Let us plan for this country of ours, Kenya,” he said.

His criticism centred instead on what he described as continued political mobilisation against his administration.

He said his administration had stabilised the economy and pointed to investments in education, housing, markets and infrastructure. During the Homa Bay leg alone, the government highlighted a Sh3.5 billion plan for 21 modern markets.

World.title: Five killed as bandits ambush police search team in Isiolo
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Five people, including two police officers killed by bandits at the troubled grazing field of Gotu in Isiolo County on Wednesday.

The victims are a senior police officer, a police constable who was the driver of the vehicle that was ambushed by bandits, a livestock farmer and two National Police Reservists (NPR). The police officers were attached to an Anti-Stock Theft Unit (ASTU) located near Gotu trading centre.

The victims were part of a search team that was looking for an elderly man who reportedly went missing within the Gotu area and was last seen around Madho Gurba Huka, a grazing area in Chari Ward in Merti sub-county.

Isiolo County Police Commander Isaac Sang said the mentally challenged man from Barambate sub-location, Kulamawe location was reported missing a day ago.

The Isiolo camel keeper, reported to be related to the man who went missing, had requested police to search for him.

The mission turned tragic when the group was ambushed by armed bandits, killing all five on the spot.

The incident took place near the junction of Lososia-Merti road and Gotu-Merti route.

Mr Sang said the bodies of the officers and other victims were removed to Isiolo County Teaching and Referral Hospital awaiting postmortem.

"A reinforcement (of security personnel) had been sent to the area which includes an armoured vehicle to pursue the attackers," said the police chief.

The police boss called for calm and cooperation from the residents while police pursue the suspects.

He said that investigation into the incident had commenced.

On Wednesday afternoon, a gunfight was reported between police reservists and the bandits on the western bank of the river.

"The reservists in the area pursued the attackers minutes after reports of the killings that led to an exchange of gunfire. We are told an unknown number of people have been injured," said a herdsman from Gotu who sought anonymity for security reasons.

A source from Isiolo County and Teaching and Referral Hospital revealed that two ambulances had been sent to Gotu to attend to the injured persons.

Gotu, along with Kom in Merti sub-county is a bandit hotspot in Isiolo that is attributed to competition over scarce pasture by rival herders from Isiolo, Samburu East and parts of Marsabit with local leaders calling for eviction of pastoralists from outside the County. Several people have been killed in the two locations since last year and hundreds of livestock stolen.

On August 1, two people were killed in the Garse Dabata area in Gotu and nearly 700 goats and sheep were stolen. Nearly all the stolen animals were recovered in operation undertaken by a multi-agency security team stationed in various locations along the Isiolo-Meru border.

Interior CS Kipchumba Murkomen on two occasions called for an operation in parts of Isiolo, Laikipia, Samburu and Meru Counties that had experienced frequent cases of banditry and rustling.

However, leaders fault the CS for failure to take decisive action on insecurity that keeps on recurring in parts of Isiolo and Meru Counties. The leaders including Governor Abdi Guyo want herders from outside Isiolo who are in Kom and Gotu areas to be evicted.

World.title: The Palestinian Authority has been banned from entering the US again. Here’s more about it
World.content:
The US has, for a second consecutive year, banned officials from the Palestinian Authority (PA) from entering the country for the United Nations General Assembly. PA President Mahmoud Abbas will once again have to speak at this week’s event virtually.

The US State Department said last week that it would not be issuing visas to PA officials, citing “ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace” in what it called the “Israeli-Palestinian Conflict.”

Among these activities are attempts to “internationalize” the conflict, including through the International Criminal Court and International Court of Justice, as well as “continuing to pay stipends to terrorists and to glorify acts of terrorism and terrorists in public pronouncements and school textbooks,” the State Department said.

The Palestinian Foreign Ministry called the US’ actions “unjustified,” saying that they undermine “efforts to rebuild trust, strengthen Palestinian-American relations, and advance the two-state solution.”

“We firmly reject the claim that pursuing Palestinian rights through the United Nations and international courts undermines peace. Resorting to international law and institutions is a legitimate and peaceful means of protecting our rights,” the ministry said.

The Palestinian Authority was formed in 1993. Though it is supposed to govern over the West Bank and Gaza, in recent decades, the militant group Hamas has run the Gaza Strip, according to the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR).

The PA is headquartered in the West Bank, operating from the city of Ramallah. It is comprised of several Palestinian factions, but excludes militant groups such as Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, CFR says.

Abbas is deeply unpopular among Palestinians. He has led the PA since the death of Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat in 2004 and has clung to power, despite being seen by critics as lacking democratic legitimacy.

In a 2025 letter, Abbas condemned the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel and pledged to hold elections and reform the PA, according to excerpts shared with CNN.

CNN’s Ibrahim Dahman, Nadeen Ebrahim and Abeer Salman contributed to this reporting.

World.title: ‘Turn the cameras off:’ London’s growing privacy pushback against smart glasses
World.content:
London/New York —

The bars, theaters and restaurants dotting central London may not seem like a conflict zone. But many venue owners are facing a difficult fight over a new and, some say, potentially dangerous device: smart glasses.

The glasses — which can capture video, photos and audio from the wearer’s perspective — are growing in popularity. Eyewear giant EssilorLuxottica, which Meta partners with for its glasses, said seven million pairs of AI glasses were sold in 2025. Meta is holding its Connect conference this week, where it’s expected to announce new smart glasses without cameras, according to The Information. Samsung and Google are expected to debut new jointly developed smart glasses this fall.

But as the technology becomes more widespread, so too has the backlash. Videos posted on social media showing men who appear to film women without their knowledge have raised questions about consent — and whether existing privacy laws can keep pace with technology that allows people to record almost invisibly.

“It makes it harder and harder to protect yourself by just looking around and screening for things,” Irina Raicu, director of the internet ethics program at Santa Clara University’s Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, previously told CNN. “So, the whole notion of consent is kind of disintegrating.”

London, along with New York and Australia, is emerging as a bellwether for how people and businesses are responding to the growing tech. Some hospitality and entertainment venues have introduced restrictions or bans, and anti-smart glasses s have begun appearing at some bus stations throughout London. One skewers Kylie Jenner’s ad campaign for Meta glasses, transforming her into a skeletal X-Ray with the tagline: “We’re Always Watching.”

A fake sign by the “Everyone Hates Elon” group is displayed on a public bin, re-designating it for a “Smart Glasses Amnesty” on September 10, 2026, in London. Leon Neal/Getty Images

The sentiment echoes a broader ban across the United Kingdom from August that prohibits smart glasses in the courtroom.

Some Londoners told CNN that smart glasses make them feel uneasy in places where people expect a degree of privacy, like bars, restaurants and other social settings.

‘Turn the cameras off’

Popular pub chain Wetherspoons has prohibited customers from recording using the glasses. “I don’t really want to be filmed when I’m just out having a couple of pints,” Zak, a student at a Wetherspoons pub in central London, told CNN. He said he had seen videos on TikTok in which people appeared unaware they were being filmed, adding that covering the glasses’ recording light was “ridiculous.”

Serena, another Wetherspoons customer, said she was particularly concerned about the possibility of being filmed without knowing where the footage might end up.

A Wetherspoons spokesperson told CNN, “With regard to Meta glasses, our instinct was to say, ‘turn the cameras off.’”

Meta says the camera on its glasses won’t record if the recording light has been covered. In August, the company said it updated its glasses to prevent users from covering the light after they started recording, coming after it previously enabled the glasses to detect whether the light had been tampered with. Meta also said it has cracked down on videos shared on social media that show wearers using their AI glasses to harass people around them.

“Naturally some places shouldn’t be filmed at all and that’s reasonable, but rules should be applied consistently,” a Meta spokesperson said in a statement to CNN. “Our glasses have a light that turns on to let people know when a photo or video is taken, something smartphones and other cameras don’t have.”

Customers drink outside a Wetherspoon public house in London on October 6, 2023. Susannah Ireland/Reuters

Google has been down this road before. It tried popularizing smart glasses more than a decade ago with its now discontinued Google Glass eyewear, which sparked similar privacy concerns.

Sameer Samat, Google’s president of the Android ecosystem, said the company isn’t surprised by the recent pushback. Details like how the glasses indicate when they’re recording and whether users can work around those safeguards “really, really matter,” he told CNN in August, adding that Google is taking those concerns into account when developing its glasses. Like Meta’s glasses, Samsung’s upcoming glasses powered by Google’s software will have a privacy light that’s tamper-resistant.

Samsung and Google declined to comment when reached by CNN.

Solving the privacy problem won’t be easy, according to Calli Shroeder, director of the AI and Human Rights program at the Electronic and Privacy Information Center (EPIC). Many potential solutions — like features that would blur peoples’ faces automatically when recording or require their legal consent before uploading videos — would be challenging to implement and still wouldn’t fully address the risks.

One possible remedy would be to make it so that glasses detect their location and automatically disable recording in sensitive areas like playgrounds and locker rooms. But that would entail making sure the glasses could sense their surroundings autonomously, which could also raise privacy issues.

Not just privacy

At London’s Piccadilly Theatre, workers and attendees said smart glasses could undermine the experience of live performance and negatively impact actors’ livelihoods.

A lot of the appeal of going to theaters is that the performance remains a mystery right up until showtime, a benefit that stealthy filming could threaten, said Bradley, a waiter and theatre director.

“It’s not a huge wide scale media like TV and film, it’s a much more enclosed environment, which you’re more intrigued to go to without those spoilers or without that pre-formed opinion of it,” he said.

Pedestrians walk along a busy West End street at night on March 22, 2024. Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images

A spokesperson for ATG Entertainment, which operates several of London’s iconic West End theatres including Picadilly Theatre, told CNN that audience members will be asked to remove the eyewear and delete any footage if caught with them.

Many movie theaters in the UK are also banning the use of smart glasses due to piracy concerns, the UK Cinema Association (UKCA) said late last month.

Race for the next big thing

The growing unease comes as technology companies continue to invest heavily in wearable devices, betting that glasses capable of capturing and processing the world around their users could become the next major consumer technology platform.

The glasses allow users to listen to music, take calls and snap photos hands-free, and some tech companies believe they could one day be the preferred way to communicate with AI assistants.

Smart glasses from Oakley Meta and Ray-Ban Meta are sitting on a table in an eyewear store in Stuttgart, Germany. Christoph Schmidt/picture-alliance/dpa/AP

A Meta spokesperson told CNN their glasses allow people to “stay in the moment, from listening to music to live translation or hands-free calls.” The glasses provide “critical new technology” to visually impaired consumers, the spokesperson said, adding that limiting how people can use this would be a “major step backwards.”

Advocacy groups, including the UK’s Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB) have warned that overregulation of smart eyewear could strip those who are blind or visually impaired of a key accessibility tool. The new tech can help with daily tasks like browsing restaurant menus, reading street signs, or describing scenery, according to RNIB.

Shipments of smart glasses grew by 212% year-over-year in the first half of 2026, according to market research firm Counterpoint Research. Meta leads the industry with about 84% of the market.

“I think there’s a huge fear of being like left behind in the race of these new technologies,” said Shroeder, the human rights director at EPIC. “I think also it’s very easy for these tech companies to fall into a bubble.”

World.title: As US steers clear of Yemen fight, the Iran-backed Huthis launch next phase of campaign
World.content:
In the last month, Iran-backed Huthi militants in Yemen have joined the Middle East conflict in dramatic fashion — capturing a swath of the Red Sea coastline, launching missiles and drones at Saudi energy infrastructure and even targeting the Saudi capital, Riyadh, over the weekend.

Now their campaign appears to be entering a new phase, with a major offensive aimed at cutting off government forces in a central part of Yemen.

Their ultimate goal, according to some analysts, is control of the entire country.

The latest Huthi advance comes as Saudi Arabia deploys fighter jets and missiles in an effort to stem the militant group’s progress south toward the port city of Aden, where Yemen’s internationally recognized government is based.

Saudi appeals for US airstrikes to reverse Huthi gains have fallen on deaf ears, according to a regional diplomatic source.

Britain, however, has answered the Saudi request for assistance. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday he has agreed to provide “defensive air-to-air refueling” for Saudi jets for a limited period, according to Reuters news agency.

In a joint statement on Monday, foreign ministers from the G7 nations called on ​Iran to end its ‌arming and support of the Huthis – and for the militant group to “cease ​all ⁠military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping.”

The Huthis have already seized a long stretch of the Yemeni coastline bordering the Red Sea — one of the world’s most important waterways — and they control the Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint at its southern end.

Now, they are trying to seize the mountainous region of Taiz, which includes important routes for government forces.

“Cutting these routes would threaten a key transport and supply connection between government-held areas,” according to Yemen analyst Mohammed al-Basha.

Women and children, who fled fighting between the Huthis and government forces in Red Sea coastline areas, walk at a camp for internally displaced people near Aden, Yemen, on Saturday. Stringer/Reuters

A commercial vessel is anchored off Yemen’s coast at Bab al-Mandeb, in the strait connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean on September 12, 2026. AFP/Getty Images

The Huthis have run into stiff resistance from local tribes, Basha told CNN.

The battlefield situation remains fluid, according to Basha, and the risk remains that the Huthis will be able to surround the city of Taiz. But it appears that defenses have not experienced a collapse comparable to what was seen on the west coast front, when a large area — including the port of Mocha — fell within hours.

Basha added that, as of Monday, the government still holds a critical road junction connecting Taiz and Aden in an area hosting hundreds of thousands of internally displaced people.

There is also heavy fighting farther east, according to several Yemen analysts, in the province of Marib. Marib is an oil-rich region long in the Huthis’ sights.

Yemeni government forces have used artillery and rocket systems — supported by Saudi airstrikes of growing intensity — to repel Huthi forces in the region, according to analysts. A senior commander claimed that his troops have now gone on the offensive.

Yemen’s internationally recognized government said Monday that its forces targeted Huthi fighters and supply lines in the strategic Bab al-Mandeb area overlooking the Red Sea and in Bayda province in central Yemen. A military spokesperson, Col. Majed al-Nazili, said government forces struck Huthi positions, personnel and supply routes, and the Information Ministry released footage it said showed attacks on Huthi sites and equipment. The claims could not be independently verified.

Huthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed Monday that Saudi Arabia has carried out 157 aircraft and missile strikes across four Yemeni provinces, bringing to 917 the total number of strikes since the latest escalation began. He vowed the attacks would be met with a response.

Saudi authorities had no immediate comment, and CNN could not independently verify the Huthi claims.

“The Huthis likely seek to capture the area in order to try to extract and export oil through the Red Sea, which could fund Huthi political and military activities,” the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington think tank, reported Friday.

The cities of Taiz and Marib are key bastions, “and if the Huthis capture both, it is game over,” Basha told CNN. “But their defenders are putting up a strong fight.”

The Huthis control a large chunk of western Yemen, where more than 70 percent of the population lives, including the capital, Sanaa. Government forces hold a slice of southern Yemen and the sparsely populated eastern part of the country.

It’s unclear whether the Huthis intend to put pressure on Aden itself. Much will depend on the ability of government forces to improve coordination after the disastrous western shore retreat.

“The Huthis do not need to defeat Saudi Arabia militarily and near certainly cannot,” said Ibrahim Jalal of the Middle East Institute in Washington.

A view of a makeshift camp for people displaced by clashes between Iran-aligned Huthi fighters and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, in Taiz province, Yemen, on September 13, 2026. Stringer/Reuters

“They, however, need to influence how much financing, intelligence, logistics, air defense and potentially airpower Riyadh is prepared to commit to the Yemeni armed forces capable of reversing their gains on the ground.”

To that end, Jalal told CNN, the Huthis are avoiding getting bogged down in urban fighting and trying to encircle government forces.

CNN has contacted Huthi officials for comment.

The New York Times reported Monday that, after a call from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman last week, US President Donald Trump agreed to launch airstrikes against the Huthis. But Trump changed his mind on Sunday, according to the Times.

Last week, Trump said the Huthis “let us know they don’t want to fight with us,” adding that they were allowing “most ships” to pass through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait but were “unhappy” with one country — obviously Saudi Arabia.

The Huthis said two months ago that they would attack Saudi shipping.

“Trump’s best option is to stay out of the Yemen quagmire as remote warfare won’t change the equilibrium on the ground while widening supply chain disruption,” according to Andreas Krieg, CEO of London-based political risk firm MENA Analytica. “It would also derail the Iran and Hormuz diplomatic track,” Krieg wrote Monday on X.

However, the “inconsistency in the US position vis-à-vis Tehran’s proxies means that the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia have had to handle the Huthis largely on their own,” Fatima Abo Alasrar, a Yemeni analyst, wrote in a piece for the Stimson Center, a US research institute.

So far, Saudi Arabia does not appear to have invoked its recently agreed trilateral defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. And Turkish officials have been careful not to offer too much.

“We see there are very serious attacks on Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity, sovereignty,” Turkish Foreign Minister Hasan Fidan said Saturday, referring to Huthi drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia.

“We are in serious solidarity on this point. … They may have some military needs, especially on some technical issues. We would have no issues in meeting these,” Fidan told Turkish channel NTV.

Saudi isolation

“Saudi Arabia is discovering how alone it is in a moment of need,” analyst Natiq Malikzada said Monday. “For years, it built its security around the hope that Washington would defend it.”

“For the US, as for any other country in times like this, Saudi security matters less when American interests are not directly at risk,” Malikzada wrote on X.

Jalal said the Saudis can count on some support from regional allies and Pakistan, and potentially from Egypt.

But for now they bear the lion’s share of the burden.

This frame grab taken from AFPTV video footage shows a fighter from the Saudi-backed Nation’s Shield Forces deployed in Yemen’s Kadha area, west of Taiz province, on September 10, 2026. AFPTV/AFP/Getty Images

Iran is banking on the Huthis as its “last resilient proxy to improve its bargaining position and leverage, while the Huthis now seek to consolidate gains and expand territorially, as well as intensify attacks into Saudi Arabia, to redraw the rules of the game,” Jalal wrote in the online publication Al Majalla.

The Huthis “will continue to punish Saudis till they get their multibillion-dollar reparations fund,” Basha told CNN on Monday. They have long insisted on Saudi compensation for the long blockade against Yemeni territory they hold.

But Huthi ambitions may go further. Their ultimate goal is control of all of Yemen, Jalal said.

Javan Online, an Iranian publication affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), recently suggested the Huthis were close to unifying Yemen under a “single center of power.”

In so doing, they would become a regional force capable of making their opponents negotiate over Red Sea security and the future of the Arabian Peninsula itself, the Javan commentary said.

That is Saudi Arabia’s nightmare.

CNN’s Nadeen Ebrahim and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed reporting.

World.title: Republican support for Trump’s handling of war in Iran shows cracks in new CNN poll
World.content:
Americans’ opposition to the war in Iran has hardened, according to a new CNN poll conducted by SSRS, with almost two-thirds saying the US is not winning the conflict and more saying President Donald Trump isn’t doing enough to end it.

Americans have never held positive views about the war, and nearly seven months after it began, broad majorities say the conflict has hurt US interests, has not been worth the costs and that the president lacks a clear plan to handle it.

The findings come as Trump prepares to address the United Nations and meet with Gulf leaders about the future of the Iran war. They also come as he is confronting a metastasizing crisis with the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

Overall, 29 percent of US adults approve of Trump’s handling of foreign affairs, a new low in CNN polling across both of his terms as president, while 71 percent say they disapprove. More see his foreign policy decisions this term as harming America’s standing in the world rather than helping it. Only 26 percent say they approve of the president’s handling of the situation in Iran, down from 33 percent a month after the war began.

Much of the decline in approval of his handling of Iran comes among Republicans. Views among Democrats and independents have been steadily negative throughout the conflict. In March, though, 73 percent of Republicans approved of the way Trump was handling it. Now, that figure stands at 60 percent. Among Republican and Republican-leaning adults, approval of Trump’s handling of Iran dips into negative territory among those younger than 45 (53 percent disapprove) and those who say they are not members of the Make America Great Again movement (54 percent disapprove).

Republicans are also less positive now than they were earlier this year about the impact of Trump’s foreign policies more broadly: About half of Republicans now say that his decisions have helped the US’ standing in the world, down 13 points since March.

Three-quarters of all adults now say Trump does not have a clear plan for handling the situation in Iran, and 78 percent say that he is not doing enough to end the war. About 7 in 10 say it’s at least somewhat likely that the conflict will be a long-term one, including majorities across party lines. About a third, 32 percent, now see a long-term conflict as very likely, the largest share to say so since the war began.

More say the war has hurt American interests than helped them (70 percent to 18 percent), and 76 percent say the war has not been worth either the toll it has taken in American lives or the financial burden it places on the US government.

Democrats and independents are near universal in their negative views of the war, with 97 percent of Democrats and 82 percent of independents saying it hasn’t been worth it. And few in either group see Trump as doing enough to bring the fighting to an end. Republicans are more divided on both questions: 55 percent say the war has been worth its costs, and 53 percent that Trump is doing enough to end it. But the president’s partisans are far more likely than others to see the US as winning the war: 70 percent say so, compared with 31 percent of independents and 13 percent of Democrats.

The president’s war Cabinet earns negative approval ratings, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 40 percent approval, Vice President JD Vance at 36 percent and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth at 34 percent.

US President Donald Trump answers questions alongside US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine during a news conference in the White House on April 6. Alex Wong/Getty Images

Among Republicans, about 8 in 10 approve of Rubio (81 percent) and Vance (79 percent), while Hegseth stands at 72 percent approval. That edge reflects some dissatisfaction with Hegseth among non-MAGA members of the GOP coalition. Among Republicans and Republican-leaning independents who do not support MAGA, 70 percent approve of Rubio and 68 percent of Vance, while just 58 percent approve of Hegseth.

Steady views toward Russia, China, but shifts on Canada, Israel

Americans’ views on Russia and China remain largely the same as they were earlier this year: Broad majorities see each as unfriendly or an enemy, but the poll finds shifting views on several countries that have been a focus of Trump’s foreign policies.

The share who view Ukraine as an ally or friendly has dipped from 76 percent in January to 70 percent now. On the flip side, more now see Cuba as friendly than did so in January (26 percent, up from 21 percent).

On Canada, most continue to see the country as an ally or friendly, but the share who consider it an ally has dropped from 51 percent in March 2025 to 38 percent now, in the wake of Trump’s tariff war with our northern neighbor. That drop comes across party lines, but is sharpest among Republicans (down 9 points among Democrats, 10 among independents and 23 among Republicans).

And the share calling Israel an ally or friendly has dropped to 61 percent, while 15 percent call it an enemy, the highest share to say so in CNN polling dating to 2000 and roughly double the share who felt that way in March 2025. This shift comes largely among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents — 17 percent in that group describe Israel as an enemy, up from 8 percent in March 2025. This view is also concentrated among younger Americans: 23 percent of those younger than 45 see Israel as an enemy, up from 9 percent a year and a half ago.

CNN’s Ariel Edwards-Levy and Edward Wu contributed to this report.

World.title: Actor Ahmed al-Awady apologizes to Yasmin Abdel Aziz following controversial car analogy
World.content:
Egyptian actor Ahmed al-Awady has addressed the controversy sweeping social media following a recent media appearance in which he used cars as an analogy for different stages of his life—a remark that sparked backlash and negative reactions online.

Clarifying his comments during his appearance on the show Qessati (“My Story”), Awady wrote in a Facebook post: “I truly meant no disrespect to anyone on Qessati, and I hold full respect for all.”

He continued: “The circulating statements regarding cars and the way they were interpreted rest entirely on those spreading them. I did not mean what some understood at all; the comparison was referring to stages of life, not romantic relationships.”

Awady added: “I apologize if anyone misunderstood the core message of my words. I hold all the respect and appreciation for the Arab world’s leading star, and I have stated repeatedly throughout the interview that I cherish fond memories of everyone who has entered my life.”

“I apologize to her if some misinterpreted my words. An apology is necessary whenever my remarks are taken out of context. This post is to set the record straight, and I reiterate my apology once more.”

The actor concluded his statement by saying: “On that note, I owe a great deal to Yasmin Abdel Aziz throughout my career. I deeply value and respect her, and I wish her continued success and brilliance, as always.”

World.title: Egyptian expat remittances surge to $29.7 billion over 7 months
World.content:
The Central Bank announced on Monday that remittances from Egyptians working abroad increased by 28.1 percent during the first seven months of 2026, recording approximately $29.7 billion, compared to around 23.2 billion dollars during the same period last year.

The bank explained that remittances from Egyptians working abroad continued their upward trajectory during last July, registering a growth of 20 percent on an annual basis to reach about 4.5 billion dollars, compared to around 3.8 billion dollars during the same month of 2025.

Banking expert Sahar al-Damaty said that the continuous rise in remittances from Egyptians working abroad reflects a clear improvement in foreign currency inflows into the banking system.

She noted that remittances reaching approximately $29.7 billion during the first seven months of 2026, compared to $23.2 billion during the same period last year, represents an increase of about $6.5 billion over the comparison period.

Al-Damaty told Al-Masry Al-Youm that the remittances of about $4.5 billion during July 2026—a 20 percent year-on-year increase—confirms the continuation of an upward trend, especially given the improved confidence of Egyptians abroad in official channels and the banking system’s enhanced ability to provide foreign currency and meet client needs.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Will Mamdani arrest Netanyahu in New York?
World.content:
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani slammed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as a “war criminal” and the “architect of the horrific genocide of Palestinians” during an interview with the American network CNN.

This came ahead of his meeting with US President Donald Trump and just days before Netanyahu’s expected visit to New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly meetings.

Can Mamdani arrest Netanyahu? The facts

The Mayor of New York, known for his strong critical stance on Israel, explained that he discussed the importance of respecting the rule of law with the Mayor of The Hague, Jan van Zanen, referencing the arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague for Netanyahu.

Mamdani clarified: “I believe this is something that should be respected, because we want to see confidence in our politics and confidence in applying the principle of accountability.”

He added: “If the ICC believes that a specific person deserves to be arrested for violating those laws, then who are we to say that someone should be above the law? I think it is very clear that everyone must be held accountable.”

About a week ago, in a move seen as a shift in his stance, Mamdani said he did not intend to participate in the upcoming protests against Netanyahu.

He stated: “If someone feels a level of frustration or opposition, protesting is something we will always respect.”

New York City officials estimated that Mamdani’s decision not to participate in the protests stems from his desire to avoid deepening divisions with the city’s Jewish community, alongside security complications that the Mayor’s participation in protests might impose.

During his electoral campaign, Mamdani had pledged to direct the New York Police Department to arrest Netanyahu if he arrived in the city, based on the arrest warrant issued for him by the International Criminal Court.

In an interview with The New York Times about two months ago, Mamdani said he still wished to arrest Netanyahu upon his arrival in New York to attend the UN General Assembly meetings in September, noting that he was engaging in an “active dialogue” with the New York City Law Department regarding the matter.

Mamdani Admits lack of authority to arrest Netanyahu

However, he later backed down from this pledge, pointing out that he does not possess the legal authority to execute an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court.

In a video clip published two months ago, he said: “We investigated every possible avenue, and we do not have the authority to do so.”

At the beginning of his remarks at the time, Mamdani pointed out that Netanyahu was “responsible for the deaths of more than 73,000 people, as well as injuring and maiming tens of thousands of children, while survivors undergo limb amputations without anesthesia.”

Mamdani also accused Netanyahu of being “responsible for targeting neonatal hospitals and maternal care centers, denying newborn children even the mere chance of survival.”

In his statements following the meeting with the US President, Mamdani focused on Trump’s decision to bar the MS NOW, CNN, and Politico networks from entering the White House, saying he informed President Trump that he intends to allow all media outlets access to the Mayor’s official residence.

Trump responded by saying: “I don’t think fake news media should be granted the right to be in very special places like the White House, given all the lies they spread regarding the war in Iran.”

Trump added: “We are in an excellent position. In fact, I am here today to hold a few meetings on this matter.”

Trump is scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, before returning to Washington, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: President al-Sisi sends Independence Day congratulations to Armenia, Malta, Belize
World.content:
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi sent a cable of congratulations to Armenian President Vahagn Khachaturyan on the occasion of Armenia’s Independence Day.

Sisi also delegated Mohamed Adel Mokhtar, Secretary at the Presidency, to the Armenian Embassy in Cairo to extend his congratulations on the occasion.

The President likewise sent a cable of congratulations to Maltese President Myriam Spiteri Debono on the occasion of Malta’s Independence Day.

He also delegated Mohamed Assi, Secretary at the Presidency, to the Maltese Embassy in Cairo to convey his congratulations.

Sisi further sent a cable of congratulations to Belize Governor-General Froyla Tzalam on the occasion of Belize’s Independence Day.

World.title: Liberia: Criminal Court “B” Releases Jerry Wrato on Habeas Corpus
World.content:
Court action comes hours after Police IG Coleman rejected VP Koung’s plea for Wrato’s release and moved to prosecute him on four cybercrime charges

By: Willie N. Tokpah

Monrovia-Criminal Court “B” of the First Judicial Circuit has released Jerry Nyantee Wrato from police custody following a petition for a writ of habeas corpus filed by his legal counsel, Cllr. Garrison Doldeh Yealue Jr.

The release came Tuesday, September 22, after Judge Pape Suah issued a writ directing that Wrato be released from further police custody and turned over to the Sheriff of the court.

The development marks a significant turn in the case, coming only hours after Liberia’s Police Inspector General, Gregory O. W. Coleman, rejected Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung’s appeal for Wrato’s release and confirmed that police had concluded their investigation and were preparing to prosecute him on four alleged cybercrime offenses.

Court Orders Release

The writ issued by Criminal Court “B” commanded authorities to release Wrato from further custody and bring him before the court pursuant to his habeas corpus petition.

The court directed that the relevant parties appear before it at 12:30 p.m. Tuesday and warned that failure to comply with the order could result in contempt of court.

Following the court’s action, Wrato was released from police custody.

The petition named as respondents the Minister of Justice, Deputy and Assistant Ministers of Justice, the Montserrado County Attorney and his deputies, Police Inspector General Gregory O. W. Coleman, the Crime Service Department and other officers or persons having custody of Wrato, among others.

The petition relied on Article 21(f) of the 1986 Constitution of Liberia and provisions of the Civil Procedure Law governing habeas corpus proceedings.

The writ was signed and sealed by Amos W. Cummings, Clerk of Criminal Court “B,” on September 22, 2026.

Police Had Announced Four Charges

The court-ordered release came after the LNP announced its decision to proceed against Wrato on four alleged violations of Liberia’s Cybercrime Act of 2025.

In a September 21 communication to Vice President Koung, Inspector General Coleman said police had resolved to charge Wrato with Misuse of Devices, Cyberstalking, Distribution of Data Messages That Incite Damage to Property or Violence, and Distribution of Harmful Data Messages.

The police identified the alleged offenses under Sections 10.1, 15.1, 18.1 and 19.1 of the Cybercrime Act.

Coleman’s communication followed a telephone conversation with Vice President Koung and the Vice President’s subsequent public appeal for Wrato’s release.

According to the Police Inspector General, once suspected criminal conduct comes to the attention of law enforcement, the matter cannot be determined solely by the wishes of the individual allegedly affected.

Coleman said the LNP had a statutory responsibility to investigate the allegations objectively and act in accordance with the law.

He also emphasized that forwarding Wrato to court would not constitute a determination of guilt and that the suspect remained entitled to the presumption of innocence and other constitutional protections.

Wrato Case Linked to AI-Generated Content

Wrato’s arrest followed the circulation of artificial intelligence-generated images and videos appearing to depict Vice President Koung in a derogatory manner.

The content surfaced amid controversy surrounding reports about Koung’s security screening at Brussels Airport, which the Vice President has denied.

The police subsequently investigated the circulation of the manipulated material under Liberia’s recently enacted Cybercrime Act.

Koung later appealed publicly for Wrato’s release, indicating that he did not wish to pursue criminal action against him over the material.

Despite the Vice President’s position, Coleman maintained that the police had an independent statutory duty to investigate suspected criminal conduct.

Habeas Corpus Leads to Release

The habeas corpus proceedings subsequently brought Wrato’s detention before Criminal Court “B.”

The court’s writ specifically directed that he be “immediately released from further custody” and turned over to the Sheriff of the court.

The subsequent release means Wrato is no longer being held in police custody pursuant to the detention challenged in the habeas corpus petition.

The court’s action, however, does not by itself constitute a determination on the underlying allegations contained in the police investigation.

The police had maintained that Wrato was to face criminal charges, while his legal counsel challenged his continued detention through habeas corpus.

Wrato remains presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

World.title: Liberia: How a Dutch Fugitive Found His Way Through West Africa’s Porous Ports, Borders, Stashing Drugs
World.content:
Ghana and Liberia sit on the same stretch of West African coast, share the same colonial-era port infrastructure, and now, investigators say, share the same weakness: officials willing to sell access to it. In Ghana, prosecutors say a container flagged by port scanners for “clear structural irregularities” was cleared anyway, allegedly by Ghana Revenue Authority officers now facing charges alongside associates of fugitive Dutch trafficker Jos Leijdekkers. In Liberia, the police chief himself says officers ran marked cruisers as paid escorts for a cocaine landing, pocketing roughly $5,000 each. No one has yet tied the Liberian case to Leijdekkers directly — but the two countries’ parallel scandals expose the same regional vulnerability: ports and patrols for sale to the highest bidder.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

MONROVIA — Two countries, an ocean apart in almost everything except geography and a shared coastline of vulnerability, are now telling versions of the same story. In Ghana, prosecutors say a port scanner flagged a shipment’s “clear structural irregularities” — and someone cleared it anyway. In Liberia, the country’s own police chief says officers ran marked cruisers as paid escorts for a coastal cocaine landing, pocketing roughly $5,000 apiece from a $10,000 envelope. Different currencies, different officers, same failure: the men who were supposed to stand between West Africa’s ports and its traffickers instead opened the gate.

Nothing yet on the public record ties the Liberian case to Jos Leijdekkers, the fugitive Dutch trafficker reportedly sheltering in Sierra Leone. But the pattern emerging on both sides of the Ghana-Liberia corridor — officials allegedly paid to look away — is precisely the kind of institutional crack that lets a network like his keep moving even as the walls close in elsewhere in the region. Leijdekkers, it now appears, isn’t just passing through West Africa’s ports. He’s paying his way through them.

The Dunkirk Shipment

It started, as these things often do, with a routine scan that wasn’t routine at all. On September 10, French customs officers at the port of Dunkirk pulled apart four containers that had sailed out of Ghana’s Tema Port and found roughly 3.9 tonnes of cocaine packed inside — a haul worth an estimated €225 million, or $261 million. Leijdekkers’ lawyers, Jan-Hein Kuijpers and Guy Weski, told the Dutch outlet NU.nl that their client denies any involvement.

Ghana’s Narcotics Control Commission moved quickly, arraigning four Ghanaians it says “represented and facilitated” Leijdekkers’ activities: Desmond Koranteng Curiel — who has also gone by “Paul Kweku Yeboah” and “Biggs” — along with Musah Attah (“Kromo”), Kweku Otchere, and Jessica Hartog. Dutch reporting fills in the backstory on Curiel, describing him as one of Leijdekkers’ “most important accomplices” and noting the two once shared a Dutch prison, where Curiel was serving time for a string of violent jewelry-store robberies. All four were remanded at the High Court in Accra on September 16 and return to court October 13.

The Officers Who Cleared It

But four tonnes of cocaine don’t leave a working port on its own — and this is where the case turns from a trafficking story into something closer to a story about the port itself. Separately from the four accused of fronting for Leijdekkers, Ghanaian prosecutors have charged three Ghana Revenue Authority officers — Frank Adu-Boahen, Andrews Tetteh Amponsah, and Togbe Agbeti — plus freight-forwarding director Francis Narh Amanor, over how the shipment made it out of Tema at all. The scan had already raised the alarm, according to the charges; the secondary inspection those red flags were supposed to trigger simply never happened. Adu-Boahen, prosecutors say, went further still — handing his own system login, the credentials used to sign off on scan results, to his co-defendants — and he’s now named as a beneficial owner of the shipment itself. Amanor was arrested September 15, Adu-Boahen the next day; all appeared in court September 17 and are due back September 24.

No filing has drawn a straight line from these three officers to Leijdekkers personally. The charges concern the shipment, not the man alleged to be behind it. But laid side by side, Ghana’s two cases sketch the same failure from opposite ends: a network with a documented personal tie to Leijdekkers on one side, a screening system allegedly hollowed out from within on the other. A scan overridden. A login shared. A shipment waved through.

Accra has noticed. MP Ntim Fordjour has publicly called for a parliamentary probe into what he’s calling Ghana’s emergence as a “cocaine coast,” and the presidency has since ordered inter-agency investigations and restored NACOC’s mandatory role in screening port cargo — the kind of response that suggests officials themselves see Dunkirk as a systemic breach, not a bad afternoon at customs.

A Familiar Pattern, Still Unconfirmed, in Liberia

Liberia’s own reckoning is unfolding on a parallel track. Inspector General Gregory Coleman has told reporters that Liberian National Police officers actively helped move roughly four tons of cocaine — “We have identified key state actors who played a role in transporting, escorting the movement of this narcotic substance,” he said. Two names have surfaced: Wadell W. Kwarbo, chief of the Highway Patrol Section, and Anthony T. Blaye, chief of the Financial Crime Division, both accused of escorting a shipment from a coastal landing site in marked police cruisers for roughly $5,000 each.

It’s a near-mirror image of what’s now public in Ghana — officials allegedly easing a shipment’s path for cash. What’s missing, so far, is the Leijdekkers connection. Coleman’s account doesn’t name him or link the seizure to a Dutch buyer or supplier, and no other source has made that connection either. Until someone does, the Liberia case stands on its own: proof of the same vulnerability across the region, not proof of the same hand behind it.

The Ghana-Liberia thread runs deeper than the two escort allegations, though. Liberian officials tell FrontPageAfrica that one of the foreign nationals now in Liberian custody carries a Ghanaian passport — one Ghanaian authority have since called fake — and a residence permit issued under two different names: Mihovil Vrhovac, also known as Michael. It’s not an isolated detail. Liberian authorities say most of the Eastern Europeans moving through these networks — Serbian, Croatian, Ukrainian, Georgian — are based in Accra and carry Ghanaian passports, some of them, FrontPageAfrica has learned, using those documents to enter Liberia as far back as 2021.

Liberia’s own case has produced two arrests so far tied to July’s $318 million bust: Spanish Colombian national Johann David Garces Grajales and Serbian former kickboxer Srđan Seleš. Prosecutors have charged five European nationals in total in the wider investigation, including Croatian nationals Nikolai Ivancic (also spelled Nicolad Avancik) and Mihovil Vrovac (Mio Vuvak), and Ukrainian national Tara Zaderieko (Taras Zargo) — the latter three indicted and now pursued in absentia through Interpol. Investigators have since traced four of them — Mihovil, Tara, David, and Seleš — to multiple visits to Freetown, with what officials describe as strong indications of ties to Leijdekkers. Mihovil, notably, was arrested in Accra at Liberia’s request — and then reportedly vanished.

A Region Under Siege

Dunkirk didn’t happen in isolation. A regional drug threat assessment obtained by FrontPageAfrica on Sunday describes an intensifying run of seizures across nearly every country on the West and Central African coast between June and September — a stretch that raises an uncomfortable question: how many of those cases, like Ghana’s, involved not just traffickers but the officials meant to be stopping them?

In Ghana alone, the Dunkirk arrests landed a week after NACOC shut down the Amsterdam Pub in Accra’s Laboma neighborhood on September 9, arresting three suspects while the principal target got away. Days before that, a joint NACOC-National Security raid in Weija caught a couple, Jibreel Hardi, 51, and his wife, Abiba Fatawu, 42, with cannabis, Tramadol, a firearm, and 50 rounds of ammunition. In August, police in the Upper East Region seized 500 cartons of Tramadol from a network allegedly running through Mali, Togo, Burkina Faso, and Senegal via the town of Widana — and earlier that month, 866 parcels of cocaine worth an estimated $6.9 million turned up hidden in sacks of gari at Tema Harbor.

Sierra Leone, where Leijdekkers is believed to be hiding, has had its own exposure: a September 10 tramadol seizure in Freetown that turned violent and left one person dead, and weeks before that, 51 kilograms of cocaine found in suitcases aboard a Brussels Airlines flight out of Freetown — leading to the arrest of a 22-year-old Belgian woman who wasn’t even on the flight’s passenger list.

Nigeria’s drug enforcement agency had one of its busiest stretches anywhere in the region — synthetic cannabis, opioids and other drugs found hidden in cargo, speakers and bread across eight states in mid-September, more than 2 million opioid pills and over 2,000 kilograms of cannabis seized in a nine-state sweep on September 6, and 329,865 kilograms of drugs destroyed in Lagos. Cabo Verde’s two main airports were hit within 24 hours of each other, couriers arrested arriving from Dakar and Bissau — one had swallowed 73 capsules of cocaine — while Brazilian authorities separately intercepted more than 100 kilograms bound for the islands hidden in drills, shock absorbers, a dental chair, and chocolate powder tins.

Liberia, for its part, has posted two of the region’s largest seizures in the same window: 3,971 kilograms in Duazon, Margibi County, on July 21 — worth roughly $317.68 million — and 237.6 kilograms at Roberts International Airport on June 8, hidden in six cargo boxes bound for Europe and valued near $19.2 million. Whether either shipment is the same one referenced in Coleman’s police-escort account remains unclear.

The wave has touched Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire, The Gambia, Guinea, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, and Senegal as well — networks dismantled, drug dens destroyed, everything from tramadol to captagon seized across a sub-region where the trade has clearly stopped respecting borders.

Ghana as the Hub

Liberian authorities, watching two major busts of their own unfold in a matter of months, believe — based on FrontPageAfrica’s reporting — that Ghana has become the operational center of drug smuggling in West Africa. The pattern keeps repeating: a Ghanaian passport later called fake, a residence permit under two names, a community of Eastern European operatives based in Accra who’ve been slipping into Liberia on those same documents since at least 2021.

“Thank God our joint security forces have intercepted or made arrests in Liberia, and not shipped [drugs] out like Ghana, Sierra Leone, and others,” a senior member of Liberia’s joint security drug force told FrontPageAfrica on Monday.

Whether that holds — whether Liberia catches what Ghana’s port let through — may be the question the rest of this story is still being written to answer.

World.title: Liberia: Police Reject VP’s Plea, Charges Wrato on Four Cybercrime Counts
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Liberia National Police (LNP) has concluded its investigation into Jerry Nyantee Wrato and will forward him to court on four cybercrime charges, rebuffing a public appeal from Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung for the young man’s release.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

In a letter dated September 21 to Koung, Inspector General Gregory O. W. Coleman said Wrato will face charges of Misuse of Devices, Cyberstalking, Distribution of Data Messages That Incite Damage to Property or Violence, and Distribution of Harmful Data Messages — alleged violations of Sections 10.1, 15.1, 18.1 and 19.1 of the Cybercrime Act of 2025. The suspect is to be forwarded to a court of competent jurisdiction “tomorrow morning,” Coleman wrote.

The letter was a direct response to a phone call Koung placed to Coleman, and to the Vice President’s subsequent public statement asking for Wrato’s release. Coleman thanked Koung for his “tolerance and restraint” but made clear the police would proceed regardless: “Once conduct potentially constituting a criminal offense comes to the attention of law enforcement, the matter is no longer determined solely by the personal wishes of the individual affected.”

He said the LNP has a “statutory responsibility to investigate the allegations objectively,” and stressed that referring the case to court “does not constitute a determination of guilt” — Wrato retains the presumption of innocence and all constitutional protections pending trial.

Wrato’s arrest followed AI-generated images and videos, circulated on Facebook, that appeared to depict Koung in a derogatory manner — content tied to earlier controversy over reports of the Vice President’s security screening at Brussels Airport, which Koung has denied. Executive Protection Service Director Sam Gaye defended applying the Cybercrime Act to manipulated political content.

The law itself is barely a month old: the Senate passed it in November 2025, and President Boakai signed it on August 19, 2026 — a fact made awkward by Koung’s role as President of the Senate, the body that passed it, while he is also the case’s alleged victim.

Former Finance Minister Samuel D. Tweah Jr. has called the law “draconian” and argued Koung should never have had to request Wrato’s release in the first place. Legal commentators have also raised a narrower question: whether a complainant can end a prosecution simply by declining to pursue it, given that criminal cases are ordinarily controlled by the state.

World.title: Liberia: Jewel Starfish Foundation Beneficiaries Share Life-Changing Stories After 25 Years of Humanitarian Service
World.content:
Monrovia – The Jewel Starfish Foundation celebrated its silver jubilee in December 2025 and continues to provide educational and other opportunities to young Liberian women from across the country.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The Foundation is a leading Liberian non-governmental organization dedicated to empowering underprivileged girls through education, leadership mentoring, and social protection.

Beneficiaries are glad, happy, and feel loved as they recounted how the former Vice President, Madam Jewel Howard Taylor, transformed their lives from uncertainty to university.

They spoke out to defend what they believe is a “life-changing” intervention in their educational journey.

In exclusive video interviews conducted on September 20, 2026, several beneficiaries from across Liberia shared emotional testimonies of how the Foundation rescued their education when all hope was lost.

From Potato Seller to Biology Major, A Story of Nancy

Narrating her story, Nancy Fayiah from Bomi County, a proud beneficiary of the Foundation, recounted how she was selling potatoes just to pay her school fees before meeting “Mama Jewel.”

“I met her in Bomi County when she gave us forms to be part of the family. Education, feeding, transportation – these are some of the things I receive from Mama Jewel,” she explained.

Nancy, who was then a student at C.H. Dewey Central High School, said she has been on the scholarship for seven years. She is now a junior student at the faith-based African Methodist Episcopal University, majoring in Biology and minoring in Chemistry.

“Imagine a girl selling potatoes just to pay her fees to be among her colleagues. That privilege was given by me and since then she started paying my fees. I never stayed out of class, even up to university level,” Nancy indicated

Reacting to her link to the drugs saga, Nancy indicated: “She is a good woman. She has inspired a lot of people. She is my mentor. She is a God-fearing woman. I feel inspired, I feel motivated, I feel important in society.”

“She Is An Angel In My Life” – Pearline Narrates

Pearline Campbell from Sinoe County, in southeastern Liberia, described Madam Taylor as “an angel in my life.”

Pearline explained with the former Vice President through her grandmother when her educational journey was uncertain.

“I was at the point where my educational journey was uncertain, and continuing my education was something difficult. Meeting her and her offering me a scholarship changed my entire life,” she narrated.

Pearline revealed she first got on the Jewel Starfish scholarship when she was in the 8th grade and has been sponsored through her first three semesters in college, where she is now studying Criminal Justice at the university.

To Liberians and fellow beneficiaries, she had this message: “She has served as a mother and mentor for so many young women.”

“Resilient Woman Who Lifts Every Girl” – Cecelia From Cape Mount

For Cecelia Bendu Freeman from Grand Cape Mount County, now a Sociology major at the University of Liberia, the Foundation came at a time when her entire class at the More Than Me Academy in West Point thought their education had ended due to “confusion” surrounding the school.

“When they took over the program, she visited the school and we explained our situation to her. We invited her as guest speaker for our 9th grade graduation. When she came, she awarded every single graduate a scholarship to attend Wells-Hairston and CWA,” Cecelia explained.

“It is such an honor, such a privilege that no matter how far I go in life, I will always appreciate that.”

Apart from educational support, Cecelia said “Mama Jewel” mentors her personally.

On the current saga facing the former Vice President, Cecelia “prayed God to be the one to take control and speak,” adding: “I know the kind of sponsor I have.”

“In a direct message to her sponsor, she said: “You are that strong woman that lifts up every young woman that comes across you. I believe in you, I believe in your work, I believe in your impact. It is a test of time, be strong and trust that God is in control.”

She described the former Vice President as a “resilient” and a “very powerful woman” who continues to impact lives.

Several other beneficiaries maintained that the Jewel Starfish Foundation is more than a scholarship scheme, stating that it is a family and a breeding ground for female leadership that has touched lives in Liberia, Ghana, Malawi and Sierra Leone.

World.title: Liberia: Three Videos Put Saudi Rice Distribution Under Fresh Scrutiny as Defense Witness Continues Testimony
World.content:
MONROVIA — Three video recordings depicting the distribution of Saudi-donated rice were presented by the defense Monday as its first witness continued testifying in the closely watched trial involving former government officials and other defendants accused of the alleged mismanagement of the humanitarian donation.

By: Willie N. Tokpah

Archievo Doe, a former National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) communications official, presented the footage before Criminal Court “C” as part of the defense’s effort to challenge the prosecution’s account of how the rice was distributed.

Doe testified that one video was recorded in 2023, during the tenure of former NDMA Executive Director Henry O. Williams, while the other two were recorded in 2024, after Williams had left the position.

The defense is seeking to use the footage, alongside media reports, community witnesses and distribution records, to challenge aspects of the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce’s investigation.
