However, the recordings’ dates, locations and the identities of those involved remain important considerations in determining whether the distributions shown relate to the specific transactions at issue in the case.

The footage alone does not establish who authorized each distribution, the quantities involved or whether the transactions complied with established procedures.

The defendants, including former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah, have pleaded not guilty and remain presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Doe Cites Media Reports, Community Beneficiaries

Doe also referenced media coverage that he said documented the distribution of the Saudi-donated rice.

He specifically mentioned Joseph Daniel, a former mainstream journalist now associated with the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce, who Doe said had previously reported on the distribution.

He also cited State Radio as another source of coverage.

Doe further told the court that the mother of the late Angel Togbah could testify that she and others received portions of the rice.

The defense maintains that such accounts could help establish that the distribution exercise was conducted openly and involved identifiable beneficiaries.

150 Bags Delivered to Caldwell Family

Testifying about the Caldwell distribution, Doe said the project’s concept note provided for two bags of rice per disaster-affected family.

However, he told the court that the Togbah family received 150 bags.

Doe testified that he signed the waybill associated with the movement of the consignment from the General Services Agency warehouse.

According to him, the rice was loaded onto an NDMA truck operated under the supervision of the Armed Forces of Liberia, with an AFL driver transporting it to Caldwell.

Doe said Williams and a team that included him followed the truck in another vehicle.

His testimony sought to place the delivery within an NDMA disaster-response operation, although the legality and significance of the transaction remain for the court to determine.

50 Bags Delivered to Flood-Affected School

Doe also testified that on October 2, 2023, Williams instructed him to deliver 50 bags of rice to Faith Caring Daycare and Elementary School in Chicken Soup Factory because the executive director was occupied with other responsibilities.

He said the school had been affected by flooding that disrupted academic activities.

Doe testified that information collected in the community identified 157 affected persons or infrastructure-related cases, including 46 infrastructure cases.

He said the rice was delivered in the presence of Staff Sergeant Zubah Blama, members of the Togbah family and community residents.

According to Doe, the consignment was transported in an NDMA Toyota Land Cruiser double-cabin pickup bearing license plate RL4704.

Explaining his broader role in the project, Doe said his responsibilities extended beyond the two distributions under scrutiny.

“My role in the Saudi rice project was not only about leading the team to deliver the 50 bags of rice to the Faith Caring Daycare Elementary School, but the Division of Communication I headed covered all the activities of the Saudi rice project,” he testified.

He added that either he or a member of his communications team was present at distribution sites.

Doe Challenges ARREPT Investigation

Doe also challenged the manner in which investigators handled his case, testifying that the two waybills associated with the Caldwell and Chicken Soup Factory distributions were not presented to him during questioning.

He said ARREPT sent him questions concerning his alleged involvement, but he considered some insufficiently specific. He testified that he requested clarification and eventually responded to approximately 18 questions.

Doe said he heard nothing further from investigators until June 27, when he was served with an indictment.

He maintained that he first saw the two waybills after his indictment, when his lawyer-wife showed them to him.

“At no time were the two willbills from Caldwell and Chicken Soup Factory presented to me,” Doe told the court.

He said he would have explained his role and the instructions he received from Williams had the documents been presented during the investigation.

Disputes Prosecution Witness’s Community Account

Doe also disputed testimony from Isaac K. Weede, General Chairman of Lakpazee Community, who previously told the court that he knew of no Saudi rice distribution in the community.

Doe referenced the death of a handicapped resident identified as Tamba and his wife in a fire incident in Lakpazee, challenging Weede’s account of events in the community.

He also cited the deaths of five children in Five-Forty Community, saying they occurred around the period of the rice distribution.

The competing accounts raise questions about the extent of individual witnesses’ knowledge of distributions across communities during the broader relief operation.

Judge Fines Defense Lawyer US$200

Monday’s proceedings also featured a tense exchange between Trial Judge Ousman Feika and defense lawyer Cllr. Jimmy Saah Bombo.

Judge Feika fined Bombo US$200 after the lawyer attempted to object to a question posed by the judge. The court ordered the fine paid within 24 hours and warned that failure to comply could result in imprisonment.

Two additional attempts by the defense to object to questions from the judge were rejected, prompting further disagreement.

The prosecution rested its case after 31 days of jury sitting, and the defense has now begun presenting its evidence.

The indictment reportedly alleges that 25,054 of the 29,412 bags of donated rice were unlawfully handled, diverted or misapplied.

As the defense continues its presentation, the jury will have to weigh the competing testimony, documentary records and video evidence to determine whether the prosecution has established the charges against each defendant beyond a reasonable doubt.

World.title: Liberia: Broken Roofs, Empty Classrooms: Beletanla and Blemeyea Schools Struggle in Bong County
World.content:
The damage has had a direct effect on attendance in the classroom. Residents said that last year, students were sent home whenever it rained because the building could not shelter them

BONG COUNTY – In the villages of District Two, the school day does not always end with the bell. At one school, it can end with the rain. At another, it can end when the only available teacher has to leave for Gbarnga. These are the daily realities at Beletanla Public School and Blemeyea Public School, two institutions that residents and staff say are being asked to educate children with far too little.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Learning at the Mercy of the Weather

Ask residents of Beletanla about their school, and the conversation quickly turns to the roof. According to those who spoke to journalist Exodus Weah of Super Bongese, a local radio station in Gbarnga, during a visit to the campus, the damaged roof and the lack of chairs have left the school in a condition that is not conducive to teaching and learning.

The damage has had a direct effect on attendance in the classroom. Residents said that last year, students were sent home whenever it rained because the building could not shelter them.

In a country where the rainy season stretches across many months, that means learning at Beletanla can stop at a moment’s notice. Residents fear the pattern will repeat if nothing is done, and they worry that the missing chairs and the failing roof will keep disrupting academic activities.

The Parents Who Pay

The pressure on Beletanla does not end with the building. The school currently has two teachers assigned by the government and two volunteers. The volunteers are not on any official payroll. Instead, residents say, members of the Parent-Teacher Association (PTA) make small financial contributions to pay them.

Kpontah explained that he dismissed the students before 1:00 PM so that he could travel to Gbarnga. The second teacher, reportedly ill, was not actively teaching on campus. With no one else to take over, the school day came to an early close

The arrangement keeps the school running, but it rests on a fragile foundation. Half of the school’s teaching staff depends on the generosity of parents rather than on a government commitment, and every contribution is a reminder that the state has not fully met its responsibility to the school.

A School with One Teacher to Spare

A short distance away, Blemeyea Public School, also known as Barsee Kpangbai Public School, faces a different but equally serious challenge. Its acting Principal, James Kollie Kpontah, says the school is operating with only two teachers, and one of them is currently unwell.

With one colleague out of action, Kpontah has taken on the teaching of students from the ABC class through the fifth grade. It is a demanding load for one person, since the range spans the youngest beginners and pupils several years ahead of them. Every child receives a smaller share of a single teacher’s attention.

The strain was visible during a news-gathering visit by journalist Weah on Monday. Kpontah explained that he dismissed the students before 1:00 PM so that he could travel to Gbarnga. The second teacher, reportedly ill, was not actively teaching on campus. With no one else to take over, the school day came to an early close.

Kpontah also disclosed that Blemeyea lacks sufficient instructional materials, a shortage he says is affecting the learning environment. For a teacher already stretched across six levels, the absence of teaching resources makes an uphill task steeper.

The Same Story, Told Twice

The damage has had a direct effect on attendance in the classroom. Residents said that last year, students were sent home whenever it rained because the building could not shelter them

The details differ from one school to the other, but the outline is the same. Beletanla has a broken roof and no chairs, while Blemeyea has a shortage of books and materials. Both rely on very small teaching teams, and both depend on individuals, whether volunteers, parents, or an acting principal doing the work of several teachers, to keep classes going.

Children bear the cost. A pupil who is sent home because of rain, or who spends the day in a crowded multigrade class, loses more than a few hours. Over time, those lost hours add up, and rural pupils risk falling behind their peers in better-equipped schools.

A Phone That Rang Without Answer

FrontPage Africa sought comment from the Bong County Education Officer, David Boakai, on the conditions at both schools and on any plans to address them. Those efforts did not materialize. The Education Officer’s phone rang endlessly without response, and no comment was available at the time of publication.

The silence leaves important questions unanswered. Is the county education office aware of the conditions at Beletanla and Blemeyea? Will more government-assigned teachers be posted to the schools? Are repairs to the roof, the supply of chairs, and the delivery of instructional materials under consideration? Residents and school officials are waiting for answers, and this newspaper remains open to hearing from the county education office.

For the people of Beletanla and Blemeyea, the requests are straightforward. They want a repaired roof, chairs for the students, additional teachers, and materials to support learning. For PTA members who have quietly carried the cost of volunteer teachers, a lasting government solution would bring long-awaited relief.

Until that support arrives, the children of District Two will keep coming to class, and their teachers will keep doing what they can with what they have.

World.title: West Africa Cannot Afford to Fight Jos Leijdekkers One Border at a Time
World.content:
Jos Leijdekkers’ fingerprints are turning up in port after port, patrol after patrol, from Freetown to Tema to a beach in Liberia — not because one fugitive is unusually clever, but because West Africa keeps fighting him one border at a time. Ghana has charged its own customs officers. Liberia’s police chief has named his own officers. Each response has been national, quiet, and separate. None has yet matched the scale of a network that treats the whole coastline as a single market. This editorial argues that unless ECOWAS states build real, shared instruments — intelligence-sharing with teeth, vetted port personnel, extradition that actually works, a joint task force built around networks rather than individual shipments — the region will keep discovering Leijdekkers-style operations one country at a time, always a step behind. The stakes go beyond narcotics: a coastline that cannot secure its ports against traffickers will struggle to secure them against anything else.

ONE MAN’S SHADOW now falls across an entire coastline. From Freetown, where Jos Leijdekkers is reported to be sheltering, to Tema, where his associates allegedly bought their way past a customs scanner, to a Liberian beach where police officers allegedly stood watch over a cocaine landing for $5,000 apiece — the footprints of a single fugitive trafficker keep turning up wherever West Africa’s ports and patrols prove for sale. That is not a coincidence. It is a diagnosis.

WHAT THE DUNKIRK CASE EXPOSED in Ghana, and what Inspector General Gregory Coleman has alleged in Liberia, are not isolated failures of two governments. They are the same failure, wearing two flags. A network built around one man has been able to move tonnes of cocaine through this region not because West African security services lack the will to stop him, but because he has found, again and again, the one official in the one office willing to look away for a price. Every country that has now stumbled onto a piece of his operation — Ghana, Liberia, Sierra Leone — has treated it as a national embarrassment to be managed quietly, prosecuted separately, and closed. None has yet treated it as what it actually is: evidence of a single, regional criminal architecture that respects no border, because the men running it long ago stopped respecting ours.

THAT HAS TO CHANGE, and it has to change now.

A Threat That Does Not Recognize Borders

LEIJDEKKERS’ NETWORK did not need a visa to move between Sierra Leone, Ghana, and Liberia. It needed a bent scanner operator in one port and a police escort in another. Eastern European operatives tied to his associates have reportedly been slipping into Liberia on Ghanaian passports since at least 2021; one suspect now in Liberian custody was arrested in Accra at Liberia’s own request — and then simply vanished. That single episode is the whole regional problem in miniature: a request for cooperation was honored on paper and defeated in practice, because no mechanism exists to make an arrest in one West African capital actually stick by the time it matters in another.

MEANWHILE THE SEIZURE numbers, taken country by country, look like separate stories: Ghana’s cocaine hidden in gari sacks and container irregularities, Liberia’s $317 million bust in Duazon and its $19 million interception at Roberts International, Sierra Leone’s cocaine-stuffed suitcases out of Freetown, Nigeria’s opioids in bread and speakers, Cabo Verde’s swallowed capsules. Read individually, each is a national success story — an arrest made, a shipment stopped. Read together, across a single June-to-September stretch, they describe a trafficking corridor running the length of the West African coast, probing every port and every patrol for the weakest link. Traffickers already treat this region as one market. It is well past time our governments did too.

What Cooperation Actually Requires

GHANA’S PRESIDENCY has ordered inter-agency investigations and restored its narcotics agency’s mandatory role in screening port cargo. Liberia’s Inspector General has named officers he says took bribes to escort a shipment. These are necessary steps, and each government deserves credit for taking them. But a scanner fixed in Tema and an internal police probe in Monrovia will not stop a network that simply moves its business to the next weak port down the coast. What this moment calls for is not two governments cleaning house separately. It is ECOWAS states finally building the shared instruments they have spent years discussing and never finishing:

A REGIONAL INTELLIGENCE-SHARING arrangement with teeth — not another memorandum of understanding, but a standing mechanism through which a customs flag in Tema, a police tip in Monrovia, and an airport seizure in Praia are treated as one file, not three.

VETTING AND ROTATION of port and customs personnel with regional oversight, so that a scanner operator’s login cannot become, as prosecutors allege happened in Ghana, a key that a trafficking network simply buys.

EXTRADITION AND MUTUAL legal assistance agreements that actually function under pressure — so that an arrest made at a neighbor’s request, as Ghana made of a suspect wanted in Liberia, does not end in a suspect who “reportedly vanished” before he can be handed over.

A JOINT TASK FORCE tracking networks, not just shipments — built to follow people like Leijdekkers and his associates across the borders they cross freely, rather than waiting for each country to rediscover the same names independently.

NONE OF THIS IS EXOTIC. Regional bodies elsewhere have built exactly these tools. What West Africa has lacked is not the blueprint but the political will to treat trafficking as a shared emergency rather than each nation’s private scandal.

The Region’s Future Is What Is Actually at Stake

IT WOULD BE A MISTAKE to see this only as a drug story. Every scanner that gets overridden for cash, every police escort sold for $5,000, is a small transaction that adds up to something much larger: a generation of West African institutions being hollowed out from the inside, one bribed official at a time. Money on this scale does not stop at corrupting a customs post. It buys judges, financiers elections, and arms the same criminal networks it enriches. A region that cannot secure its own ports and highways against traffickers will find it just as hard to secure them against anything else.

JOS LEIJDEKKERS WILL eventually be caught, or he will not; that is, in the end, a matter for Dutch, Sierra Leonean and Interpol investigators. But whether West Africa produces the next Leijdekkers-scale network, and whether it takes years or weeks to unravel next time, is entirely within this region’s own hands. Liberia, Ghana, Sierra Leone and their neighbors have now each been handed unmistakable proof that their ports, their patrols and their own officials are being tested for weaknesses by organized crime on an industrial scale. The only responsible answer is to close that gap together, before the next shipment — and the next bribe — finds it first. The choice in front of West Africa’s governments is not complicated. Cooperate now, or explain later why they didn’t.

World.title: Liberia: Freeman Challenges Liberia’s US$1 Billion Revenue Story, Says US$400M Is Being “Squeezed” From Economy
World.content:
Liberia’s Economist and Politician Mr. Simeon Freeman

MONROVIA — Liberia’s historic crossing of the US$1 billion domestic revenue mark is being celebrated by the government as a major fiscal achievement.

By Edwin G. Genoway, Jr

Liberia’s economist and politician Simeon Freeman has raised fresh questions over Liberia’s revenue system, claiming that approximately US$400 million is being squeezed out of the local economy through charges that are not reflected in the government’s budgetary revenue figures.

Freeman said the amount includes payments associated with port operations, terminal charges, shipping companies, tracking fees and other costs incurred when goods enter Liberia.

While acknowledging that international trade taxes account for a significant portion of government revenue, he argued that the broader financial burden imposed on importers and consumers extends beyond what appears in the national budget.

“If you put all of that inflow together, you’re talking about US$400 million that is squeezed out of the local economy,” Freeman stated.

Freeman argues that these additional costs ultimately find their way into the prices Liberians pay for goods and services, particularly in an economy heavily dependent on imports. “By mopping money from the local economy, it makes the cost of goods very expensive,” he said, linking the alleged unbudgeted charges to rising consumer prices and declining purchasing power.

“How much money is circulating out of the pockets of Liberian consumers and businesses through charges that do not appear as direct government revenue in the national budget,” he intimated.

In a pointed economic commentary, Freeman challenged the growing celebration around government’s record revenue performance, arguing that the headline figure alone does not tell the full story of Liberia’s economic condition.

His argument is that government can increase revenue while ordinary Liberians simultaneously become poorer in real terms if the cost of raising that revenue is ultimately transferred to consumers through higher prices. “Every aspect of this budget is mopping money from the local economy,” Freeman said.

“By mopping money from the local economy, it makes the cost of goods very expensive.” The comments come days after President Joseph Nyuma Boakai announced that Liberia had raised more than US$1 billion in domestic revenue during the first nine months of 2026.

The President described the achievement as a historic milestone and said the money was mobilized through taxes, duties, fees and other lawful payments from individuals and businesses. He also said the government intends to ensure that the revenue translates into benefits that Liberians can see and feel.

But Freeman’s analysis challenges Liberians to look beyond the revenue headline.

‘The money is coming from somewhere’

Freeman’s argument rests on a basic economic principle: government revenue does not appear in isolation from the economy, he said

Taxes, duties, fees and other government charges are ultimately paid by individuals and businesses. Where businesses incur higher costs, those costs can be passed on to consumers through higher prices. That, Freeman argues, is the part of the US$1 billion story that deserves greater public scrutiny.

“The government gets the money by mopping and squeezing it from the economy,” he said “What that means is, when tuition goes up, it’s not the school that you blame.” For Freeman, the issue is therefore not whether government should collect revenue.

It is whether the country’s revenue system is increasing the productive capacity of the economy or simply extracting more money from an economy whose businesses and households are already under pressure.

Freeman focused particularly on Liberia’s import-dependent economy

He argued that the official tax figures do not necessarily capture the full range of costs associated with moving goods into Liberia.

According to his analysis, importers face customs-related taxes alongside port, terminal, shipping, tracking and other charges.

The economist contends that when those costs accumulate, they eventually become part of the price paid by consumers. “Something costs one dollar in China, very cheap. One dollar in China comes to Liberia and costs about 10, 15 dollars. Now you understand why.”

Freeman’s specific estimate that approximately US$400 million is being removed from the economy through additional charges is still subject to independent verification. But his broader economic argument is more fundamental: the price consumers pay at the end of the supply chain reflects not only the original cost of the product, but also the taxes, fees and other costs accumulated along the way.

The uncomfortable connection between revenue and prices

Freeman linked government revenue collection to the everyday economic struggles facing Liberians. He pointed to rising transportation costs, food prices, rent and education expenses as examples of the pressure households are experiencing.

“When government mop up the money, they spend it on themselves and not necessarily on us,” Freeman argued.

The IMF has reported that Liberia’s recent revenue performance has been supported by stronger income and international trade taxes, among other sources. It has also emphasized the importance of maintaining a prudent fiscal stance and improving the quality of public spending.

Freeman also turned his attention to Liberia’s debt

He argued that a significant portion of the government’s fiscal resources is already committed to servicing debt.

The FY2026 budget and subsequent fiscal planning have indeed placed substantial emphasis on debt management, while the IMF has continued to monitor Liberia’s debt position as part of its economic program.

Freeman’s concern is that Liberia could find itself in a cycle where government collects more revenue, borrows more money to finance development, and then uses an increasing amount of future revenue to service those obligations.

“You have to keep borrowing repeatedly for every major project,” Freeman said. His broader warning is that revenue growth without corresponding growth in production, investment and household incomes may not fundamentally transform the economy.

President Boakai has argued that the billion-dollar milestone must ultimately translate into tangible improvements in the lives of Liberians.

World.title: Kawambwa bar owners warned against under age patrons
World.content:
Kawambwa Town Council has issued a final warning to bar and nightclub owners against admitting persons under the age of 18 into their premises.

Council Secretary, George Biemba emphasised that allowing underage patrons into bars and nightclubs is prohibited under the Liquor Licensing Act No. 20 of 2011.

Mr Biemba noted that despite an earlier warning issued in February this year, some establishments in the district have continued to entertain minors.

“We are reminding all licensed premises that the law forbids admitting persons below 18 years, selling or supplying them with liquor, or permitting them to consume alcohol on the premises. This is a final warning and all should comply,” MrBiemba said.

Mr Biemba said bar and nightclub owners found violating the law risk facing fines, prosecution, and closure of their businesses.

He urged all operators to strictly comply with the law, stressing that the stated penalties will be enforced without further delay by the local authority.

The Council has since called on liquor-licensed premises to cooperate with the local authority and ensure that underage persons are not allowed to access or consume alcohol.

The warning by the local authority comes in the wake of a surge in the number of underage persons patronizing bars and nightclubs in the district.

World.title: ZRA calls integrity in tax administration
World.content:
The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) has called for collective responsibility from stakeholders in Nakonde District in Muchinga Province in ensuring integrity in tax administration within the trading ecosystem.

Nakonde ZRA Station Manager, David Mungela, said integrity is tested when financial interests and pressure come into play.

Mr Mungela was speaking during an ethics engagement meeting with the business community held at Izukanji Lodge in Nakonde district.

The meeting was held in collaboration with the Anti-Corruption Commission.

Mr Mungela stated that ZRA has adopted an outward looking approach to its integrity agenda by engaging beyond its officers to include taxpayers and other players.

“Corruption, smuggling and fraud do not only affect ZRA, they increase the cost of doing business and undermine resources meant for national development,” he said.

Meanwhile, Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) Corruption Prevention Officer, Chindika Mtonga, said corruption disproportionately affects the vulnerable in society.

Mr Mtonga noted that while institutions such as ZRA, the Drug Enforcement Commission and Zambia Police support the Commission in fighting the vice, citizen participation remains critical.

“Citizens must join the fight against corruption because without your involvement our efforts will be in vain,” he said.

And speaking during the same meeting, Nakonde Chamber of Commerce and Industry President, Thomas Botha called for enhanced collaboration between ZRA and the ACC to curb corrupt practices.

Mr Botha further commended ZRA for simplifying the process of acquiring a Taxpayer Identification Number (TPIN).

“We need to collaborate more to reduce corrupt practices and we commend ZRA for automating the issuance of TPINs,” Mr Botha said.

World.title: Hichilema underscores the importance of diplomatic ties
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says diplomacy is a critical tool in achieving the Grow Zambia Agenda, as it nurtures mutually beneficial relations for countries.

President Hichilema has underscored Zambia’s focus on growth in his second term, noting that diplomatic relationships are critical for mutually beneficial economic development.

The Head of State said this in a speech read for him by Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mulambo Haimbe at the United Nations General Assembly, in New York.

“Diplomatic relations mean new markets for our farmers, new partners for our investment drive and new friends for Zambia in the institutions that shape the global economy,’’ he stressed.

This is contained a statement issued to the media in Lusaka by First Secretary for Press at the Permanent Mission of Zambia to the UN, Namatama Njekwa, Zambia signed Joint Communiqués with Uruguay and Vanuatu.

Ms Njekwa revealed that the agreements open avenues for cooperation in agriculture, livestock, climate change adaptation, eco-tourism, trade, and investment.

She stated that Zambia also held talks with Malawi, agreeing to enhance collaboration in trade, energy, infrastructure, and connectivity, including Malawi’s interest in the Lobito Development Corridor.

Ms Njekwa further indicated that Zambia also held talks with Cuba where the two countries reaffirmed their longstanding friendship and solidarity, pledging continued cooperation in health, education, and multilateral coordination.

She added that Zambia also exchanged support with Cuba for respective candidatures to the UN Human Rights Council and other committees.

Ms Njekwa revealed that the Zambian delegates further engaged UN officials, focusing on rule of law, human rights, misinformation, and the country’s cooperation with the UN development system.

She however stated that Minister of Health, Roma Chilengi participated in the launch of the Accra Reset High-Level Panel report on reforming global health governance, which aligns with Zambia’s principle of strengthening national priorities through international cooperation.

Ms Njekwa further disclosed that Zambia will co-host the follow-up meeting on the Sevilla Commitment on Wednesday, with additional bilateral engagements on investment, energy, and infrastructure scheduled throughout the week.

The Assembly is convened under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.”

World.title: Masebo cautions the public against fake social media messages
World.content:
United Party for National Development (UPND) Senior Management Committee Member and Former Minister of Lands , Sylvia Masebo has urged Zambians to ignore social media messages allegedly aimed at promoting hatred and division by individuals who want to destroy the good name of the country.

Ms Masebo has cautioned the public that social media is heavily laden with falsehoods, disinformation, and manipulated content targeting the UPND members especially former cabinet Ministers.

She has noted that all online content or insinuations tagging her name are all fake, adding that she has never given an interview to any media platform, individual journalist or blogger since the August 13 , 2026 general elections.

Ms Masebo who is an entrepreneur and politician who has served in various portfolios said this during a media engagement in Lusaka today.

“All they want is to create division between the President and his former Ministers like myself and others which will never work.

Masebo has pledged deep loyalty to President Hichilema, stating that she will remain committed to the UPND regardless of electoral losses or results of her petition in court.

“President Hakainde Hichilema’s administration has stabilised Zambia’s macroeconomic environment and all the constitutional laws that have been made by this government. I was part of them so I am still in the government, I am in the senior management committee of the party;” she said.

“Zambia must remain under the leadership of President Hichilema as the country is on a stable path of economic recovery and democratic governance, the country is in safe hands under President Hichilema,” she said.

She further denied social media reports claiming that she called the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) a corrupt institution, saying that she fully respects the constitutional mandate of the commission as an independent body managing national elections.

Ms Masebo stressed that taking a petition to court is her constitutional right and not undermining the ECZ.

“I took the matter to court because I was aggrieved by how I was maligned by my competitor, how I was defamed by one competitor which is my constitutional right and I have no issues with the ECZ,” she stated.

She further revealed that attempts to divide UPND party members by enemies of the government should be ignored.

Ms Masebo stressed that following the August 2026 general elections, quite a number of parliamentary election petitions have been lodged at the high court by various losing candidates, saying that she is not the only one who has petitioned her opponent.

World.title: Govt. launches of Transformative Sustainable Food Systems programme
World.content:
Government has called for stronger coordination among sectors and institutions in addressing Zambia’s food security and nutrition challenges.

Permanent Secretary for Administration in the Office of the Vice President, Lillian Kapusana, says the challenges affecting food systems are interconnected and require a coordinated, systems-based approach rather than isolated interventions by individual institutions.

Ms Kapusana was speaking today at the official launch of the US$500,000 two year Technical Cooperation Programme, on Catalysing Transformative and Sustainable Food Systems in Zambia, supported by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations.

She said the programme provides an opportunity to bring institutions together around a common food systems agenda and shared results, saying the initiative would also support the review of nutrition coordination guidelines and Zambia’s food systems pathways developed in 2021.

Ms Kapusana said the two year programme will support government and FAO in catalysing practical and institutional changes aimed at improving nutrition outcomes and strengthening the resilience of Zambia’s food systems.

She further said the project will focus on strengthening food systems coordination and governance, as well as promoting sustainable production, markets and consumption, surveillance and compliance mechanisms.

Ms Kapusana said the project will be implemented in Solwezi and Zambezi districts of North-Western Province, targeting vulnerable farming households and building the capacity of agriculture and nutrition extension workers.

She said combining targeted local implementation with national systems strengthening would allow lessons from the pilot activities to inform policy, guide future investments and support scaling up of successful interventions.

Ms Kapusana observed that Zambia has made progress in agricultural production and nutrition, with stunting levels declining from 35 percent in 2019 to 32 percent in 2024, but the progress remains insufficient to achieve Sustainable Development Goal number Two, of ending hunger by 2030.

She however, said Zambia continues to experience production and consumption patterns heavily centred on maize, while diversification into nutrient-dense crops, livestock, fisheries and other nutritious foods remains low.

“The situation contributes to low dietary diversity, while smallholder farmers continue to face climate variability, post-harvest losses, market access constraints and limited integration of crop and livestock systems,” added Ms Kapusana.

Ms Kapusana has since assured stakeholders that the Office of the Vice President would support government ownership, inter-sectoral coordination and strategic partnerships throughout the project cycle.

Meanwhile, FAO Representative in Zambia, Suze Filippini, said the project will support the government in strengthening coordination across sectors while promoting nutrition-sensitive and climate-smart agriculture, improving food safety systems and market linkages, operationalising the animal identification and traceability system.

Ms Filippini explained that the project is intended to catalyse lasting transformation by strengthening national institutions, partnerships, approaches and investments beyond the lifespan of the programme.

She said food systems affect production, household food choices, nutrition and health, environmental sustainability, employment, markets and the resilience of communities to climate and economic shocks.

Ms Filippini pointed out that Zambia continues to face interconnected challenges, including limited production diversity, market barriers, post-harvest losses, climate vulnerability, food safety risks and persistent malnutrition which need coordinated action.

She further said improved food safety and traceability systems will help protect consumers, strengthen livestock disease surveillance and create opportunities for producers to access domestic, regional and international markets.

Ms Filippini said the success of the project will ultimately be measured by improvements in the livelihoods of Zambians, stating that the project will support efforts to make rural communities more resilient to climate-related and economic shocks.

World.title: SEC in Muchinga to sensitise public on financial literacy
World.content:
Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary Brian Sichande says financial literacy remains key to Government’s agenda of creating a financially informed population.

Mr Sichande said Government was committed to implementing progressive policies, with financial literacy being an important area of focus.

He said this when a team from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Financial Inclusion and Education Unit visited him at his office.

Mr Sichande emphasised the need to promote financial literacy among young people, stressing that youths were the future of the country and needed to understand the value of money and how to use resources appropriately.

He said a lack of financial literacy could lead to the misuse of resources.

“If you did not have this lesson from the onset on how best to spend money, you risk taking the money somewhere it is not supposed to go. If a resource was meant to build schools, let it build schools. If it was meant to build markets or buy medicine, let it do that,” he said.

Meanwhile, SEC Manager for Financial Inclusion and Education Sitali Mugala said the Commission was targeting young people under the National Strategy on Financial Education initiative.

Ms Mugala said the initiative was aimed at promoting a culture of saving and investment from an early age.

She said SEC was conducting a National Capital Markets Debate across the country to encourage youth participation in capital markets.

“We are going around the country conducting financial literacy sensitisation. The debate is a build-up to the national debate that will be held in Chipata next month. As we move from province to province, tertiary institutions that have expressed interest will compete amongst themselves,” she said.

Ms Mugala said the Commission was targeting students from six institutions in Muchinga Province, including Kapasa Makasa University in Chinsali and Zambia College of Agriculture in Mpika.

World.title: Lusaka DEBS hails 2026 Grade 6 Literacy Quiz Competition
World.content:
The Ministry of Education has called for greater investment in literacy programmes that equip learners with knowledge and skills beyond the classroom.

Lusaka District Education Board Secretary, Christopher Nyungila, says the 2026 Grade Six (6) Literacy Quiz Competition is helping learners gain knowledge in museum education, financial literacy, general literacy and road safety.

Mr Nyungila said this in a speech read on his behalf by Ministry of Education Standards Officer, Anderson Katete during the competition hosted by the Lusaka National Museum in partnership with the Bank of Zambia(BoZ) .

He said museum education is important in helping learners understand the country’s heritage, culture and scientific knowledge.

Mr Nyungila also encouraged learners to develop financial literacy from an early age by learning how to use resources prudently.

He further called for strengthened road safety education, saying learners remain vulnerable to road traffic accidents caused by reckless driving and vandalism of road safety infrastructure.

Mr Nyungila said Government’s investment in education should be complemented by initiatives that develop practical knowledge and skills among learners.

And BoZ Assistant Director for Communications, Besnert Mwanza who was represented by BoZ Strategic Communications Manager, Daniel Tonga said more than 2,000 pupils have benefited from the Lusaka National Museum Schools Literacy Programme since its inception in 2019.

Ms Mwanza said the programme has helped strengthen literacy and critical thinking skills while promoting financial literacy, road safety awareness and museum education.

“I encourage you to cultivate good financial habits from an early age and make responsible financial decisions,” she advised.

She commended the Lusaka National Museum, Ministry of Education, Road Transport and Safety Agency (RTSA) and other partners for their contribution to the education and development of children.

Meanwhile, Lusaka National Museum Director, Perrice Nkombwe has called for stronger collaboration between museums and schools to give learners practical opportunities to understand Zambia’s history, culture and heritage.

Ms Nkombwe said regular interaction with museums can complement classroom teaching and help learners develop cultural awareness alongside academic knowledge.

“Museums are centres of learning that reflect our national identity,” she said.

She also encouraged learners to develop good reading habits and observe road safety practices, saying the skills will contribute to building informed and responsible citizens.

World.title: Serenje DC urges workers to embrace a clean environment
World.content:
Serenje District Commissioner, Ellen Mibenge, has urged workers in the area to embrace the “Keep Serenje Clean, Green and Healthy Campaign” as part of efforts to keep the town clean.

Ms Mibenge says every worker should participate in the campaign as part of the Government’s efforts to promote cleanliness and environmental sustainability across the country.

Speaking during a meeting with Government workers, Ms Mibenge said a clean environment is a catalyst for human and socio-economic development, as healthy citizens are more productive.

“The Keep Serenje Clean, Green and Healthy Campaign aims to involve every citizen of Serenje, not just the Council. Let us all participate in cleaning our surroundings to help prevent outbreaks of diseases in the district,” she said.

Ms Mibenge observed that some workers were using the campaign as an excuse for reporting late for work on Fridays.

The DC further expressed disappointment with some companies, traders and local residents who have continued to shun the exercise, which is aimed at promoting the development of the district.

She said authorities will seriously consider sanctioning business owners and workers who refuse to participate in the campaign.

The Keep Serenje Clean, Green and Healthy Campaign is conducted every Friday from 08:00 hours to 10:00 hours to promote environmental sustainability, public health and community development.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 22, 2026
World.content:
Monrovia — South Africa Pushes for Permanent African Seat on UN Security Council

South Africa is leveraging ongoing intergovernmental negotiations on UN reform to advance the African Union's demand for permanent representation. Speaking at the 81st UN General Assembly, South Africa's Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Mxolisi Sizo Nkosi, highlighted Security Council reform as a core priority for Pretoria as it rallies support across member states.

The Security Council currently comprises 15 members: five permanent and ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. South Africa maintains that the body must expand to reflect contemporary global realities, specifically addressing Africa's historic absence from the permanent category.

UN Voices Deep Concern Over Escalating Security Crisis in Ethiopia



The UN has expressed strong concern over a deteriorating security situation in Ethiopia, pointing to the formation of a new coalition of armed groups, widespread instability, and repeated drone strikes.

Speaking at a press briefing on September 21, UN Secretary-General Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the UN was "deeply concerned" by the ongoing escalation. The warning comes amid heightened tensions across the country, including fresh clashes between federal forces and regional troops in northern Tigray.

South West Somalia Steps Up Flood Preparations Ahead of El Niño Rains

South West State President Sheikh Adan Mohamed Nur Madobe convened a high-level ministerial committee and the Somalia Disaster Management Agency (SoDMA) to review emergency preparations ahead of expected El Niño rains.

Officials outlined risk mitigation plans aimed at preventing flood damage, safeguarding communities, and enhancing disaster response capabilities across the state. President Madobe urged government agencies and humanitarian partners to streamline coordination and ensure emergency equipment is pre-positioned in high-risk zones.

South African Women Need Protection, Not Warnings, Says Human Rights Watch

The discovery of several women's bodies on the outskirts of South Africa's commercial capital, Johannesburg, has caused fear, anxiety and outrage across the country. All the women were found naked or partially clothed, according to police. Some of the bodies had bruising. At least three suspects are already in custody as authorities continue to examine possible links between the killings

Writing for Human Rights Watch, researcher Stacey-Leigh Manuel emphasized that these horrific killings are not isolated incidents, but rather symptom of South Africa's ongoing national emergency regarding gender-based violence.

World.title: Niger: Junta Strips 5 More Exiled Critics of Nationality
World.content:
press release

Nairobi — Latest Crackdown Heightens Rights Concerns Amid Renewed Political Tensions

Niger's junta has provisionally stripped five more exiled opposition figures of their nationality, extending a controversial policy increasingly used against critics of the military authorities, Human Rights Watch said today.

On September 17, 2026, Gen. Abdourahamane Tiani, who has led Niger's junta since the July 2023 coup, signed a decree removing the nationality of five prominent Nigeriens living in exile. The decree derives authority from a 2024 order creating a national terrorism database with overbroad inclusion criteria and inadequate due process requirements and safeguards for redress. The order jeopardizes privacy and data protection rights and increases the risk of statelessness.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"The Niger junta's use of a terrorism database to deprive people of their nationality without any meaningful legal safeguards raises serious human rights concerns," said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. "Nationality is a fundamental legal status, not a privilege that governments can take from people for political reasons."

The five affected are former Prime Minister Ouhoumoudou Mahamadou; Amadou dit Ange Barou Chekaraou, Oumarou Moussa Ibrahim, and Ousmane Abdoul Moumouni, all former advisers to President Mohamed Bazoum, who was ousted in 2023 and remains arbitrarily detained; and Boubacar Seyni Souley, a social media activist critical of the junta.

The September 17 decree accuses the men of various offenses, including disseminating information capable of disturbing public order, providing intelligence to foreign powers, electronic defamation, demoralizing the armed forces, and threatening state security.

The decree raises questions about compliance with Niger's existing legal framework. The 1984 Nationality Code does not provide for "provisional loss" of nationality. Where deprivation of nationality is permitted, the law requires the authorities to notify the person concerned and give them one month to submit a written defense before the measure is published in the official journal.

"Nothing of the sort is happening here," the Alliance of Sahel Democrats, a coalition of Nigerien, Malian, and Burkinabè diaspora political opposition groups advocating a return to constitutional rule, said in a statement on September 18. The alliance also noted that the September 17 decree is depriving individuals of their nationality while they are still being prosecuted, in contravention of the 2024 order, which states that deprivation of nationality can only be imposed after a conviction.

According to Niger's press agency, the junta's latest action brings the number of people provisionally deprived of Nigerien nationality under the 2024 order to 25. In October 2024, the junta provisionally stripped nine people linked to former President Bazoum of their nationality. In June, authorities revoked the citizenship of Mariama Djibrine, an opposition figure living in exile.

In a September 19 statement, the G25-Niger, an opposition coalition of civil society groups and media organizations formed in 2025, said the 2024 order "is being used as a tool of political repression ... to crack down on opponents and other dissenting voices."

Since taking power in 2023, Niger's military junta has entrenched authoritarian rule and consolidated sweeping and unchecked powers, systematically weakening institutions capable of holding the military authorities to account.

In the past year alone, the military authorities have dissolved all political parties and several independent unions, suspended dozens of civil society groups, detained journalists under a broad cybercrime law, criminalized consensual same-sex relations, announced Niger's withdrawal from the International Criminal Court, and prolonged the country's political transition without any roadmap toward democratic elections. In addition to Bazoum, the junta continues to arbitrarily detain Moussa Tchangari, a prominent human rights defender.

The authorities have also taken steps to curb criticism from abroad. In June, Niger's foreign affairs minister instructed diplomatic missions to monitor online criticism of the military authorities, signaling growing scrutiny of the diaspora's discussions of the country's political and human rights situation.

The political climate in Niger has become increasingly tense in recent weeks, Human Rights Watch said. On August 28, mutinous soldiers attacked a military base at the international airport in Niamey, Niger's capital, and the presidential palace, with hours of gunfire. The mutineers also briefly seized the headquarters of the state-run national television, disrupting broadcasts. General Tiani called in Russia's government-controlled Africa Corps, whose intervention, including the use of armed drones, helped loyalist forces suppress the mutiny.

Close 

Niger is a party to the United Nations Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, which restricts states from depriving people of their nationality when doing so would leave them stateless. Colleagues of the five affected by the September 17 decree said that at least four of them only possess a Nigerien passport.

Those who are without a nationality as well as their families risk being deprived of legal and social protection abroad. It could prevent them from returning to Niger, which is their right under international human rights law.

"The Niger junta has been depriving perceived political opponents of their nationality without meaningful due process, and contrary to Niger's obligations to prevent statelessness and protect fundamental rights," Allegrozzi said. "The junta should immediately revoke the decree and suspend the use of the easily abused terrorism database."

World.title: Djibouti: Djibouti Frees Top SA Investigative Journalist Micah Reddy
World.content:
South African investigative journalist Micah Reddy of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists was detained on Saturday, but is now on his way back to South Africa.

Micah Reddy, the South African investigative journalist who was detained by government authorities in Djibouti on Saturday, 19 September, was released on Tuesday and is on his way home to South Africa, unharmed.

His family announced this on Tuesday following two days of anxiety after he and his local fixer Kooki Mahmoud disappeared from their hotel in Djibouti at about 1pm on Saturday. Reddy's family said in a statement that Mahmoud had also been released without charge.

"It is with immense relief and delight that we share the news that he is on his way back to South Africa, unharmed," the family said.

Reddy, a journalist and Africa Coordinator at the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), had been held in the custody of Djiboutian authorities "from 1pm on Saturday, 19 September 2026", the announcement added.

"Despite numerous efforts to establish his whereabouts and condition, no official information was provided until today," the family said.
