World.title: 12 Michelin Key hotels in Hungary – what makes each one stand out?
World.content:
Hungary has secured 12 places in the 2026 Michelin Key hotel selection, with ten properties in Budapest and two beyond the capital. Two Budapest hotels received Two Michelin Keys, while another ten properties earned One Key, giving travellers an unusually varied collection ranging from grand Art Nouveau palaces to a tiny adults-only hotel by Lake Balaton.

All 12 Hungarian properties in this year’s selection were also recognised in 2025. The only hotel to disappear from last year’s 13-property Hungarian list is BOTANIQ Castle of Tura, whose business model has since changed.

What does a Michelin Key actually mean?

The Michelin Key is essentially the hotel counterpart of the restaurant world’s Michelin Star. Inspectors visit anonymously and consider five broad criteria: architecture and interior design, the quality and consistency of service, personality and character, value for money, and how significantly the property contributes to the experience of its destination.

One Key signifies what Michelin describes as a very special stay, Two Keys an exceptional stay, and Three Keys an extraordinary one. No Hungarian hotel currently holds the maximum Three-Key rating, but two have reached the second level.

Michelin Key hotels in Hungary with Two Keys

Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace Budapest – Two Michelin Keys

Few hotels are as closely tied to Budapest’s cityscape: the Four Seasons occupies the spectacular Gresham Palace, completed in 1906, directly opposite the Chain Bridge and looking towards Buda Castle. Its restored Art Nouveau architecture is combined with traditionally elegant rooms, while the top-floor spa includes an infinity pool overlooking the city. The combination of internationally recognisable architecture, one of Budapest’s most prestigious locations and a building that is itself a landmark makes the Gresham Palace much more than simply a luxury hotel.

Source: Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace Budapest

Matild Palace, a Luxury Collection Hotel – Two Michelin Keys

Matild Palace occupies one of the twin Belle Époque palaces commissioned by Archduchess Marie Clotilde near Elizabeth Bridge and has been transformed into a 130-room hotel without erasing the building’s historic identity. Guests find contemporary luxury inside, alongside Danube views, the Swan Spa, Spago by Wolfgang Puck and the rooftop bar The Duchess. It stands out for combining a genuine piece of Budapest architectural history with a distinctly modern hospitality concept rather than treating its historic shell merely as decoration.

Photo: Matild Palace

If you missed it: FirstMed and Daily News Hungary bring diplomats together for exclusive Budapest reception – photos, video

Eight One-Key hotels in Budapest

Anantara New York Palace Budapest – One Michelin Key

The defining feature of the Anantara is the legendary New York Café, which opened in 1894 and remains one of Budapest’s most elaborate historic interiors, with frescoes, chandeliers, gilding and monumental columns. The hotel continues that grand style in its rooms and suites and adds a 500-square-metre spa in the middle of the busy Grand Boulevard district. Few hotels allow guests to sleep in the same building as one of Budapest’s most famous cafés, making the property particularly strong for travellers interested in the city’s literary and architectural past.

Dorothea Hotel, Budapest, Autograph Collection – One Michelin Key

Opened in 2023, the Dorothea combines three buildings from different periods into a single 216-room hotel designed by Italian architect Piero Lissoni. Contemporary interiors contain references to Hungarian craftsmanship, while its large colonnaded atrium, garden restaurant and rooftop dining create very different spaces within the same property. What distinguishes the Dorothea is the way it uses several layers of Budapest architecture rather than relying on a single historic building or a purely contemporary design concept.

Hotel Clark Budapest – One Michelin Key

Hotel Clark sits in an almost impossible-to-beat location between the Chain Bridge and the Buda Castle funicular, with many rooms opening directly towards the Danube. Its interiors are contemporary and playful, while the Leo Rooftop has become known for its panoramic views over central Budapest. The hotel’s strongest characteristic is therefore its relationship with the city outside: some of Budapest’s most recognisable landmarks are effectively part of the view from the building.

Visual plan: Clark Ádám Square renovation. Source: budapest.hu

If you missed it: Inside Hotel Clark Budapest: Luxury, design and Danube views at the foot of the Chain Bridge

Kimpton BEM Budapest – One Michelin Key

One of the newest names on Budapest’s luxury-hotel scene, Kimpton BEM opened in 2024 inside a restored 19th-century palace on the Buda side of the Danube. Designer Marcel Wanders mixed the historic architecture with unusually bold contemporary interiors, incorporating references to Hungarian nature, Lake Balaton, mythology and animals, alongside the Agos restaurant and rooftop feNNen Skybar. Among the Michelin Key hotels in Hungary, it is particularly distinctive for rejecting restrained hotel minimalism in favour of theatrical colours, motifs and visual storytelling.

Kozmo Hotel Suites & Spa – One Michelin Key

The Kozmo occupies a protected building erected in 1910 that once housed what the hotel describes as the largest telecommunications centre in Central and Eastern Europe. Its monumental staircase, tower, high ceilings and historic architectural details have been retained, while contemporary art and large rooms and suites give the former institutional building an entirely different purpose. Its appeal lies in this unusual conversion: instead of a former palace or aristocratic residence, guests are staying inside a grand piece of Budapest’s early telecommunications history.

Párisi Udvar Hotel Budapest – One Michelin Key

Párisi Udvar is arguably the most visually extravagant property on the list, occupying a former shopping arcade whose architecture brings together Art Nouveau, Gothic, Moorish and Arabic influences. Its spectacular passage features details including Zsolnay ceramics, stained glass associated with Miksa Róth and a huge glass dome, while the guestrooms themselves adopt a more restrained contemporary style. What makes it exceptional as a hotel setting is that the lobby is not simply inspired by historic Budapest architecture: it is one of the city centre’s remarkable surviving architectural spaces.

Verno House – One Michelin Key

Verno House takes a smaller-scale approach, with 48 rooms in central Budapest near Szabadság Square and St Stephen’s Basilica. Rather than palace-like grandeur, its interiors use warm colours, rich textures and greenery to create the feeling of an urban retreat, complemented by an intimate spa and the Flava restaurant. That quieter, residential character gives Verno a different identity from Budapest’s monumental five-star hotels and makes it one of the more intimate properties in the Hungarian Michelin Key selection.

W Budapest – One Michelin Key

W Budapest occupies the historic Drechsler Palace on UNESCO-listed Andrássy Avenue, directly opposite the Hungarian State Opera House. Its design deliberately plays with contrasts – ballet and nightlife, historic architecture and modern luxury – with references to Hungarian culture, chess and even Harry Houdini appearing throughout the interiors. The result is one of the boldest reinterpretations of a Budapest landmark, with the former palace functioning not as a solemn heritage hotel but as an intentionally energetic contemporary space.

Two Michelin Key hotels in Hungary outside Budapest

The 2026 selection is heavily dominated by the capital, but its two non-Budapest hotels demonstrate that Michelin is also looking at smaller destinations. One is beside Lake Balaton, while the other forms part of a remarkable hospitality and gastronomic complex in Tata.

Hotel Petit Bois, Balatonfüred – One Michelin Key

Hotel Petit Bois is by far one of the smallest properties in the group, with just 13 rooms in the Lake Balaton resort town of Balatonfüred. The adults-only hotel combines Belle Époque elegance with contemporary technology and offers a rooftop restaurant, terrace and pool, while rooms look towards either its namesake park or the lake. Its scale is what makes it particularly interesting: Michelin recognition here is attached to a highly intimate boutique experience rather than the grand urban luxury offered by most of the Budapest hotels.

Platán Manor, Tata – One Michelin Key

Platán Manor stands immediately beside Tata Castle and offers just ten individually designed rooms overlooking the castle and its restored moat, with additional accommodation available nearby at Platán Street. Its unusual Mirror Spa has been constructed in the moat itself, while the wider Platán complex has a particularly strong culinary identity, including Platán Gourmet, which retained Two Michelin Stars in the 2025 restaurant guide. The combination of tiny scale, castle-side setting, destination gastronomy and spa facilities gives Platán an identity that no city-centre luxury hotel on the Hungarian list can really replicate.

Photo: Erika Gáncs

Budapest dominates, but the list is more varied than it first appears

The 12 Michelin Key hotels in Hungary reveal a clear strength in historic-building conversions: former palaces, a shopping arcade and even an early telecommunications centre have all become high-end hotels. Yet Michelin’s inclusion of the much smaller Petit Bois and Platán Manor shows that size, an international hotel brand and a Budapest address are not prerequisites for recognition.

The 2026 results also underline how closely Hungary’s luxury hospitality offer has become tied to architecture, history and gastronomy. For international visitors, that means the Michelin Key list can serve not only as a guide to where to sleep, but also as a compact introduction to some very different ways of experiencing Budapest, Lake Balaton and historic Tata.

World.title: Hungarian central bank makes a move towards the euro
World.content:
Hungary’s central bank has decided to lower its medium-term inflation target from 3 per cent to 2.5 per cent from 2028, a move that could support Hungary euro adoption by bringing domestic monetary policy closer to conditions prevailing in the euro area. However, several other economic, fiscal and legal requirements still need to be met before Hungary can introduce the common currency.

The Monetary Council of the National Bank of Hungary (MNB) decided after reviewing its inflation target that the new 2.5 per cent target will take effect on 1 January 2028, HVG reported.

The current target is 3 per cent, with a tolerance band of plus or minus one percentage point. According to the central bank, lowering the target brings Hungary closer to regional practice and to the European Central Bank’s 2 per cent inflation target.

The change will nevertheless begin influencing monetary policy before 2028 because central banks set interest rates based on their medium-term inflation outlook rather than current inflation alone.

Lower inflation target supports Hungary euro adoption

The MNB said Hungary’s economic convergence with the euro area and the decline in inflation expectations created room to lower the target. The central bank expects a lower-inflation environment to contribute to more predictable economic conditions and, over the longer term, lower nominal interest rates and financing costs.

It also explicitly linked the decision to Hungary’s preparations for joining the euro area.

MNB Governor Mihály Varga said earlier in September that euro adoption required a disciplined and coordinated strategy between monetary and fiscal policymakers. He said Hungary should introduce the euro in a way that allows the economy to continue converging both before and after joining the currency union.

The Hungarian government has meanwhile said it aims to meet the Maastricht criteria required for euro adoption around 2030. That does not amount to a formal date for replacing the forint with the euro: meeting the criteria would be a prerequisite for entering the final stages of the process.

If you missed it – Hungary sets 2030 euro target: Government reveals when budget deficit could fall below 3%

What Hungary still has to do before introducing the euro

Lower inflation is only one element of euro-area accession.

EU countries seeking to adopt the single currency must meet convergence requirements covering price stability, sustainable public finances, long-term interest rates and exchange-rate stability. They must also participate in the Exchange Rate Mechanism, known as ERM II, for at least two years without severe exchange-rate tensions.

Hungary is not currently part of ERM II, and the European Commission states that the country has no formal target date for adopting the euro.

The Commission’s June 2026 Convergence Report also concluded that Hungary did not yet fulfil the conditions for joining the euro area. At the time of the assessment, Hungary failed the price-stability criterion, while Hungarian legislation, including rules governing the MNB, was not considered fully compatible with requirements for participation in the Eurosystem.

Inflation has since fallen, which helps explain why the MNB now sees scope for setting a lower target.

Public finances remain a major challenge

Fiscal policy remains another important part of the equation. Hungary is still subject to the EU’s excessive deficit procedure, although the procedure is currently held in abeyance following the Commission’s assessment of government measures.

The European Commission’s spring forecast projected Hungary’s general government deficit at 6.2 per cent of GDP in 2026 and 5.8 per cent in 2027. Public debt was forecast to rise from 74.6 per cent of GDP in 2025 to 75.1 per cent in 2026 and 76.8 per cent in 2027.

As a recent HVG analysis noted, euro preparations therefore require coordination between the government’s fiscal policy and the MNB’s monetary policy.

The reduction of the inflation target is a concrete change on the monetary side. For Hungary euro adoption to progress further, however, the country will also need sustainable public finances, exchange-rate stability, legal alignment and eventually entry into ERM II. The latest MNB decision therefore marks one step in a process that is likely to extend over several years.

What’s next? New analysis: Hungary’s government is full steam ahead with adopting the euro

Just in: interest rate decision – Monetary Council leaves base rate unchanged

The Monetary Council of the Hungarian National Bank (MNB) left the 5.50 per cent base rate unchanged at its meeting on Tuesday, the central bank announced.

Source: MTI

Both ends of the interest rate corridor also remained unchanged: the overnight (O/N) deposit rate stands at 4.50 per cent, whilst the upper end of the corridor, the overnight (O/N) lending rate, stands at 6.50 per cent.

The decision was in line with analysts’ expectations.

The committee last cut the base rate in August, by a unanimous decision, by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent.

World.title: BREAKING! Hungarian immunity rights: Prosecutors seek suspension for PM Magyar and two former Fidesz ministers
World.content:
Hungarian immunity rights have returned to the spotlight after prosecutors asked parliament to suspend the immunity of two former government ministers, while a separate request has also been filed concerning Prime Minister Péter Magyar. The three requests relate to separate criminal investigations and do not in themselves constitute findings of guilt.

According to 24.hu, prosecutors have requested the suspension of the parliamentary immunity of former culture and innovation minister Balázs Hankó, a Fidesz MP, and former national development minister Miklós Seszták, a KDNP MP. The authorities have also renewed proceedings concerning Magyar over an incident dating back to 2024.

Hungarian immunity rights and the investigation into Miklós Seszták

The most serious allegations outlined by prosecutors concern Seszták, who served as national development minister between 2014 and 2018.

According to the prosecution’s account cited by 24.hu, investigators suspect that Seszták and the former chief executive of the Hungarian National Asset Management company received more than HUF 11 billion (approximately EUR 30.4 million) in unlawful benefits between 2015 and 2018 from a representative of companies that had contractual links to the state-owned Volánbusz transport company.

Investigators also suspect that a representative of a construction group offered to return 10 percent of the value of certain contracts to Seszták through an intermediary in exchange for anticipated state orders. Prosecutors say the company group won several major state projects between 2015 and 2018 and allegedly provided more than HUF 1 billion, or around EUR 2.8 million, in unlawful benefits.

The broader Volán investigation is examining suspected losses of around HUF 10 billion (EUR 27.6 million) linked to allegedly overpriced bus purchases and other transactions. These remain allegations under investigation, and criminal liability can only be established by a final court judgment.

Prosecutors also seek to lift Balázs Hankó’s immunity

A separate request concerns Balázs Hankó and an investigation into the National Cultural Fund, known by its Hungarian abbreviation NKA.

Prosecutors suspect that a temporary NKA committee was used to distribute public funds for purposes that differed from those authorised by legislation and the body’s founding documents. According to investigators, some applications submitted under a funding scheme launched in July 2025 were approved without substantive assessment, with money allegedly used for election campaign-related expenses or personal purposes.

The case concerns funding decisions worth more than HUF 17 billion, equivalent to roughly EUR 46.9 million. Prosecutors believe Hankó’s alleged conduct could qualify as breach of trust causing particularly significant financial damage. Hankó and other people concerned by the investigation are entitled to the presumption of innocence.

Former prime minister Viktor Orbán previously rejected the accusations surrounding the NKA case, describing the investigation as politically motivated and arguing that the fund’s decision-makers had merely distributed money allocated to Hungarian culture.

As we wrote earlier, Hungarian billionaire Jellinek and former state asset manager chief arrested

Péter Magyar’s immunity is also at issue

In an entirely separate case, prosecutors have once again sought the suspension of Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s parliamentary immunity over an alleged theft dating back to June 2024.

Authorities allege that during an altercation at a Budapest nightclub, Magyar took a man’s mobile phone after noticing that he was being filmed. The phone was later allegedly thrown into the Danube. Prosecutors first sought to have Magyar’s immunity lifted while he was serving as a Member of the European Parliament.

The European Parliament refused to waive his immunity in October 2025, citing concerns over possible political motivation behind the proceedings. The European Parliament stressed at the time that an immunity procedure was not a determination of criminal responsibility.

Magyar’s European Parliament mandate, and the immunity attached to it, ended on 8 May 2026. He became a member of Hungary’s National Assembly the following day and was elected prime minister on 9 May following TISZA’s victory in the April parliamentary election.

As a Hungarian MP, however, Magyar again enjoys parliamentary immunity. Prosecutors therefore need parliament’s consent before the criminal proceedings can continue against him.

Under Hungarian rules on parliamentary immunity, criminal proceedings against an MP generally cannot be initiated or continued without the prior consent of the National Assembly. Parliament will therefore have to decide separately whether the immunity of the politicians concerned should be suspended, making the requests the next major procedural step in all three cases.

World.title: In neighbouring countries: Austrian government agrees to extend mandatory military service
World.content:
The Austrian governing coalition has agreed on a new model to extend military service, Yannick Shetty, leader of the New Austria and Liberal Forum (NEOS), announced on Tuesday.

According to Anadolu, under the proposed reform, the current six-month basic training will be immediately followed by one month of active drills. Conscripts will then complete the remaining two months of reserve training at a later date.

Currently, military service in Austria is limited strictly to six months of basic training.

To pass the reform, the coalition requires a two-thirds majority in Parliament, meaning it must secure votes from the opposition.

The largest opposition party, the far-right Freedom Party of Austria (FPÖ), is calling for an even longer extension of both military and civilian service. The Austrian Greens, on the other hand, remain opposed to the planned changes.

If you missed it – Hungarian Gripen crash: Swedish Saab offers support as investigation begins

Not just Austria

Austria is not the only country in Europe making changes to its conscription system in response to the war in Ukraine and perceived security threats from Russia.

Latvia reinstated mandatory military service in 2024 after a nearly two-decade hiatus. Croatia, following a 17-year hiatus, reintroduced mandatory two-month basic training for men starting in January 2026.

Denmark implemented a comprehensive reform starting in 2026. Military service will be drastically extended from four to eleven months.

Similarly, in Germany, which suspended a draft in 2011, a new model has emerged.

Under the new Military Service Act passed under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, conscription was not fully reinstated, but it was comprehensively reformed.

Starting in 2026, all 18-year-old men will be required to complete a digital questionnaire on physical fitness and military readiness.

Based on the responses, candidates will be invited to a physical examination in, with the goal of recruiting approximately 20,000 volunteers each year.

Hungary has no mandatory military service in peacetime

Unlike Austria, Hungary does not have mandatory military service in peacetime. Conscription was suspended in November 2004, when the last conscripts left the Hungarian Defence Forces, and the country switched to a professional, voluntary military system. Today, Hungarians can join the armed forces voluntarily as professional, contract or reserve personnel.

Hungary’s legal framework nevertheless retains the possibility of compulsory military service under exceptional circumstances. Under Hungarian law, citizens’ preparation for national defence is based on voluntary participation in peacetime, while military obligations may be activated under the special legal order applicable in wartime.

World.title: Péter Magyar and Ukraine clash over new Carpathian Eight initiative
World.content:
Péter Magyar and Ukraine have become embroiled in a public diplomatic dispute after Budapest rejected claims that Hungary had joined the newly launched Carpathian Eight regional initiative. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha criticised the Hungarian government’s position as unnecessarily confrontational, while Magyar insisted that no sovereign country could be declared part of an international cooperation format without its consent.

The exchange unfolded on social media after Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said in parliament on Monday that Hungary was not a member of the Carpathian Eight, or C8, launched by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy days earlier.

Sybiha described Budapest’s reaction as surprising and unnecessarily confrontational. He argued that the initiative was designed to strengthen regional development, cross-border relations and mutually beneficial investment.

Sybiha also criticised Budapest’s reaction to a separate cooperation agreement between Ukrainian and Hungarian energy companies.

Péter Magyar and Ukraine disagree over Hungary’s C8 status

The dispute centres on a fundamental question: whether Hungary ever actually joined the new regional format.

Zelenskyy announced the Carpathian Eight at its inaugural summit in western Ukraine on 18 September. Ukrainian officials described the initiative as bringing together Ukraine, Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, Czechia, Austria and Serbia. Its proposed areas of cooperation include security, energy, logistics, investment and cross-border economic development.

However, the Hungarian government says Budapest never agreed to become a member.

Hungary was represented at the meeting by Ádám Ceglédi, chargé d’affaires at the Hungarian Embassy in Kyiv, but the Foreign Ministry said his presence did not amount to Hungary joining the initiative.

Hungary also did not sign the declaration adopted at the summit. According to the ministry, the document was endorsed by Ukraine, Austria, Romania, Poland, Serbia and Slovakia. Czechia also did not sign.

Magyar told parliament that Hungary had received an invitation but had decided not to join.

In his response to Sybiha, he argued that declaring Hungary a member without prior agreement was unacceptable. He illustrated his point with a football analogy, saying it would be like someone forming a team in a neighbouring village and then informing another person that they were already a member and expected to bring the ball.

If you missed yesterday: Russia election 2026: What Putin’s strengthened majority means for Hungary

Ukrainian foreign minister invokes the Orbán era

Sybiha went further in his criticism, linking the current dispute to Hungary’s foreign policy under former prime minister Viktor Orbán.

He suggested that although Orbán was no longer in office, what he described as a policy of “obstruction and isolation” remained visible in Budapest’s approach.

The Ukrainian foreign minister also referred critically to “Orbánism”, while stressing that Kyiv remained open to pragmatic and mutually beneficial cooperation with Hungary.

The remarks are notable because Magyar’s government has sought to distinguish its foreign policy from that of its predecessor, although the C8 dispute shows that significant disagreements between Péter Magyar and Ukraine remain.

MOL–Naftogaz deal adds another layer to dispute

The diplomatic argument has also become entangled with a planned energy project involving Hungarian oil and gas group MOL and Ukraine’s state-owned Naftogaz. Details: Ukraine could store fuel in Hungary as MOL and Naftogaz strike deal amid Russian attacks

Naftogaz announced on 20 September that the companies had signed a memorandum during the first C8 summit concerning the development of facilities in Hungary, close to the Ukrainian border, that could store petroleum products for the Ukrainian market.

The Hungarian government reacted cautiously.

Magyar said in parliament that no such oil storage facility would be built near the Ukrainian-Hungarian border under his government. Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány also said MOL had not informed the cabinet before signing the memorandum. According to the Hungarian side, the agreement begins a longer preparatory process rather than immediately authorising construction.

Sybiha, however, characterised the arrangement as direct and pragmatic cooperation between companies from the two countries and argued against political interference in such commercial relations.

What is the Carpathian Eight?

The C8 is intended as a new regional framework rather than a military alliance or a supranational organisation.

Its organisers say the initiative should connect governments, regional authorities, businesses and investors across the wider Carpathian region, with cooperation focusing on energy, security, transport, logistics and cross-border development.

The inaugural summit took place in Ukraine’s Ivano-Frankivsk region from 18 to 20 September. Zelenskyy presented the initiative as a way of creating a stronger framework for regional cooperation and closer coordination at European Union level.

Whether Hungary will eventually participate remains unresolved. Budapest says it will continue to follow the development of the initiative, but for now insists that attendance at the inaugural summit should not be interpreted as membership.

The public exchange between Magyar and Sybiha therefore goes beyond terminology: it highlights unresolved questions over how Budapest and Kyiv intend to manage regional cooperation, energy projects and bilateral relations under Hungary’s new government.

World.title: Hungarian food industry urges government to scrap price margin cap
World.content:
Hungary’s food producers and retailers are jointly calling on the government to abolish the country’s price margin cap immediately, arguing that the measure has outlived its original anti-inflation purpose and is now distorting the market. The debate puts Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s new government in a difficult position: while inflation has fallen sharply and both businesses and the central bank see room for an exit, consumers have become accustomed to direct state intervention keeping some supermarket prices down.

What is Hungary’s price margin cap?

The Hungary price margin cap is not technically a traditional price freeze. Instead of fixing the final shelf price of a product, the state limits the difference between the price at which a retailer buys a product and the price at which it sells it.

The measure was introduced by Viktor Orbán’s government in March 2025 as food inflation was accelerating again. For the food categories covered by the regulation, retailers generally cannot apply a margin above 10%, while a lower average margin used in January 2025 must also be respected where applicable.

This distinction matters. A retailer can still increase the shelf price if its purchase price rises, but it cannot freely determine its mark-up. Moreover, the retail margin is not the same thing as a company’s net profit: wages, rents, logistics, energy bills, taxes and other operating costs must also be paid from the difference between purchase and retail prices. The European Commission has specifically criticised Hungary for treating the margin as if it were equivalent to profit.

The intervention was originally presented as temporary. However, successive extensions followed, and shortly before leaving office in April 2026, the Orbán government removed its automatic expiry. The new parliament subsequently incorporated the restrictions into statutory law, meaning that they remain in force until the legislation is changed.

If you missed it: Hungary reveals new diesel subsidy details: Who gets EUR 55 and when will payments begin?

Food industry calls for immediate abolition

In a joint statement on Tuesday, organisations representing Hungarian food manufacturers, agricultural producers and retailers said the time had come for the price margin cap to be removed.

They pointed to months of improving inflation data.

According to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH), consumer prices were only 1.3% higher year on year in August 2026. Food prices actually fell by 1.4% compared with August 2025, or by 4.8% when catering services are excluded.

The organisations argue that maintaining the restriction under these circumstances is no longer justified.

They also claim that the Hungary price margin cap interferes with normal market pricing, prevents real production costs from being fully reflected in retail prices and weakens suppliers’ negotiating position.

Another concern is imports. According to the industry organisations, when retailers cannot achieve viable margins on domestically produced goods, they may have a stronger incentive to replace them with cheaper imported alternatives, potentially hurting Hungarian farmers and food processors.

Among those calling for the immediate withdrawal are the Federation of Responsible Food Manufacturers, the Hungarian mineral water and soft drinks industry association, confectionery, meat, refrigeration and canning industry organisations, the National Federation of Agricultural Cooperators and Producers, the Hungarian Chamber of Agriculture and the Milk Interprofessional Organisation and Product Board.

The Hungarian Chamber of Commerce and Industry separately reached a similar conclusion last week, saying the measure had become a distortion of competition rather than an effective long-term tool against inflation.

Central bank sees limited inflation risk from removing the cap

The strongest argument for an exit may come from the National Bank of Hungary (MNB).

In its June Inflation Report, the central bank estimated that abolishing the margin restrictions would cause only a limited rebound in prices because much of the adjustment following their introduction had already worked its way through the supply chain.

The MNB estimated that only around one-quarter of the original 1.4-percentage-point technical price-reducing effect would return. Its modelling suggested an inflationary impact of up to roughly 0.4 percentage points, with inflation remaining below the central bank’s 3% target even after an immediate withdrawal of the measure.

This does not mean that every affected product would remain at its present price. Some could become more expensive once retailers regain freedom to set margins. However, the central bank also expects competition between supermarket chains to limit the extent of such increases.

Why has Péter Magyar’s government kept the policy?

This is where economics and politics collide.

The measure was inherited from the Orbán government, but Péter Magyar’s administration did not dismantle it upon taking office. Before the transfer of power, TISZA had indicated that it would initially retain the system because there was not enough time for an abrupt withdrawal. In August, Magyar said the government had not yet discussed ending the measure, while acknowledging that inflation had fallen to levels not seen for years.

By 18 September, his position had moved further: the prime minister said the government was examining either abolishing or transforming the scheme because of the damage it could cause to Hungarian agricultural producers, particularly dairy farmers. He also said the decline in inflation meant an exit might no longer produce a major jump in supermarket prices.

The government therefore faces a policy-exit problem familiar from other forms of administered pricing. Once consumers become accustomed to a lower regulated shelf price, removing the intervention can look and feel like a government-induced price rise, even when the underlying inflation rate is low.

That creates a political incentive to postpone reform.

Yet maintaining the scheme carries costs of its own. Producers and retailers warn of distorted supply chains and greater import pressure, the MNB says the inflationary justification for maintaining it has weakened, and the European Commission argues that the restrictions breach EU single-market rules.

In July, Brussels referred Hungary to the Court of Justice of the European Union over both the food and drugstore price margin restrictions. The Commission argues that the system disproportionately affects non-Hungarian companies and can force retailers to sell products at levels insufficient to cover their wider operating costs.

If you missed it – Hungary new home VAT 2027: developers and buyers brace for a costly shift

What can the government do next?

The government has several possible routes without necessarily moving from full regulation to complete deregulation overnight.

It could abolish the margin cap immediately, relying on supermarket competition and falling producer prices to limit the resulting price increases. The MNB’s estimates suggest that this is considerably less inflationary today than it would have appeared when the policy was introduced.

A second possibility would be a phased withdrawal, for example by gradually increasing the permitted margin or removing individual product groups from the regulation. Such an approach could limit sudden changes in shelf prices while giving producers and retailers time to renegotiate contracts.

A third route would be to replace broad price intervention with targeted assistance for lower-income households if food affordability remains a concern. That would separate social policy from retail price-setting, although any such programme would have its own fiscal cost.

The government could also rely more heavily on competition enforcement, price transparency and measures aimed at reducing costs along the supply chain rather than determining commercial margins directly.

For the Magyar government, the decision is therefore broader than whether a litre of milk or a kilogram of meat becomes slightly more expensive after the cap disappears. It is an early test of how quickly the new administration is prepared to unwind direct market interventions inherited from its predecessor when the original emergency conditions have eased.

With food prices now falling year on year, businesses demanding an exit, the central bank seeing manageable inflation risks and an EU court case pending, the pressure for a decision is becoming increasingly difficult to postpone.

World.title: Croatia Pushes for Stronger Frontex Role on Western Balkan Migrant Route
World.content:
Members of FRONTEX at a launch ceremony in Skopje, North Macedonia, April 2023. Photo: EPA-EFE/GEORGI LICOVSKI.

Croatia’s Interior Minister Davor Bozinovic said on Tuesday that his country advocates deploying the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, Frontex, in neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, noting that more than 95 per cent of migrants using the so-called Western Balkan Route to enter Croatia come from that direction.

“Our goal, and the goal of the European Commission [in talks with Bosnia] was to resolve the status of Frontex there,” Bozinovic said, adding that Frontex is currently establishing some activities in the country, mainly along Bosnia’s eastern border.

“However, what interests us the most is the western border, where migrants mostly try to cross illegally into the territory of Croatia,” Bozinovic said. “That is one of the issues that I think we will discuss in the future,” he added.

Bozinovic said Frontex’s future mission was to strengthen the capacities of countries through which migrants travel to reach the European Union, and improve returns.

He said an organisation with such a large budget could play a much more effective role in returning migrants caught entering the EU irregularly to their countries of origin.

“Our three countries share a common goal of ensuring citizen safety, managing migration effectively, and further strengthening the [borderless] Schengen Area,” Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi said, adding that cooperation had produced positive results, citing a 28-per-cent drop in irregular border crossings recorded in the first eight months of this year.

Bozinovic also noted a further decline in irregular migration along the Western Balkan route this year but warned that the route remained active and needed close monitoring.

“We will therefore continue with trilateral border patrols, as they have proven effective, particularly in the fight against migrant smugglers,” Bozinovic said.

He noted that 842 smugglers had been arrested this year and that prevention efforts had produced stronger results than in the previous period, with nearly 25 per cent more attempted entries into EU territory prevented than last year.

He was speaking at a meeting of the interior ministers of Italy, Croatia and Slovenia in Pordenone, Italy. The ministers confirmed their readiness to further improve cooperation through regular information sharing, joint operational activities and coordinated responses to security challenges.

“Today, there is no security challenge, especially for police forces, that does not have a cross-border dimension. The better we cooperate, the more successful we will be,” Slovenian Interior Minister Franci Matoz said.

World.title: Albania’s Intelligence Chief Suspended for Allegedly Aiding Crime Group
World.content:
The head of Albania’s State Intelligence Service, Vlora Hyseni. Photo: LSA.

Anti-corruption prosecutors on Tuesday placed Vlora Hyseni, head of Albania’s State Intelligence Service, SHISH, under house arrest and suspended her for allegedly revealing state secrets and assisting an offender.

The Special Prosecution Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK, has also questioned the former Chief of Police, Ilir Proda, it announced. Media reported that Hyseni is not currently in Albania.

SPAK added that a sector head of the Forensic Police and a businessman had been arrested in relation to the same case.

Hyseni is being investigated over a corruption scandal surrounding tenders of the national agency overseeing the development of state information systems, the National Agency for Information Society, AKSHI.

Hyeni has headed the SHISH, the most important institution handling national security, since 2023, and her alleged involvement with the AKSHI corruption scandal potentially marks the most serious crisis over national security in the country’s history.

Hyseni was appointed head of SHISH after serving as Prime Minister’s Edi Rama national security adviser for about two years. She had earlier been deputy director of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency, KIA, but was dismissed from that post in June 2021 by Kosovo President Vjosa Osmani and Prime Minister Albin Kurti.

Her appointment as head of SHISH in 2023 was controversial because of her Kosovo citizenship and the unclear reason for her dismissal from Kosovo’s top security institution.

Meanwhile, former police chief Proda was seen at SPAK offices on Tuesday where, according to the media, he was questioned in relation to the AKSHI scandal and his house was searched.

AKSHI coordinates the development of state information systems and digitalisation procedures and administers the state public services portal, e-Albania.

The agency has managed a massive budget; some 19 of its procedures investigated by SPAK alone had an estimated total value of 5.9 billion lek, or about 59 million euros.

The SPAK investigation alleges that AKSHI’s director, Mirlinda Karcanaj, and her deputy, Hava Delibashi, placed many of these funds in the hands of a group linked to organised crime, pre-selected tender winners and ensured the diversion of tens of millions of euros into the accounts of IT businessman Ermal Beqiraj and Ergys Agasi.

Agasi is accused of forming a criminal group with Beqiraj to rig and extort tenders from the AKSHI, even using violence and hostage-taking.

Agasi was arrested in August 27 after being on the run for months. Beqiraj was arrested earlier in France on July 24 while flying a light aircraft through restricted airspace over a nuclear power plant.

Karcanaj, Delibashi and Agasi all deny charges while Beqiraj is still under arrest in France. SPAK alleges that he transferred a portion of his illicit proceeds to France, using the cash to purchase a château, two apartments and motor vehicles, while also depositing over 2 million euros in bank accounts.

The alleged involvement of top security officials in this scheme, providing criminals with information and assisting them, has left many in the country in shock.

“Whenever something happens, we say: ‘This is the end; nothing worse than this could possibly happen.’ But in this country, the problem is that even the end has no end,” Mentor Kikia, a journalist and analyst, wrote on Facebook.

The opposition has urged President Bajram Begaj to call an urgent meeting of the State Security Council.

Ruling Socialist Party MPs are urging caution. “We must await the final judicial verdict. Nothing is true until proven by the courts,” Blendi Cuci, a Socialist MP, told a meeting of parliament’s Committee on Internal Affairs and Defence, after opposition MPs asked for the issue to be urgently included in parliamentary sessions.

World.title: As Tech Giants Harvest Data, Montenegro Struggles to Track Them
World.content:
Mirko Radunovic from Podgorica planned to organise and monitor his gym training sessions by registering on a mobile fitness app.

Knowing the app's purpose, he did not find it off when it asked him to enter information about his age, health and exercise habits.

“I entered information about my age, health, nutrition and life habits, to create an appropriate training plan. After some time, I started receiving s for fitness equipment and supplements,” Radunovic told BIRN.

“When the app suggested that I add progress photos, I stopped using it. I removed it from my phone – but didn't ask for my data to be removed," he added.

World.title: Albania to Adopt EU Disability Access Standards – But Will They Be Enforced?
World.content:
Katerina Jaupaj understood from an early age that she could not take a step without thinking about the consequences. She was 18 months old and had only just started walking when she broke her leg for the first time.

Jaupaj was diagnosed with osteogenesis imperfecta, better known as brittle bone disease, a rare genetic disorder that affects the production of collagen and renders bones fragile. Those with the condition face a high risk of fractures, even from impacts or movements that would be considered ordinary for others.

The fear of injury followed Jaupaj throughout her childhood. While at school, she began using a wheelchair, but this only proved another source of anxiety.

World.title: ‘Our War is Being Judged’: In Kosovo, Outrage at Hague Verdict Simmers
World.content:
Thaci, Krasniqi, Veseli, and Selimi were sentenced to 25, 25, 18, and 13 years in prison respectively. They were found guilty of the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder, committed from April 1998 to June 20, 1999, in Kosovo and two locations in Albania. They were found not guilty of crimes against humanity.

On Monday, the parliamentary group of the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK – the party widely seen as originating from the KLA, which has been led by both Thaci and Veseli in the past – announced it was initiating an attempt to change the law underpinning the court.

The PDK proposed that the trial proceedings to continue through to the conclusion of the appeals phase. However, if the case is sent for retrial, it should not start over in The Hague but instead in Kosovo.

In the case of a potential retrial, “new jurisdiction applies, and once the conditions are met, the case will be transferred to Kosovo for proceedings,” PDK leader Bedri Hamza told media on Monday.

He argued that the protests cannot be ignored, saying that “the parliament of Kosovo cannot act as if this matter does not affect the Republic of Kosovo”.

It’s not yet clear how much support the PDK proposal will get. But anger about the verdict is also shared by the ruling party, Vetevendosje. Prime Minister Albin Kurti, the leader of Vetevendosje, wrote on X on Monday that the court’s findings “were based on factual inaccuracies, historical misunderstandings, and legal errors. We expect these to be fully corrected on appeal.”

The Specialist Chambers were established under a law adopted in 2015 by the Kosovo Assembly, under pressure from Pristina’s Western allies. The court is part of Kosovo’s judicial system but located in The Netherlands and staffed by internationals as part of efforts to prevent witness-tampering during trials. Thaci was one of the politicians who supported the court’s establishment, saying it would prove the KLA’s war was just.

Kosovo’s former ombudsperson, Hilmi Jashari, told BIRN on Friday that a change of regulations on appointing and overseeing the judges at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers would be beneficial for a fair trial. But Jashari cautioned that demands to fully repeal the law on the court would not be a good way forward.

“I have heard recently that the only solution is to repeal the law [governing the Specialist Chambers]; then one hears suggestions that the president should pardon the convicted individuals, but practically speaking, embarking on such an undertaking is impossible from a legal and juridical standpoint,” Jashari told BIRN and Internews Kosova’s Kallxo Pernime TV programme on Friday.

Edward P. Joseph, a lecturer at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies in Washington DC, told Kallxo Pernime that the anger towards the court in Kosovo is understandable – particularly as the verdict comes soon after Bosnian Serb wartime general Ratko Mladic, who was convicted of genocide, was buried with military honours in Belgrade.

“Consequently, this decision appears to Serbs in Belgrade as a form of vindication or absolution, while casting a shadow over the realities of the 1990s in Kosovo. That is why I find it very concerning,” Joseph said, claiming that Serbia and its supporters in Russia and China would exploit the verdict to spread their own narratives.

Serbia’s Interior Minister Ivica Dacic has welcomed the guilty verdict in exactly this way, saying it represents a “clear, though long-overdue, confirmation of what Serbia and the Serbian people have been saying loudly for more than a quarter of a century – that the so-called KLA was a criminal and terrorist organisation”.

Meanwhile on Monday evening in Pristina, protesters gathered again in the main square, determined that their message will be heard.

World.title: UN Chief Condemns Mladic Glorification in Meeting with Bosnian Leader
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Monday condemned the ongoing glorification of the late convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic during a meeting in New York with Denis Becirovic, chair of Bosnia’s three-member state presidency.

The encounter took place at the UN’s New York headquarters to discuss international law, regional stability and Bosnia’s current challenges. Guterres targeted recent revisionist actions and the denial of genocide in Bosnia, describing them as direct violations of international legal and civilisational norms.

According to the statement released afterwards, the conversation focused on implementation of the UN General Assembly’s Srebrenica Genocide Resolution, adopted in 2024, and the need to combat historical revisionism in the region.

“The UN maintains an unyielding stance against historical revisionism and the glorification of war criminals, which continues to jeopardise reconciliation efforts,” Guterres stated. “International law and civilisational standards must be respected to maintain regional stability.”

Becirovic invited Guterres to visit Sarajevo and the Srebrenica Memorial Centre in the future. He emphasised the importance of establishing permanent international outreach educational programmes on the 1995 genocide to prevent future historical revisionism and protect the historical truth established by international courts.

Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade on September 7 was attended by ministers and high officials both from Serbia and Bosnia’s Serb-led entity, Republika Srpska and was organised with military honours.

EU officials have condemned the government of Serbia – an EU membership candidate state – over the glorification of Mladic, saying it was incompatible with the bloc’s values.

World.title: Across Croatia, Protesters Demand Tougher Response to Violence Against Women
World.content:
Women’s organisations staged symbolic public protests in 17 towns and cities across Croatia on Monday, titled “While the Minister Sheds Light, Women Remain in the Dark” – a slogan pouring scorn on a comment made by Family and Social Policy Minister Alen Ruzic after a woman’s murder.

The groups’ demands include moving violence against women from the realm of misdemeanours into the criminal justice sphere.

“We demand a specific law against all forms of gender-based violence,” the organisations and initiatives said ahead of the National Day Against Violence Against Women, observed on September 22.

They also called for a unified, mandatory and standardized assessment of the risk of recurring violence and femicide, as well as mandatory specialized training for everyone involved in risk assessment and decisions concerning the protection of women.

World.title: Serbia ‘Still Ignoring’ UN Court Monitor over Vojislav Seselj Case
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Vojislav Seselj. Photo: EPA/KOCA SULEJMANOVIC.

Monitor Dagmara Albrecht told the UN’s International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals in her latest report that she has not received any new information from the Serbian authorities about the status of the contempt-of-court case against Serbian Radical Party leader Vojislav Seselj and four of his party members.

The International Residual Mechanism transferred the contempt-of-court case against Seselj and his followers to Serbia in 2024, saying that conditions were adequate for it to be processed there, and appointed Albrecht to monitor progress.

But since then, Serbia has been ignoring questions about the status of the case, according to Albrecht. In her latest report, she said that since her previous report in May, she had “received no response to my numerous inquiries addressed to the Ministry of Justice of Serbia”.

In the May report, she also said that although the Ministry of Justice had promised to provide her with information, her emails went unanswered.

Her latest report suggests the case may not have moved forward. “Based on information previously received, the Seselj et al. case is still awaiting a preliminary opinion of the Ministry of Justice,” she added.

The case against Seselj and his followers – Miljan Damjanovic, Miroljub Ignjatovic, Ljiljana Mihajlovic, and Ognjen Mihajlovic – relates to his 15-year trial in The Hague for wartime crimes.

The indictment charges them with having “knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice; disclosed information in violation of court orders, including orders for the protection of witnesses; and failed to comply, without just excuse, with court orders to cease and desist from the publication of confidential information”.

Seselj already has a conviction for inciting crimes with his wartime speeches. The UN war crimes tribunal sentenced him to ten years in prison in April 2018. He did not serve any jail time, however, because of the time he had spent in custody prior to the verdict.

The Serbian Radical Party leader has been charged with contempt of court several times by the Hague-based tribunal. In 2011, he was convicted of revealing information about witnesses in a book he authored.

In 2012, Seselj and Radical Party colleagues Vjerica Radeta and Petar Jojic were also charged with pressurising witnesses in his trial using threats, blackmail and bribes to change their statements or not testify. This case is still ongoing in The Hague after the tribunal declined to transfer these proceedings to Serbia.

World.title: Croatia’s Končar Presents Hybrid Electro-Diesel Train at InnoTrans
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – Croatia’s well known Končar has presented its impressive hybrid electro-diesel train at InnoTrans in Berlin.

The InnoTrans fair in Berlin once again brought together the world’s leading manufacturers, carriers, operators and experts from the fields of transport technology, railways, public transport and sustainable mobility. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that Končar officially presented its latest step forward in Croatian industry in the field of urban mobility and infrastructure at the world’s largest transport technology fair, InnoTrans in Berlin. The train is an ultra-modern hybrid (bimodal) electro-diesel train intended for long-distance transport.

After it was put into regular service on the Zagreb – Split route a week earlier in cooperation with the customer HŽ Passenger Transport, the second train from this series has now also been presented to the international public. With the global premiere of its latest solution for more modern, more comfortable and more sustainable passenger transport, Končar has once again confirmed that the knowledge, competences and technological solutions developed in Croatia compete on equal terms with the biggest names in the European railway industry.

The InnoTrans fair in Berlin once again brought together the world’s leading manufacturers, carriers, operators and experts from the fields of transport technology, railways, public transport and sustainable mobility. Among the most visited parts of the fair was the outdoor exhibition area with 3,500 metres of track, on which 130 exhibitors from 17 countries of the world exhibited a total of 113 vehicles, including the latest generations of trains, locomotives and vehicles with alternative propulsion systems.

Precisely in such an international environment Končar is presenting technological solutions developed and produced in Croatia for the 10th time, confirming its position among the relevant European manufacturers of modern rail vehicles and advanced solutions for sustainable urban mobility. After two years ago it was the only one at InnoTrans to present a battery train, which then also became the first such product in commercial use in Europe and one of the first such products in the whole world, Končar has also displayed its new bimodal electro-diesel train at one of the most attractive positions on the outdoor exhibition area of the fair – on 75-metre-long tracks.

At the same time, the latest solutions for railway infrastructure, electrification, urban mobility and traffic digitalisation were presented on the spacious indoor area, further emphasising the ability of the domestic company to independently develop and deliver integrated technological solutions for the transport systems of the future.

World.title: New Obligations for Traders in Croatia Soon, Fines Reach €30,000
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – New obligations are coming for traders and service providers in Croatia as of the first day of October, with fines reaching a staggering €30,000.

Fuels are more expensive across Croatia once again, and by expanding the so-called anchor prices, the government wants to increase transparency and prevent the spilling over of higher costs onto other products and services. Poslovni reports that whether the measure can help in the fight against inflation or will create an additional burden for entrepreneurs and craftsmen was discussed by guests on HRT’s Otvoreno.

price hikes will be more noticeable

Željko Krevzelj from the Ministry of the Economy said that the dual display of prices is part of the Government’s 11th package of measures, and the goal is to increase transparency and encourage consumers to monitor price changes more closely. “It’s an expansion of the measure that entered into force back on the 2nd of May 2025, while from the 10th of September, it was expanded to additional categories of products and services,” he explained. When it comes to the new products, he noted that the measure applies to products that existed up to the 10th of September and that the Ministry has sent additional clarifications on the application of anchor prices to economic associations.

“Fines for non-compliance with the measures are from three to 30,000 euros. The decisions enter into force on the 1st of October and we expect them to be applied,” Krevzelj said. According to the official government decisions, as of the 1st of October, alongside the current price of products and services, the price that was valid on the 10th of September 2026 must also be displayed. For the categories that were already covered by the earlier measure – food, drink, cosmetics, cleaning agents, toiletries and household products – the reference remains the price from the 2nd of May 2025.

The second new obligation relates to the publication of price lists on websites. Traders and service providers who have established websites will have to publish price lists there in XML or CSV format. Traders must update them once a day, no later than 08:00, while service providers must update them with every price change, also no later than 08:00 that same day. Published price lists must be available for 30 days.

where does inflation come into it?

Kristina Bakula from the Association Voice of Entrepreneurs assessed the expansion of the measure as extremely worrying. She warned that anchor prices have so far been applied by large systems that have their own IT departments, while now similar requirements are being placed in a short time on farmers, car mechanics, hairdressers and other small craftsmen.

“You’re talking about an anti-inflation package, and I am telling you that no additional cost falls under the fight against inflation. On the contrary, it encourages its growth,” Bakula said. She warned that additional costs for entrepreneurs have previously also been justified by transparency or the fight against inflation and that the new requirements could force some to hire an IT specialist to maintain websites and price lists.

“This isn’t the first situation in which additional costs for people are justified by ‘transparency’ or the fight against inflation. Let us remember that the problem of craftsmen where some craftsmen’s costs rose by 200 percent has not been extinguished. We have not solved that problem either, and you are pouring oil on the fire. People have to hire an IT specialist. Is a farmer supposed to become an IT specialist overnight? An inspector will come and say: ‘You have great tomatoes, but you have to refresh your price list if you have a website. You didn’t update it at eight in the morning.’”

Krevzelj replied that the measure applies to those who already have price lists and displayed products and that the Ministry is not imposing an obligation to publish prices where a price list on the website has not existed so far. Bakula then asked him whether that means that an entrepreneur who has services listed on the website but does not have a price list will not have to start publishing prices. “You’re loading us with new things that will achieve nothing,” Bakula said.

Krevzelj replied that the rules, instructions and clarifications are clear and announced new rulebooks that should further clarify the implementation of the measure.

some may close their online shops…

President of the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts Dalibor Kratohvil said that those operating crafts are calling the Chamber and that nervousness has appeared among them because of the new rules and the short deadline for adaptation. HOK has therefore requested the withdrawal of the decision. As an example he cited the owner of a second-hand clothing shop who sells products for two, five or seven euros, and whose website is maintained by a neighbour who deals with IT and occasionally changes the prices.

“She’s worried about how she will manage everything. I’m afraid we are not going in a good direction,” Kratohvil said. He also warned that some craftsmen, because of the new obligations, are thinking about closing their web shops.

“Many have stated that they want to close their web shops, which is today a window to the world. People want to give up on those stories, and that is not desirable,” he emphasised. Kratohvil said that he does not agree with the Association Voice of Entrepreneurs on many issues and the manner of communication, but that craftsmen need to be enabled to work instead of being additionally burdened with administrative requirements. He added that HOK understands the Ministry’s intention, but considers that the existing Consumer Protection Act already prescribes how to deal with base prices. “We consider that this decision should be withdrawn,” Kratohvil concluded.

there’s a limit to how far the government can realistically go

Former Minister of the Economy Davor Štern warned that the discussion is taking place in a period of major disruptions on the world energy market. He noted that the price of diesel has risen 50 percent in the last six months, while the oil price is continuously oscillating. He said that he understands the positions of the Ministry, consumers, craftsmen and entrepreneurs and that a way needs to be found to prevent large jumps in fuel prices from being used for unjustified increases in other prices. One possibility, he said, would be the taxation of unjustified revenues and profits realised because of market disruptions. But he warned that even a tax on excess profit is not direct protection of consumers because that money ends up with the state.

“By displaying prices the consumer is still somewhat protected. That is good for consumers and the political environment,” Štern said. Speaking about the fuel price increase that has entered into force, he noted that a litre of diesel in Germany costs more than three euros. To the question of how the price in Croatia is still kept below two euros, he replied that the government has shown good will with its interventions, but that the possibilities of such a policy are not unlimited. “There is a limit to how far one can realistically go,” Štern concluded.

World.title: European Heat Dome at the End of September Will Also Affect Croatia
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – Another European heat dome at the end of September will bring about unusual heat levels, and it will also affect Croatia.

Yet another unseasonably warm spell will hit a large part of Europe at the end of September, and unusually high temperatures could persist into early October. According to the forecast by Severe Weather Europe, a strong area of high pressure will develop over the continent that will draw very warm air northward from the Mediterranean and northern Africa. Index reports that in parts of western, central and northern Europe the air temperature aloft will be 8 to 12 degrees higher than the average for this time of year. At the surface temperatures in many areas will exceed 25 degrees, and in places even 30 degrees, which is very unusual for the end of September and the beginning of October.

high temperatures for croatia

Such a weather pattern is often called a heat dome. It is a large and long-lasting area of high pressure that keeps warm air over the same area. The air sinks towards the ground, heats further and makes the formation of clouds more difficult, so high temperatures can last for days, and sometimes even weeks. The heatwave is expected to gradually spread across the continent by the end of September, and stable and dry weather could continue into early October. For southern Europe and the Balkans warmer air is expected from Saturday and the beginning of next week.

Temperatures in northern Italy and the central part of the Balkans should reach between 28 and 30 degrees. The warming will also affect Croatia. According to the maps, on Sunday the 27th of September in Croatia, the highest daily temperatures are mostly expected between 22 and 26 degrees. By Tuesday the 29th of September it will warm further so temperatures in parts of the country will rise to around 27 degrees. The most pronounced deviation from usual temperatures is expected over the Po Valley and Tuscany in neighbouring Italy, the northern and central part of the Balkans and Greece.

heat across the iberian peninsula

The greatest heat during this week is expected on the Iberian Peninsula. In central and southern Spain and Portugal temperatures will exceed 35 degrees, and from Thursday to Saturday in places they could approach 40 degrees. It will also be very warm in France. In the central part of the country temperatures around 35 degrees are expected, while in the south they could reach approximately 36 degrees. In the north of France and in the Benelux countries, temperatures hovering at around 30 degrees are expected over the weekend. Warm air will then spread towards Germany, Poland and the Baltic countries. In western, central and northern Germany temperatures from Sunday to the beginning of next week could reach between 27 and 29 degrees, and in places approach 30.

heavy rain for northwestern europe

In England, the warming will be shorter, with temperatures mostly between 25 and 28 degrees. In Ireland and Scotland it will be significantly cooler, with temperatures mostly around 15 degrees. While a large part of the continent will be under the influence of warm and dry air, western Ireland, Scotland and southwestern Norway can expect very moist air from the Atlantic. By the beginning of October more than 150 millimetres of rain could fall locally there. Forecasts show that the warm period could continue into early October. Then the area of high pressure would expand further towards the north and east of Europe, and the largest deviations from usual temperatures could appear in Sweden and Finland.

World.title: HRejting: Croatians Fear Corruption and Inflation the Most
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – The latest HRejting poll has revealed that Croatians still fear corruption and inflation more than climate change or wars.

Corruption and the complete non-functioning of the rule of law are the greatest threat for the citizens of Croatia, according to a new HRejting survey. Index reports that the poll was conducted for HRT by the agency Promocija plus between the 15th and the 18th of September on a sample of 1,000 respondents. The maximum sampling error is +/- 3.04 percent, at a 95 percent confidence level.

what do croatians fear the most?

Respondents were asked 21 questions about the threats they fear the most. As many as 73.4 percent of respondents listed corruption and the non-functioning of the rule of law as one of the greatest. Immediately behind that are inflation and the rise in the cost of living, followed by ecological incidents and pollution.

69 percent of citizens fear serious illnesses, while almost 64 percent fear poverty. Immediately behind is the fear of a rise in crime. A decline in the quality of public healthcare worries 62 percent of those surveyed, followed by alienation among people and the mass departure of young people. Around 56 percent of citizens fear climate change and natural disasters. Around 53 percent of respondents fear political instability. A slightly smaller percentage worries about the loss of personal freedoms, cyber attacks and the uncontrolled development of artificial intelligence. Mass migrations and demographic collapse are seen as a threat by around 52 percent of those polled. At the bottom of the list of threats are terrorism, job loss and technological lagging. The fewest respondents, 39 percent, fear war and military conflict in the region.

most expect a less secure future for croatia

The survey also covered the question of Croatia’s security in the next ten years. More than half of the respondents, precisely 51.6 percent, believe that life in the country will be significantly less secure. That the security situation will remain roughly the same is thought by 29 percent of those polled. Only 10 percent expect that Croatia will be significantly more secure, while 8.5 percent did not know how to assess the future state.

World.title: New Law for Foreign Workers in Croatia Faces Criticism
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – A new law facing foreign workers in Croatia as of 2027 is already causing a stir and facing criticism from migration experts.

You go to another country, get a job, learn around thirty basic phrases of its language and that is, according to the law, enough to be considered “integrated.” Most would argue that this statement is so ridiculous that it’s difficult to quantify. Poslovni reports that the aforementioned notion is all that will be required of foreign workers in Croatia as of 2027. They will have to prove knowledge of the Croatian language at level A1.1 in order to extend their residence and work permit. Apparently, that’s “integration”.

Is basic knowledge of a few dozen words really the same as integration into society? According to Ivan Balabanić, senior research associate at the Institute for Migration Research, the answer is very clearly “no.” The data that his institute collects shows that Croatia is only beginning to scratch the surface of a problem that, as the number of foreign workers grows, will become ever more complex. Balabanić views the obligation to pass A1.1 Croatian simultaneously as an integration measure and as an administrative condition, but emphasises that its meaning should primarily be integrative.

“Knowledge of the language of the country in which a person lives and works is one of the first preconditions for beginning to feel part of society. Nevertheless, such a low level of language knowledge by itself does not resolve questions of the legal security of foreign workers nor their finding their way in Croatian administration. Integration does not begin with a language course, but at the moment when a foreign worker knows their rights and can actually exercise them,” Balabanić highlighted.

croatia’s responsibility as a state

Precisely for that reason, while the worker hasn’t mastered Croatian, information about residence, work, the healthcare system and the protection of rights must be available to them in a language they understand, and that, Balabanić emphasises, in one place, and not scattered across a series of different institutions. Alongside economic integration, which in Croatia today mainly comes down to the relationship between the worker and the employer, the social dimension is equally important, and that, according to his words, cannot be one-way. Foreign workers need to get to know the norms and values of the society they are coming into, but the domestic population must also accept that Croatia is becoming culturally more diverse.

How weak that readiness is at this moment is shown by a study by the Institute for Migration Research from November 2025, conducted on a sample of 1,000 respondents: only 2.4 percent of citizens would accept a foreign worker as a friend, 5.7 percent as a neighbour, and as a family member only a negligible number of respondents. “That’s why I would say that Croatia is still in an early phase of the integration of foreign workers. Language is an important first step, but without legal security, available information, social contacts and the readiness of the domestic population to accept new fellow citizens we cannot speak of a serious integration policy,” Balabanić said. When it comes to the financing of integration, Balabanić clearly emphasises that the largest part of the cost should be borne by the state.

“The logic is simple: foreign workers come to Croatia primarily because of the needs of the domestic labour market and the shortage of labour in certain sectors. If the state creates a system that encourages the arrival of foreign workers, then it must also take on the largest part of the responsibility for their integration,” he is clear.

That, he emphasises, does not mean that the responsibility must be exclusively state. Local self-government has an important role because integration takes place in concrete communities – the needs of workers in Istria are not the same as the needs of those in Lika or Zagreb. Employers bear their share of responsibility within the work environment, but Balabanić warns that it would be wrong to shift the entire burden onto them, since they already bear significant costs of employing foreign workers. The least burden, he believes, should be shifted onto the workers themselves, although they too have the obligation to actively participate in integration by learning the language and respecting the law.

the so-called information vacuum

Precisely there Balabanić sees the real danger that integration becomes something that the state formally requires of the foreign worker, while at the same time not providing them with the tools to fulfil that requirement.

“It wouldn’t be logical for Croatia to actively attract foreign workers because its economy needs them, and then declare their integration exclusively their personal problem,” he said. When it comes to the biggest obstacles in the everyday life of foreign workers, Balabanić avoids singling out only one. The language barrier, inadequate accommodation, violation of labour rights, difficult access to healthcare and social isolation, he says, are intertwined – but the common denominator of most of these problems is the chronic lack of available and reliable information.

Croatia, he admits, is gradually responding regulatorily to the new situation; amendments to laws and regulations are being adopted, but the open question remains how many of them the administration manages to implement in practice. Tightened criteria for employers, for example, were supposed to regulate the market, but at the same time increased the administrative burden, so some workers waited months for the extension of their permit. A particular problem is the healthcare system – according to another study by the Institute from November 2025, conducted on 429 foreign workers from Asia and Africa in Zagreb and Zagreb County, only 28.7 percent of respondents have a chosen general practitioner, which seriously complicates regular health care.

Language remains an obstacle even when workers themselves try to find information, because the official websites of institutions are very often available exclusively in Croatian. Because of that many find themselves in what Balabanić calls an information vacuum, in which the main, sometimes the only, source of information becomes the employer or the employment agency. “A series of entirely practical questions, from whether the employer can keep the passport, whether they have the right to unemployment benefit, whom to turn to if their rights are violated – for a large number of workers remain without a reliable answer. Croatia today does not primarily lack regulations. It lacks a system that will enable the foreign worker to actually exercise the rights they have,” Balabanić highlighted.

financial burden

Particularly vulnerable, he warns, are workers in whom several unfavourable circumstances overlap – those who went into debt in order to reach Croatia at all through long chains of intermediaries, and therefore more readily accept poor working conditions, as well as those employed by an employer on whom they depend for salary, accommodation and information about their own rights. The education of children is for now not among the most pronounced problems, since a large part of labour migrants still live in Croatia without family, but with the growth in the number of those who stay long-term and bring families, that topic, Balabanić estimates, will become increasingly important.
