World.title: Jollibee enters the menu as impeach court scrutinizes Sara Duterte businesses
World.content:
Even the country’s top fast food chain was not spared in the expansive investigation into Vice President Sara Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.

Could Jollibee hold a piece of the smoking gun that the prosecution has been searching for to remove her from office?

Jollibee was implicated in the mess because documents show that its Bolton Street branch in Davao City is owned by Gencorp Industries Inc., described in one of government documents as a franchisee of the casual dining giant.

Duterte said in her sworn Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) that she is a stockholder of Gencorp, although her name is not in Securities and Exchange Commission documents (SEC) filings of the company.

Other companies associated with the Vice President or her husband Mans Carpio are Metro City Chow Food Corporation, City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation, Timesquare Bee Foods Corp., and Great Jolly Times Food Corp.

The names of several of these companies appear to echo those of Jollibee and its sister fast-food chain, Chowking.

“This P2.1 billion in sales — these are restaurants, right? Are they Jollibee or Chowking?” Senator Kiko Pangilinan asked. “I would assume there are many Jollibee and Chowking franchises, which is why sales reached billions over a period of time.”

“One of the financial statements that the witness identified yesterday contains the word ‘Jollibee’ in reference to Gencorp,” prosecutor Erwin Matib said. “Yes, there are franchises.”

Jollibee Davao Bolton is a known hangout spot of the Dutertes. It is in the same building as the listed address of Gencorp.

Rappler previously reported that Gencorp has cornered at least P14 million in contracts with Davao City Hall since 2022, coinciding with the time that Sara became VP, and her brother Sebastian assumed the mayorship of their hometown.

The Davao City mayor later not only confirmed the existence of the deals, but even updated the actual total value of the contracts bagged by Gencorp — P33 million over 19 contracts. Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System division chief Rendell Sopeña told the impeachment court that there are 15 Gencorp-Davao City deals worth P34 million in its database.

The arrangement raises questions on conflict of interest, and potential violation of the Constitution. The 1987 charter explicitly prohibits the Vice President from having business interests while in office.

The Jollibee connection did not escape the prosecution and her critics, which used its slogan to take a swipe at the Vice President.

“Bida ang sarap, bida ang ebidensiya (the star is the flavor, the star is the evidence),” prosecutor Terry Ridon said.

Play Video

“Inday, pa-Jollibee ka naman diyan (Inday, how about treating us to Jollibee),” former presidential adviser Ronald Llamas said in jest on Facebook.

Spectators of the trial might just be craving two things after Tuesday’s proceedings: a one-piece Chickenjoy, and an explanation from the Vice President. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan to Auction Rights to 56 Hydrocarbon Subsoil Blocks
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Energy Ministry will hold an electronic auction for the right to use 56 hydrocarbon subsoil blocks, with most lots offered for exploration and production as the country seeks to attract investment into its oil and gas resource base.

The auction is scheduled for Dec. 25 on the e-Qazyna platform. Applications to participate will be accepted through Nov. 18, inclusive.

Most blocks are intended for geological exploration and subsequent hydrocarbon production, while four lots are designated specifically for production, Kazinform reported on Sept. 21.

Most blocks are located in Kazakhstan’s western regions, including the Aktobe, Atyrau, West Kazakhstan and Mangystau Regions. The Western Ulytau block spans the Kostanai and Ulytau Regions.

Block sizes vary considerably. The Tyubedzhik (Karakum) block in the Mangystau Region covers 58.95 square kilometers, while Ustyurt Block 4, also in the Mangystau Region, spans 4,058.53 square kilometers. The Karasu block, located in the Atyrau and Aktobe Regions, covers 2,339.49 square kilometers.

The upcoming auction forms part of Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to expand geological exploration and attract investment into the country’s subsoil sector. Kazakhstan has been increasingly digitizing the process, with electronic auctions and access to geological information available through the e-Qazyna infrastructure. The electronic auction process has been fully automated since 2020, while a unified digital platform launched in 2025 further expanded online access to subsoil-use services.

In March, Kazakhstan also signed a long-term geological exploration agreement with Shell Kazakhstan covering the Zhanaturmys field in the Aktobe Region, highlighting continued efforts to expand the country’s hydrocarbon resource base.

World.title: Kazakhstan, UK Seek to Deepen Trade Through Higher-Value Exports and Mineral Processing
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and the United Kingdom are seeking to build on rapidly growing bilateral trade by expanding Kazakh exports beyond raw materials and deepening cooperation in mineral processing and higher-value production.

The push reflects a broader shift in the bilateral relationship. As outlined in a recent analysis for The Astana Times, the entry into force of the UK-Kazakhstan Strategic Partnership and Cooperation Agreement (SPCA) in July has created a wider institutional framework for cooperation in critical minerals, trade, logistics, education and technology.

The agreement points to a gradual shift from a relationship centered largely on resource extraction toward one focused on processing, technology, investment and higher-value production. Recent developments, including a $107 million agreement on rhenium recycling and Kazakhstan’s first multimodal fertilizer shipment to the UK via the Middle Corridor, illustrate how that shift is beginning to translate into practical projects.

Minister of Trade and Integration Arman Shakkaliyev discussed the priorities with the UK Government’s Trade Envoy to Azerbaijan and Central Asia, Lord John Alderdice, focusing on trade diversification, industrial cooperation, investment, and scientific and educational ties.

Trade between Kazakhstan and the UK reached $1.63 billion in 2025, up 83.7% from 2024. In January-July, turnover reached $1.25 billion, up 68.5% from the same period the previous year, reported the ministry’s press service on Sept. 22.

Despite the strong growth, Kazakhstan is seeking to diversify its trade structure. Current exports to the UK are dominated by silver, crude oil, copper and copper cathodes.

“It is important for us to move from the achieved growth to deeper and more diversified trade. First and foremost, we are interested in expanding the export of Kazakh products to the British market beyond raw materials,” Shakkaliyev said.

To support this effort, Shakkaliyev proposed organizing a trade and economic mission for British importers and retail chain representatives to visit Kazakhstan and establish direct contacts with domestic producers. The officials also discussed British requirements for product quality, certification, packaging and standards.

Critical minerals emerged as another key area, with the officials highlighting opportunities to move beyond extraction toward processing and the production of higher value-added products.

Lord Alderdice said British companies and universities could work with Kazakhstan not only in resource extraction but also in developing processing capacity.

“Kazakhstan has significant natural resources, but it is especially important that you set the task not to limit yourselves to their extraction, but to create added value and develop processing. It is precisely here that we see great opportunities for cooperation,” he said.

The meeting also covered prospects for British investment in manufacturing, energy, logistics and high-tech industries, alongside efforts to strengthen direct links between companies.

The officials also discussed standardization and export readiness as part of efforts to help Kazakh producers enter the British market. Kazakhstan expressed interest in exchanging expertise with the British Institute of Export and International Trade and expanding cooperation between KazStandard and the British Standards Institution (BSI).

The officials also considered preparations for carbon-related trade requirements, including the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), as well as cooperation between universities and research institutions in mining, mineral processing and the nuclear industry.

Following the meeting, Shakkaliyev and Lord Alderdice confirmed their interest in developing specific trade, investment, industrial and research projects and expanding direct contacts between businesses and relevant organizations in Kazakhstan and the UK.

World.title: Kazakhstan Hotels Receive MICHELIN Keys for First Time
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has been included in the MICHELIN Guide’s global hotel selection for the first time, with five hotels receiving the prestigious One MICHELIN Key distinction and nine others entering the guide’s recommended hotel selection.

The MICHELIN Guide has unveiled its MICHELIN Key Selection 2026, a global selection of outstanding hotels assessed through independent and anonymous inspections. Kazakhstan’s inclusion marks the country’s debut in the MICHELIN Guide’s hotel geography.

Five Kazakh hotels received the One MICHELIN Key distinction: The Veil Hotel, The St. Regis Astana and The Ritz-Carlton in Astana, as well as The Ritz-Carlton and Tenir Eco Hotel in Almaty, reported Kazakh Tourism on Sept. 22.

The MICHELIN Guide also included nine more hotels in its recommended selection. They are Sheraton Astana Hotel, Swissôtel Wellness Resort Alatau Almaty, Qazaq Auyl Eco Hotel, Qazaq Garden, Donatello Premium Almaty, Radisson Blu Hotel Almaty Airport, Zvezdnaya Eco-Hotel, YURTA Boutique Hotel and Medina Palace Hotel.

The MICHELIN Guide highlighted Kazakhstan’s growing appeal as an international tourism destination, placing the country among destinations that offer travelers experiences beyond established global tourism routes.

“The first MICHELIN Key is a celebration. It is also an invitation for travelers to look beyond the world’s most established destinations,” the MICHELIN Guide said, highlighting the diversity of experiences identified by its inspectors, from remote safari destinations to architectural landmarks in Kazakhstan’s capital.

The inclusion of Kazakh hotels followed strategic initiatives by Kazakh Tourism to develop tourism infrastructure and raise hospitality standards.

Kazakh Tourism Chairman Talgat Gazizov said the recognition could help strengthen the country’s position in the international premium tourism market.

“Having Kazakhstan appear on the global MICHELIN map is a significant recognition of the quality of service and authenticity offered by domestic hotels. The presence of 14 properties in the international selection confirms the competitiveness of Kazakhstan’s hospitality sector and provides a strong multiplier effect for tourism infrastructure development. Our key task is to translate this international recognition into sustainable growth in inbound tourism and strengthen Kazakhstan’s image as a key destination in Central Asia,” Gazizov said.

The MICHELIN Key was introduced in 2024 as a hotel distinction based on a methodology comparable to the rigorous standards that the MICHELIN Guide has applied to restaurants since 1900.

Anonymous inspectors assess hotels against five universal criteria: their ability to provide guests with a destination experience; the quality of architecture and interior design; consistency of service and comfort; the consistency between price and the experience offered; and the property’s individuality and authenticity.

The One MICHELIN Key distinction is awarded to hotels with a distinct character that provide a level of hospitality above the standard expected within their category.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands Digital Road Safety Measures as Astana Traffic Grows
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is expanding artificial intelligence, automated traffic enforcement and average-speed monitoring as road safety indicators improve, while rapidly growing vehicle numbers are driving the development of smart transport systems in Astana.

Road safety indicators improve

At a Sept. 22 government meeting, Minister of Internal Affairs Yerzhan Sadenov reported a 5% decline in road accidents nationwide, a 15% decrease in fatalities and a 6% reduction in injuries following measures to strengthen road safety.

On national roads, Transport Minister Nurlan Sauranbayev reported that from January to August, accidents fell by 10%, fatalities by 14% and injuries by 11%.

The authorities are expanding digital enforcement. The number of automated traffic-violation detection systems has increased from 28,000 to 32,000. The TOR platform brings together the Internal Affairs Ministry’s relevant digital services, while artificial intelligence monitors vehicles, identifies drivers who have been behind the wheel for more than eight hours, and helps locate stolen vehicles.

Average-speed monitoring is another key measure. The system currently operates on 12 sections covering 2,800 kilometers. Another 16 sections, covering an additional 2,800 kilometers, are planned by the end of the year, bringing total coverage to 5,600 kilometers across 28 sections.

Astana manages growing traffic

The capital is facing increasing pressure on its road network. Astana currently has 471,000 registered vehicles, compared with 420,000 in 2024 and 446,000 in 2025. The number increases by 25,000- 30,000 vehicles annually.

In addition, around 150,000 vehicles enter and leave the city every day, reflecting the scale of commuter traffic.

To manage these flows, Astana is implementing a comprehensive transport development program supported by an Intelligent Transport System (ITS). Some 80% of the city’s traffic-light facilities – 664 out of 847 – have been adapted to the system, with another 79 planned for adaptation this year.

AI supports the Smart City

As part of Astana’s Smart City project, more than 1,200 traffic-violation detection complexes operate in the capital, and more than 60,000 cameras are integrated into the city’s Situation Center.

The number of violations that can be detected automatically has increased from four to 15, while 35 types of AI-based video analytics have been introduced. Detection of the new violation types began in April.

These technologies are being developed alongside infrastructure measures to improve traffic flow and road safety.

Public transport expansion

Astana is also expanding public transport in response to growing mobility demand. Dedicated Bus Lanes now extend for 146 kilometers, 6.6% more than a year earlier.

The city’s bus fleet has increased by 60% over the past several years, from 1,200 to 1,900 vehicles. The city purchased another 80 buses this year, with 350 more planned for 2027.

The Tarlan Astana light rail transit (LRT) system will be integrated with bus routes and transport hubs as it develops. The city expects public transport users to reach 60% by 2030.

The city is also implementing new road infrastructure projects to redistribute traffic and improve connectivity across the capital.

World.title: Astana and Almaty Enter Global Top 300 Cities, Stand Out for Human Capital
World.content:
ASTANA – Astana and Almaty have placed among the world’s 300 highest-ranked cities in the 2026 Global Cities Index by Oxford Economics, with both Kazakhstan’s major urban centers showing their strongest performance in human capital. Almaty ranked 265th globally and Astana 281st among 1,000 cities assessed by the international economic research firm.

Kazakhstan’s cities in the global ranking

Almaty ranked higher overall at 265th, while Astana placed 281st. The index evaluates cities across five categories: Economics, Human Capital, Quality of Life, Environment and Governance.

Almaty’s strongest result came in Human Capital, where it ranked 66th globally. Astana also entered the global top 100 in the category, ranking 98th.

The two cities’ category profiles show different strengths. Almaty ranked 288th in Economics and 269th in Quality of Life, while Astana ranked 264th and 360th, respectively. In Environment, Almaty was 845th and Astana 630th. Both received the same Governance rank of 622nd.

Oxford Economics defines Human Capital through indicators including population growth, age profile, universities, corporate headquarters, educational attainment and the share of foreign-born residents.

Human capital as a source of growth

The report emphasizes the relationship between human capital and economic development. According to Oxford Economics, cities that move into higher-value sectors can attract and retain skilled workers, while strong industries encourage investment in education and skills.

“The end result is an increase in the stock of human capital, which further incentivises investment, accelerating economic growth further still,” the report said.

This dynamic is increasingly important as the global urban economy changes. Oxford Economics notes that many cities in Asia and the Middle East are gaining ground by expanding labor markets and moving into technology, advanced manufacturing and financial and business services.

The report also identifies Astana as a Regional Leader, an archetype comprising important cities that are significant within their regions and tend to outperform their respective countries on indicators such as economic growth and income per person.

A changing global urban landscape

The 2026 index places New York first, followed by London and Paris. Seattle, San Francisco, Dublin, Boston, San Jose, Tokyo and Zurich complete the top 10. The report says North American and European cities still dominate the top positions, but the global economic landscape is becoming increasingly multipolar.

Asia is central to this shift. Oxford Economics expects cities across Asia Pacific and the Middle East to record significant gains in the coming years as economic growth improves living standards and quality of life.

For Kazakhstan, the results put Almaty and Astana firmly within the global top 300, while their relatively strong human capital rankings highlight the role of education, skills, labor markets and demographic factors in their position among the world’s major urban economies.

World.title: Dimash Qudaibergen Joins Kazakhstan’s Reading Nation Marathon
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen has joined the nationwide Reading Nation marathon in its Parasat category, a non-competitive initiative that promotes reading through the personal example of public figures. Unlike participants in the competitive stages, those in Parasat do not compete for cash prizes; the category focuses instead on promoting a culture of reading through personal example.

The marathon’s competitive stages offer substantial cash prizes: regional winners receive 600,000 tenge (US$1,337) for first place, 450,000 tenge (US$1,000) for second and 300,000 tenge (US$668) for third, while the 10 top readers selected at the national final will each receive 10 million tenge (US$22,293), bringing the total value of the main national prizes to 100 million tenge (US$222,937).

Dimash chooses Karipbek Kuyukov’s story

For the marathon, Qudaibergen selected the autobiography of Kazakh artist and anti-nuclear movement activist Karipbek Kuyukov, “Life Without Hands”, which recounts the artist’s life and his work despite being born without arms as a result of the effects of nuclear testing in the Semipalatinsk region, reported the Ministry of Culture and Information on Sept. 21.

Qudaibergen said he had met Kuyukov personally in Karagandy before a Miner’s Day concert.

“His life journey, unyielding perseverance in the face of hardship and strength of spirit made a particular impression on me,” he said.

The Reading Nation marathon runs from September to April 2027. It includes Kazakh and Russian-language leagues and seven areas involving schoolchildren, students, teachers, families, civil servants and other participants.

National focus on reading

The initiative follows a presidential decree signed in May on measures to develop reading culture and form a “reading nation.” The document sets reading promotion as a priority in culture, education and innovation policy and envisages measures to expand access to books and modernize the country’s literary and library infrastructure.

The campaign comes amid broader discussion about reading and foundational skills in the digital and AI era. Kazakhstan’s latest PISA results showed that 15-year-old students performed below the OECD average in reading, mathematics and science.

Against this backdrop, the government is also preparing measures to promote reading through new library formats, wider access to literature and a national concept for developing reading culture in the AI era.

World.title: Who Will Pay for Processing Kazakhstan’s Copper?
World.content:
The new methodology for calculating copper concentrate processing tariffs raises a broader question: how competitive and predictable will Kazakhstan’s copper value chain be for international business?

Kazakhstan is seeking to develop domestic processing and create more value within the country. This is particularly important for copper, as the country has a significant resource base while the metal is becoming increasingly important for global industry, energy and technology.

Against this backdrop, the Ministry of Industry and Construction has proposed a new methodology for calculating the tariff for processing copper concentrate. The aim is to establish a unified and transparent mechanism for determining the cost of processing raw materials at copper smelting facilities in Kazakhstan.

Under the proposed approach, the tariff would be based on processing costs, a normative profit margin and investment components, including investment in new copper smelting capacity.

For the domestic market, this is primarily a question of tariff regulation. For international businesses, however, the issue is broader: how will the economics of Kazakhstan’s copper value chain be structured, and how competitive will these conditions be compared with the global market?

Global market, global benchmarks

Copper concentrate processing is part of an established international supply chain. Smelters and concentrate producers operate in a market where processing economics depend not only on domestic costs, but also on global supply and demand.

One of the key market benchmarks is the Treatment Charge (TC). When concentrate is abundant and smelting capacity is relatively limited, treatment charges tend to be higher. When concentrate becomes scarce, smelters compete for feedstock and TC declines.

In some market conditions, treatment charges can reach zero or even become negative.

This does not necessarily mean that smelting is uneconomic. Rather, it reflects the broader revenue structure of copper processing.

One concentrate, multiple sources of value

A copper smelter generates economic value from more than the treatment charge itself.

Copper and other metals, including precious metals, are recovered from the concentrate. Sulphur contained in the feedstock can be used to produce sulphuric acid, which also has an independent market value.

As a result, an international processor assesses the overall economics of the operation rather than simply the cost of the processing service. This includes the value and composition of the concentrate, recoverable metals, prices for final products, potential revenues from sulphuric acid and production costs.

This is why a zero or negative TC does not automatically indicate that processing is loss-making. Under certain market conditions, a smelter may accept concentrate without a treatment charge in order to maintain capacity utilisation and generate value from the metals and by-products recovered during processing.

What does this mean for Kazakhstan?

The proposed Kazakh methodology is primarily cost-based, taking into account processing expenses, a normative profit margin and investment costs.

This raises an important question: how does the calculation account for the revenue side of the business, including the economic value of additional metals and sulphuric acid?

For domestic regulation, this is a question of tariff design. For international investors, it is also a question of competitiveness and comparability.

A copper concentrate producer does not assess processing costs in isolation. The economics of the entire chain matter: mining, transportation, processing, financing and the sale of copper and associated products.

A change in the economics of one stage can therefore influence the attractiveness of the entire project.

From raw materials to global value chains

This issue is particularly relevant as Kazakhstan seeks to move from the export of raw materials towards higher-value production.

Developing domestic copper processing is consistent with this objective and could also strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in emerging international supply chains for critical minerals.

For investors, however, the equation goes beyond the availability of mineral resources or processing capacity. It includes the long-term predictability of regulations, logistics and processing costs, access to infrastructure, export opportunities and the overall stability of a project’s economic model.

At the July 2026 meeting of the Council of Foreign Investors, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev again identified critical minerals and the production of higher value-added products as promising areas for investment.

Asian Development Bank Vice-President Fatima Yasmin, in turn, noted that global capital is becoming more selective, with investors paying particular attention to predictable rules, transparent procedures and projects that can be clearly assessed from a financing perspective.

More than a tariff

The discussion around the methodology therefore goes beyond the relationship between a concentrate producer and a smelter.

If Kazakhstan wants to attract international capital into deeper copper processing, investors need to understand how the economics of each stage of the value chain are determined.

Can the new methodology support the development of domestic processing while maintaining the competitiveness of Kazakhstan’s copper industry?

Will the resulting tariff remain comparable with international commercial conditions?

How will foreign companies factor it into long-term investment decisions?

And how will the new regulatory framework fit into Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to create a more predictable investment environment?

These questions matter because a country’s competitiveness is not determined by a single tariff or incentive. It is shaped by the overall investment and operating environment.

For Kazakhstan, the debate therefore goes beyond the price of processing copper concentrate. Ultimately, it is about the country’s position in the global copper value chain — whether Kazakhstan remains primarily a supplier of raw materials, becomes a processor, or develops into a fully-fledged participant in international value chains, creating greater value through processing, technology and industrial capabilities.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans to Launch Driverless Taxi Service in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to introduce a driverless taxi service in 2027, with an autonomous vehicle already undergoing testing in Almaty and a pilot project underway in three cities.

The first driverless vehicle is currently being tested in Almaty, where it is collecting data and creating a digital map of the city, Yandex Qazaqstan CEO Timur Shalekenov said during a Sept. 22 government meeting.

The vehicle must cover several thousand kilometers in test mode before the first commercial passenger trips can begin, he noted.

Meanwhile, the government is working on the regulatory framework needed to operate autonomous vehicles. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said the pilot project covers Almaty, Astana and Kosshy.

The development comes as Kazakhstan is also exploring other forms of next-generation urban mobility, including passenger air taxis, with the country recently taking its first steps toward testing eVTOL aircraft.

World.title: A pair of porcupines, Khrashuna and Khramuna, at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Tbilisi Zoo is home to two Indian porcupines, a female and a male named Khrashuna and Khramuna. Their keepers chose the names for a reason: the porcupines make funny “crunching” sounds when they eat. Khrashuna is the bolder of the two, while Khramuna is more cautious.

Life at the Tbilisi Zoo: ALL VIDEO

______________________________________________________________________________

Contrary to popular belief, porcupines have nothing in common with either badgers or hedgehogs. Badgers are carnivores, hedgehogs are insectivores, while porcupines are rodents.

Their most distinctive feature is their long, thick quills, which they mainly use for defence. When threatened, their first response is to flee rather than attack. And no, porcupines do not shoot their quills — that is simply a myth. When they sense danger, they

Alongside their varied diet, Khrashuna and Khramuna always have branches in their enclosure. They gnaw on the wood, which helps keep their teeth strong.

Porcupines are nocturnal animals. During the day, especially in summer, they prefer to stay in their shelter. They become active in the evening and start looking for food. That is why visitors who come to their enclosure during the day may see nothing more than a nose or head poking out of the burrow.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Porcupines at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: European Court of Human Rights to review case of Georgian activist Irakli Miladze
World.content:
The Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has accepted the case of Georgian activist Irakli Miladze. The case concerns freedom of expression online and administrative proceedings brought against the activist.

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) asked the court to refer Miladze’s case to the Grand Chamber in August 2026.

According to GYLA chair Tamar Oniani, this means that until the Grand Chamber delivers its judgment, Georgia’s city and appeals courts cannot cite the case as a precedent when restricting freedom of expression on social media.

Irakli Miladze case

In 2022, authorities fined activist Irakli Miladze for using profanity in a video in which he criticised Tbilisi’s transport policy. He directed some of the offensive language at the city mayor, municipal officials and police officers.

Authorities brought the case under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences, which covers petty hooliganism, including the use of obscene language in public places. Tbilisi City Court ordered Miladze to pay 2,000 lari [~$740], but the Court of Appeal reduced the fine to 500 lari [~$185].

On 19 May 2026, the ECHR’s Fourth Section ruled on the case and found that the authorities had not violated Miladze’s freedom of expression, which Article 10 of the Convention protects.

Irakli Miladze

The court found that Miladze’s statements did not form part of a public debate and therefore did not warrant the same level of protection for freedom of expression as statements on matters of political or public interest.

The court also considered the size of the fine and its consequences, noting that the sanction did not prevent Miladze from continuing his civic and political activities. At the same time, the court confirmed that the concept of a “public space” also covers online platforms when they are widely accessible to the public.

The case will now be reconsidered, but this does not mean that the Grand Chamber has already found that Miladze’s rights were violated. In its final judgment, it may uphold the previous ruling or take a different position.

The key question will be whether Miladze’s statements on TikTok were protected by freedom of expression and whether imposing an administrative fine on him was justified.

According to GYLA, the significance of referring the case to the Grand Chamber is further underscored by the fact that, after the May 2026 ruling, the Interior Ministry established a so-called “censorship department”. GYLA says its activities are linked to administrative cases brought against citizens over opinions they post on social media.

Irakli Miladze case

World.title: ‘One cashbox’ for two parties: Transparency International Georgia study
World.content:
According to a study by Transparency International Georgia (TI), a significant share of the funding for the pro-government and anti-Western People’s Power party comes from people who have previously funded, or continue to fund, the ruling Georgian Dream party.

The study found that, as of August 2026, 28 people had donated a total of 861,750 lari [~$320,000] to People’s Power, which split from Georgian Dream in 2022. Of these, 21 had previously donated 1,969,169 lari [~$730,000] to Georgian Dream. Another three continue to fund both parties.

TI says these financial links indicate that People’s Power is not independent of the political and business circles surrounding Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili.

The study highlights a group of businesspeople and companies linked to Ivanishvili’s circle. According to the organisation, members of this group donated a total of 381,000 lari [~$141,000] to People’s Power between 2024 and 2026.

One of them is Archil Mamatashvili, CEO of JSC Cartu Insurance Company and a member of the supervisory board of Ivanishvili-linked Artu Holding. In 2025–2026, Mamatashvili donated 70,000 lari [~$26,000] to People’s Power. He had previously donated 55,600 lari [~$20,600] to Georgian Dream.

According to the study, Cartu Insurance Company received government and municipal procurement contracts worth around 3.5 million lari [~$1.3 million]. Other company representatives — Alla Kakhniаuri, Kakha Kobiashvili, Zaza Verdzеuli, Givi Lebanidze and Zurab Chachkhiani — donated a total of around 1 million lari [~$370,000] to Georgian Dream.

Another major donor to People’s Power is Giorgi Damenia, a business partner of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s brother, Alexander Ivanishvili, in the company Tornado+. In 2025–2026, he donated 120,000 lari [~$44,400] to the party. Damenia had previously donated 170,000 lari [~$63,000] to Georgian Dream, while Tornado+ itself donated 85,000 lari [~$31,500] to Ivanishvili’s party between 2016 and 2018.

Another member of Ivanishvili’s business circle is Irakli Bekaури, CEO of Bolero & Company, owned by Vakhtang Karichashvili. Karichashvili, who holds Georgian and Russian citizenship, has been described as a business partner of Ivanishvili’s cousin, Ucha Mamatshvili. According to the study, his companies rank among Georgia’s largest wine exporters to Russia. Between 2014 and 2024, his companies received 56 million lari [~$20.7 million] in subsidies from Georgia’s Agriculture Ministry.

In 2026, Bekauri donated 60,000 lari [~$22,200] to People’s Power. He had previously donated 327,000 lari [~$121,000] to Georgian Dream.

Among people linked to Bekauri and Karichashvili is Levan Getsadze. Public Registry records list him at various times as a representative of companies linked to Ucha Mamatshvili’s business partners. Getsadze donated 13,000 lari [~$4,800] to People’s Power, which the study says was his first political donation.

For many years, Getsadze owned Trezor, a company founded in 2019 that operated a medical laboratory in Tbilisi. Soon after its establishment, the company began taking part in public procurement and has since received contracts worth around 3.2 million lari [~$1.19 million]. The laboratory is now owned by the US company Quest Biosciences LLC.

The study also links another major People’s Power donor, David Balanchivadze, to Ucha Mamatshvili’s business circle. In 2016–2017, the investigative journalism studio Monitor linked Balanchivadze’s appointment as executive director of RMG GOLD to Mamatshvili’s interests.

Balanchivadze began making political donations to Georgian Dream in 2016. According to the study, he donated a total of 532,000 lari [~$197,000] to the party. In 2026, he donated 60,000 lari [~$22,200] to People’s Power.

Among the donors to People’s Power is Giorgi Meskhi, who served as director of the state-owned company Sakspetstrans from 2017 to 2020. In 2024, he donated 58,000 lari [~$21,500] to the party.

While running the state-owned company, Meskhi founded the construction company Hiteco Group with his business partner Giorgi Khujadze. Meskhi now owns 100% of the company and serves as its director. Hiteco Group is building a multi-storey hotel in Tbilisi. Meskhi also owns a 33% stake in Gonio Group.

Another People’s Power donor, Guram Tetrashvili, is director of Georgian-Israeli Business Group LLC. The company is owned by Besik Papismedov, who is involved in several construction projects in Tbilisi. Tetrashvili donated 10,000 lari [~$3,700] to the party. According to the study, this was also his first political donation.

According to Transparency International Georgia, three of the 28 donors — Aleksandre Tushuri, Mamuka Gogrchiani and Givi Gabunia — fund both People’s Power and Georgian Dream.

All three donated a total of 60,000 lari [~$22,200] to People’s Power on 11 December 2025. Three months later, on 18 February 2026, the same people donated another 60,000 lari [~$22,200] to Georgian Dream.

People’s Power was founded in August 2022 by three MPs who left Georgian Dream: Sozar Subari, Dimitri Khundadze and Mikheil Kavelashvili. It initially operated as a civic movement and registered as a political party in March 2024. Sozar Subari is the party’s chairman.

When they launched the movement, its founders said their goal was to provide the public with more information about developments in Georgian politics and defend the country’s national interests. People’s Power has been particularly vocal in criticising the influence of Western political forces and non-governmental organisations. The party initiated the draft law on the “Transparency of Foreign Influence”.

From 2022 to 2024, People’s Power formed part of the Georgian Dream parliamentary majority. In the 2024 parliamentary election, the party ran jointly with Georgian Dream. Today, People’s Power has its own parliamentary political group.

Transparency International Georgia study

World.title: “The ritual is complete”: Why the Kremlin needs elections to the State Duma
World.content:
Russia State Duma elections

Based on a report by Novaya Gazeta Europe

Russia’s first State Duma elections since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine have brought few surprises. According to preliminary official results, the ruling United Russia party has retained its constitutional majority.

Political observers say there is now little genuine political competition left in the country.

But if the vote does little to determine either the composition of the real centers of power or the direction of the Kremlin’s policies, why does the Kremlin continue to hold elections? And what significance do they still have for the authorities and for Russian society?

To explore those questions, Novaya Gazeta Europe spoke with political scientists, a sociologist, a political strategist and an electoral expert.

Yabloko disrupted the script of a quiet campaign

According to an electoral expert who asked not to be identified for security reasons, the authorities had initially planned a campaign that would be as uneventful and tightly controlled as possible.

“Overall, all the candidates and parties that made it onto the ballot tried to run their campaigns as inconspicuously as possible, so as not to give the authorities grounds to target them. Everyone except Yabloko played by the system’s current rules. Yabloko, by contrast, played by the rules the system had five years ago,” he said.

The situation surrounding Yabloko became the campaign’s main development to break from the prescribed script. According to the expert, the party’s position had not changed, but after years of war, the authorities had come to view it as radical.

The federal list of Yabloko was barred from the election by a decision of the Supreme Court. The Central Election Commission removed information about the party from the federal ballot.

“In the end, the authorities chose the coercive route: they removed Yabloko, barred all the more or less prominent candidates, and eliminated the regional lists — with the exception of Novgorod Region. This really became the central story of the election campaign,” the expert said.

Sociologist Igor Eidman said that Yabloko’s attempt to take part in the election at least demonstrated that opponents of the war still exist in Russia. But it produced no meaningful electoral result.



Political analyst Ivan Preobrazhensky does not consider the campaign a genuine election at all. In his view, it was closer to a “performance” or a “special electoral operation,” resembling the Soviet-era plebiscitary votes in which voters were offered no real alternative.

Eidman likewise argues that voters had little meaningful influence over the distribution of political power.

“This was pure political farce — a staged performance, a fake imitation of a political process that does not exist in Russia. The script was written long ago, and all the figures were determined in advance,” he said.

Yet the predetermined outcome does not make the elections meaningless for the Kremlin.

State Duma elections as a political ritual

Political strategist Stanislav Belkovsky describes the elections as a political ritual.

“The event is meaningless in terms of the actual political process, but it is an integral part of the rituals of power. In that sense, it can be compared with the Victory Day parade on Red Square or the Kremlin reception held to mark June 12.”

In his view, Vladimir Putin regards adherence to such rituals as part of maintaining the stability of his own rule.

Alexei Nechaev, chairman of the New People party, left, at the party’s campaign headquarters during a meeting to discuss preliminary results of the State Duma elections. Moscow, Sept. 20, 2026. Photo: Pavel Seleznev / TASS / ZUMA Press / Scanpix / LETA

Belkovsky says the Kremlin is also interested in preserving a liberal façade in the form of the New People party. In his view, its presence allows the authorities to project an image of Russia as a country where legal liberal political forces still exist.

At the same time, he argues that on fundamental issues, the party does not differ from the other established political forces.

There was also uncertainty surrounding A Just Russia, which was hovering near the 5 percent electoral threshold. According to preliminary official results, the party cleared the threshold.

Preobrazhensky argues that even if the party disappeared from Parliament, it would not fundamentally change Russia’s domestic politics.

“There is not a single genuine political party that would be allowed to take part in Russian elections today,” he said.

Yabloko party chairman Nikolai Rybakov casts his ballot at a polling station. St. Petersburg, Sept. 20, 2026. Photo: Olga Maltseva / AFP / Scanpix / LETA

Was there any point in voting?

Preobrazhensky believes that taking part in the election may have had a primarily psychological significance. For some people, simply going to the polls, deliberately spoiling a ballot or taking part in the “Noon for Peace” protest became a way to engage in at least a symbolic political act.

Eidman takes a different view. He argues that mass participation helps the authorities maintain the appearance of a normal electoral process.

He points to the 2024 presidential election as an example. At the time, large lines of Putin opponents formed outside polling stations abroad. Yet the official election results remained unchanged.

An independent electoral expert disagrees.

“The greatest joy for anyone rigging an election is absenteeism — people staying away from the polls. It makes their job much easier. High natural turnout is always a problem for those who manipulate elections,” he said.

What happened with election fraud

According to the anonymous expert, opportunities for independent election monitoring have sharply diminished in these elections. As a result, it has become far more difficult to compare the official results with what actually happened at polling stations.

“In my view, even the information that is available is enough to conclude that, in the overwhelming majority of regions, the official results do not correspond to how people actually voted,” he said.

That is the assessment of the newspaper’s source. Russian authorities, by contrast, said the voting took place without violations capable of affecting the outcome. Independent observers and opposition groups reported violations and restrictions on election monitoring.

The expert believes the nature and scale of possible manipulation may also be changing. In the past, observers focused primarily on precinct-level election commissions. Now, he said, some manipulation may be taking place higher up, at territorial election commissions where results from individual polling stations are consolidated.

As an extreme example, he points to Chechnya, where, according to official figures, Ramzan Kadyrov received 99.85 percent of the vote.

“That would mean that across the entire republic, fewer than 1,000 people supposedly voted against Kadyrov, despite turnout being virtually 100 percent. That is even more extreme than in the Soviet Union,” the expert said.

The source also drew particular attention to Moscow. On the final day of voting, the system for issuing paper ballots experienced a failure there.

The expert stressed that there is no evidence that the disruption was deliberate. But many voters who had deliberately chosen not to vote electronically were planning to go to polling stations precisely on the final day.

Preobrazhensky points to another change. In the past, he said, discussion centered on individual regions with particularly conspicuous electoral anomalies. Now, in his view, the anomalies are becoming regions where the alleged falsifications are less extensive and less obvious.

The question of how to legitimize the results, however, remains. Preobrazhensky argues that it is important for the Kremlin to convince both Russians and audiences abroad that the official figures genuinely reflect public sentiment.

“In the West, there is, in my view, a mistaken argument: ‘Perhaps no one elected Putin, but we know anyway that he is supported by an absolute majority of Russians.’ That is not true, because no one knows that,” the political analyst said.

What will change after the election

Belkovsky believes it would be a mistake to view the State Duma election as a turning point after which the Kremlin should embark on a fundamentally new course.

In his view, the State Duma is not an independent center of key political decision-making.

“The State Duma election in itself is neither a milestone, nor a turning point, nor a ‘barometer’… It is simply part of a ritual, and that ritual has been completed,” he said.

Belkovsky said any decision on a new formal mobilization would likewise not be directly linked to the election results. At the same time, he said, the Kremlin still has ways of replenishing the armed forces through less visible and indirect means.

Eidman believes the official results could serve a different purpose for the authorities — as evidence of a public “mandate” for further decisions.

Preobrazhensky points to another possible consequence of the campaign: a struggle for influence within the Russian government itself.

In his view, the election exposed a conflict between the Federal Security Service, or FSB, and the presidential administration over control of domestic politics.

“The main question that emerged during the election was: Who controls domestic policy? During the so-called election campaign, domestic policy was quite clearly controlled primarily by the FSB,” the expert said.

According to Preobrazhensky, the future direction of Russia’s domestic politics will depend to a significant extent on whether the FSB retains that control.

exchange

World.title: ‘My arrest was political from start to finish’ – Georgia’s ex-PM writes seventh letter from prison
World.content:
Garibashvili writes seventh letter from prison

Former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili, who is serving a five-year prison sentence, has said in his latest – seventh – letter that the real purpose of his arrest was not the criminal case against him, but to neutralise him politically and prevent him from returning to politics in the future.

According to Garibashvili, the authorities initially changed the terms of a plea deal they had agreed with him. Later, when his imprisonment proved more politically damaging to the ruling team itself, they offered him a deal under which he would admit to a new corruption charge.

‘I was screwed over again’

The former prime minister says that on the day he was detained, he received a message telling him that he had to withdraw from politics. In return, he says, he was promised that he would not go to prison but would instead receive a lengthy suspended sentence and a fine.

“I was screwed over again,” Garibashvili writes.

However, he continues, on 4 January 2026 he was unexpectedly informed that the terms had changed and that he would face five years in prison. By that point, he had already pleaded guilty, been released on bail and was awaiting the formalisation of a plea agreement.

20-year relationship with Bidzina Ivanishvili

In one of the key parts of the letter, Garibashvili discusses his longstanding relationship with Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of the ruling Georgian Dream party. He says that because of his 20-year political and personal relationship with Ivanishvili, he did not want to enter into a political confrontation with him.

“I silently walked to the political slaughterhouse and went to prison because I did not want to enter into confrontation,”the former prime minister writes.

He says that by making this decision, he sacrificed himself to protect the team and the country.

“I made my sacrifice and also spared the team and the country. In return, I was screwed over for a third time,”Garibashvili says.

‘Authorities suffered more from my arrest than I did’

Garibashvili says that in February he communicated with the authorities through an intermediary. Their main message, he says, was that the ruling team had suffered more from his arrest than Garibashvili himself.

He says this left him with the impression that the authorities were preparing a new provocation because his detention and the campaign against him had failed to produce the result they had expected.

“They failed to discredit me sufficiently in the eyes of the public; they failed to achieve the effect they had expected from my arrest and the accompanying propaganda,” the former prime minister writes.

‘My reputation was not significantly damaged’

Garibashvili says there was no further communication with him until July, when the authorities made a new proposal.

According to Garibashvili, this time the authorities acknowledged that his arrest had damaged the ruling team itself, while the former prime minister’s reputation had not suffered significantly.

Garibashvili writes that public sympathy for him had grown, particularly among some Georgian Dream voters.

He says this was also because other people convicted of offences against the authorities had been released with suspended sentences, making his five-year prison term difficult for the public to understand.

Admitting to new corruption charge

According to the former prime minister, it was after this that the authorities developed a new fear that he would return to politics after his release from prison. Garibashvili says he was asked to admit to a new corruption charge.

He says the aim was twofold: to destroy his reputation once and for all and further prevent any possibility of his return to politics:

“Because of this, they demanded that I admit to a new, dirty corruption charge so that, on the one hand, my name would be completely destroyed and, on the other, they could further guard against the risk of my return to politics.”

‘My imprisonment was political from start to finish’

Garibashvili gives a clear assessment of his own case:

“Based on all this, my imprisonment was political from start to finish, from the very first day, and everything that has been done against me is politically motivated and has nothing to do with a legal process.”

The former prime minister says he believes he is in prison because of “absurd suspicions, fears and envy”.

He describes it as an injustice committed not only against him but also against his family.

Response to state propaganda

The second part of the letter contains direct and strongly worded accusations and criticism of the authorities.

Garibashvili says that “false and dirty propaganda” against him has continued over the past two weeks.

The former prime minister describes statements by government representatives as “hypocritical” and “false”.

“As I see it, you have got rather carried away and really settled into your role. Don’t be hypocrites! First take the log out of your own eye, and then talk about corruption,” Garibashvili writes.

He says the public is well aware that the campaign being waged by the authorities is a “farce”.

Irakli Garibashvili

‘You have made state institutions a laughing stock’

Garibashvili also accuses the authorities of damaging state institutions. He says their actions both at home and abroad have made state institutions “a laughing stock”.

“You have given enemies at home and abroad grounds to talk,” he writes.

He says the ruling team’s policies have plunged the country into “continuous chaos and an endless crisis”.

Garibashvili also says the authorities’ own voters have been left confused by their policies, while a sense of hopelessness, instability and uncertainty about the future has taken hold in society.

Parallel with Saakashvili era

The sharpest part of the letter is Garibashvili’s comparison of the authorities’ actions with the rule of Mikheil Saakashvili.

“You are already following Saakashvili’s path and bringing back the methods of rule used by the United National Movement,” Garibashvili writes.

The former prime minister argues that the authorities’ current policies are ultimately harming both Georgian Dream itself and the country.

“You have caused enormous, irreparable damage to your own state, your government and the ruling party itself,” he says.

The letter ends with a warning:

“You are doing evil. Be careful!”

The case against Garibashvili

Garibashvili was first charged with corruption in October 2025. Investigators accused him of large-scale money laundering.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, Garibashvili provided false information in his asset declarations in an attempt to make illegally obtained income appear legitimate.

In January 2026, Garibashvili pleaded guilty and reached a plea agreement with prosecutors. The court sentenced him to five years in prison.

In a second case, the former Georgian prime minister is accused of accepting a particularly large bribe. Prosecutors allege that he received 750,000 lari (approximately $289,000) from a scheme involving classified procurement by the Defence Ministry.

The new case followed statements by Garibashvili in which he accused the authorities of pressuring him and demanding that he admit to a new charge.

The case concerns the procurement of medical equipment and supplies for the Defence Ministry. According to prosecutors, the ministry carried out three classified procurements from late 2022. At the time, Juansher Burchuladze was defence minister and Irakli Garibashvili was prime minister. Prosecutors, however, plan to reach a plea agreement with Burchuladze, saying the decision was made in view of the extent of his co-operation with the investigation.

World.title: Armenia marks 35 years of independence: the country’s gains and losses, according to AI
World.content:
Armenia’s 35 years of independence: an AI assessment

Armenia is marking Independence Day. Thirty-five years ago, on 21 September 1991, an overwhelming majority of the population (94.39%) voted in a referendum to leave the USSR and establish an independent democratic state.

JAMnews asked artificial intelligence to analyse Armenia’s journey over the past 35 years.

According to the AI assessment, the past 35 years present a highly mixed picture. Armenia has made significant progress in democratisation, international integration and the development of state institutions.

At the same time, Armenia has suffered major losses. Wars have cost thousands of lives, driven emigration and resulted in the loss of territory. Above all, the country has yet to fully resolve its security concerns.

“The greatest achievement is the survival of an independent state. The greatest loss is the human cost and demographic price Armenia has paid over 35 years,” the AI concluded.

From survival to state-building

“35 years can be divided into three major stages.

1991–1998: survival and state-building — the declaration of independence, war, blockade, an energy crisis and economic collapse, but also the creation of the foundations of state institutions.

1999–2017: stabilisation and economic growth — macroeconomic stability, rapid growth and infrastructure development, but also emigration, corruption, a closed political system and the unresolved Karabakh conflict.

2018–2026: democratic transformation, war and a new foreign policy strategy — the 2018 “Velvet” Revolution, the 2020 war, the loss of Nagorno-Karabakh, the exodus of Karabakh Armenians from their homeland in 2023, the arrival of more than 100,000 forcibly displaced people in Armenia, and efforts to build a new security system and new foreign policy relationships.”

Key achievements

“Building an independent state”

The greatest achievement is that Armenia has existed for 35 years as an internationally recognised independent state, with its own Constitution, state institutions, army, currency, diplomatic system and international commitments.

Developing an international presence

Armenia joined the UN in 1992 and later joined numerous international organisations. This means that the Armenian state acts as an independent subject in international relations and makes its own decisions.

Building an army and defence system

During the war of the 1990s, Armenia established its armed forces. This became one of the key institutions underpinning its independent statehood.

Economic recovery and long-term growth

After the severe crisis of the early 1990s, the economy began to recover in 1994, followed by rapid growth in the 2000s. According to the World Bank, Armenia’s economy grew by an average of around 6.3% a year between 2000 and 2023. During this period, the economy shifted significantly from agriculture towards industry and services.

Development of the technology and services sectors

IT, services, finance and tourism now play a much larger role in the economy than they did during the early years of independence. This is particularly important for a small landlocked country.

Some improvement in living conditions

The World Bank notes an increase in life expectancy and improvements in several social indicators. Extreme poverty has been virtually eliminated. However, “ordinary poverty” remains a serious problem, particularly in rural areas.

Political change and the ability to transfer power

The peaceful transfer of power in 2018 demonstrated the potential for mass civic mobilisation and political change. Subsequent elections, including the 2021 early parliamentary election, were competitive and well organised, according to international observers, although political polarisation persisted.

Strengthening civil society and national identity

Independence created an environment in which the Armenian language, state symbols, national culture and the idea of statehood became the foundations of an independent country rather than a Soviet republic.”

Losses and setbacks

“Human losses

The First Karabakh War, the four-day war of 2016 and especially the 2020 war claimed thousands of lives and left deep trauma across Armenian society.

Consequences of the 2020 war

Armenia lost control over a significant part of the territories of Nagorno-Karabakh and its previous security system. After 2020, Armenia’s security environment changed radically. In 2024, the prime minister himself described 2020 as a moment when Armenia found itself on the verge of losing its independence.

The loss of homeland for Karabakh Armenians and population displacement

After the military escalation in September 2023, more than 100,000 people moved to Armenia. The International Committee of the Red Cross noted that Armenian social services and the accommodation system struggled to cope with such a large influx of displaced people. For Armenian society, this became not only a territorial loss but also a major demographic, social and psychological one.

Emigration and demographic problems

Mass emigration, which began in the early years of independence, became one of Armenia’s most persistent long-term problems. The World Bank identifies low birth rates, an ageing population and significant emigration as serious constraints on the country’s economic future.

Social inequality and poverty

Despite years of strong economic performance, economic growth has not always translated evenly into higher living standards. According to the World Bank, as of 2022, around half of the population still lived below the international poverty line of $6.85 a day. This threshold applies to upper-middle-income countries.

Weak institutions and political polarisation

Over 35 years, Armenia has not achieved full judicial independence, eliminated corruption or overcome political polarisation. A 2026 analysis by Human Rights Watch says that, despite reforms, serious problems remain concerning the independence of the judiciary, the media and the police, as well as the protection of human rights.

Excessive reliance on external security partners

For 35 years, Armenia has had to build its security system amid difficult regional and geopolitical conditions. Its long-standing reliance on Russia for security and, in recent years, the need to diversify its partnerships show that full strategic autonomy remains a work in progress.”

Independence as a fact

“Armenia has managed to create and preserve an independent state, but it has not yet transformed that independence into a state system that is sufficiently secure, demographically sustainable and socially prosperous.

It is important to distinguish between independence as a legal and statehood fact and independence as a real characteristic of a state. Armenia achieved the former in 1991. The latter — economic, military, demographic, institutional and diplomatic independence — remains an ongoing process.

At the same time, the picture of recent years is not limited to losses. In 2025, Armenia and Azerbaijan made progress towards a peace settlement. The prospect of restoring regional ties has also created an opportunity for a new stage to begin, although it is still too early to assess its long-term results.”

Armenia’s 35 years of independence: an AI assessment

World.title: Why are pensions in Abkhazia so low? Officials explain
World.content:
A 71-year-old resident of Abkhazia Marina Kachubeevna recently submitted documents to apply for Russian citizenship. Without a Russian passport, she cannot receive a Russian pension, which is relatively generous by local standards.

Her Abkhaz pension, which totals 6,000 roubles [$65] a month including all basic payments and supplements, is not enough to live on. So the woman has to continue working to have money of her own.

“I have wonderful children. My son and daughter-in-law never refuse me anything. When I started having health problems last year, they took full responsibility for paying for my medicines and doctors.

But every time I have to ask them for money for the pharmacy or basic personal needs, I feel uncomfortable. I don’t want to be a burden. At 71, I want to remain independent and be able to buy even small gifts for my grandchildren myself, without having to ask my children for the money,” Marina Kachubeevna says.

This desire to ease the financial burden on her family is the only reason she decided to apply for Russian citizenship.

Intergenerational solidarity and the reality of pension payments

The story of Marina Kachubeevna reflects broader systemic trends in Abkhazia’s social welfare system.

At present, around 33,000 people receive the basic old-age pension of 6,000 roubles. As the chairman of the republic’s Pension Fund, Denis Gularia, acknowledges, this amount falls far short of what is needed to live on.

However, Gularia points to a traditional model of social support in Abkhaz society, based on assistance from relatives.

“There is such a concept as intergenerational solidarity: children should help their parents. Of course, some pensioners do not have children, but this is the kind of society we have. Neighbours help each other as much as they can.

We constantly hear criticism directed at us. We hear it and understand it. But people have to help each other,” the Pension Fund chairman says.

He also stresses that the number of people receiving additional domestic payments continues to grow:

“The number of people receiving supplementary payments is approaching 17,000 and will continue to grow. Many of our citizens no longer have enough Soviet-era work experience to qualify for a pension from Russia’s Social Fund, so they will receive only our payments. We will try to find the funds to increase these payments in the future.”

41,000 workers supporting 50,000 pensioners

The main obstacle to a significant increase in pensions is the imbalance between the number of officially employed residents and the number of people receiving pensions and benefits.

According to statistics, Abkhazia has a working-age population of 144,000. Of these, around 40,000–41,000 people officially work and pay social insurance contributions. Meanwhile, around 51,000 people receive supplementary payments or pensions.

“With this ratio, high pensions are simply impossible. The remaining part of the population, around 100,000 people, work but do not contribute to the Pension Fund,” Gularia explains.

Commercial businesses also create an additional problem by avoiding full payment of social insurance contributions:

“Unfortunately, not everyone declares their full salary. The minimum salary in commercial organisations here is 20,000 roubles [$215]**. But if someone earns more, employers and employees often agree to declare only the minimum.

People themselves should have an interest in ensuring that social insurance contributions are paid. Remember, the contributions made by the 40,000 people who work today support the entire older generation.”

Reforms, collection orders and individual records

To change the situation, the Pension Fund plans to introduce individual records for insurance contributions and tighten fiscal discipline.

“A flat-rate system is unfair to those who pay honestly. One person pays contributions based on their actual salary, while another declares the minimum, yet they both receive the same pension. That is unfair.

Once we introduce individual records for insurance contributions, it will benefit people who plan to remain economically active: in addition to the basic 6,000 roubles, they will receive substantial payments based on the contributions recorded in their personal account,” Gularia says.

At the same time, the fund is actively working with employers who fail to meet their obligations. According to the chairman, the agency can issue collection orders when contributions are overdue. A collection order allows a bank to debit money from a payer’s account without prior consent. In 2025, the fund recovered 49.9 million roubles [around $537,000] in this way.

Some businesses also voluntarily repay old debts.

“We need to adopt legislation that strengthens the responsibility of managers and accountants who fail to submit reports on time,” Gularia says.

Re-registration for oversight and transparency

The re-registration of pensioners, which runs from 1 September to 1 December 2026, is another necessary step towards putting the system in order.

“There are cases when relatives do not always register a pensioner’s death promptly or submit the death certificate to social welfare offices. The money saved as a result of these checks will go into a fund for future increases in supplementary payments to the most vulnerable groups,” the official explains.

Apparently, bringing businesses out of the shadow economy, introducing individual records and ensuring that people pay their contributions properly offer the only way to ensure that, in a few years, pensioners such as Marina Kachubeevna can retire without financial worries, feel secure and afford to buy gifts for their grandchildren without having to work at the age of 71.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Features of the pension system in Abkhazia

World.title: Georgian authorities ‘suspect’ Tbilisi School of Political Studies of receiving grant without their consent
World.content:
The Georgian State Audit Office has launched an investigation into the financial activities of the Tbilisi School of Political Studies. The Audit Office’s Financial Transparency Department said the investigation concerns the possible receipt of a grant without the Georgian government’s consent.

“To examine the matter comprehensively, the State Audit Office will act within the powers granted to it by Georgian law, including the Law of Georgia on Grants,” the Audit Office told Interpressnews.

The Tbilisi School of Political Studies was founded in 1999 as a non-governmental organisation. The school operates under the auspices of the Council of Europe and is headed by politician Armaz Akhvlediani.

What happened

Government officials have repeatedly spoken about the Tbilisi School of Political Studies in recent weeks. Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said the school had held a seminar in the village of Bakhmaro with funding from the Council of Europe. He suggested that the funding for the event may have bypassed Georgian law.

According to Papuashvili, the school did not seek the government’s consent to receive the grant, while the Council of Europe’s media office said the event in Bakhmaro did not constitute a grant.

“So what was it, then?” Papuashvili asked.

He said the original version of the Law on Grants required government approval for all forms of foreign funding, including direct spending by organisations. The final version retained an exception for diplomatic activities. However, Papuashvili argued that organisations should not use this exception to circumvent the law.

ПPapuashvili suggests that, in the case of the seminar in Bakhmaro, the Council of Europe’s local office directly paid for hotel accommodation, transport and food, as well as fees for experts and speakers.

“If that is the case, we are dealing with an attempt to circumvent the law,” the speaker said.

According to Papuashvili, the law also covers cases where an agreement is described as a service contract but in substance amounts to a grant.

What the Law on Grants provides

The legislative package approved on 4 March 2026 significantly broadens the definition of a “grant”. It covers both financial and non-financial support if it can be used to influence the country’s domestic or foreign policy, including activities linked to the interests of a foreign state or political force.

The law also strengthens the State Audit Office’s oversight of the awarding and receipt of grants. If a foreign legal entity funds a branch operating in Georgia without government approval, it can face sanctions, including a fine equal to twice the value of the grant.

Violating the grants law can also result in criminal liability. Penalties include a fine, community service or up to six years in prison.

The changes also affect the political process. People who work for organisations that receive predominantly foreign funding will be barred from joining political parties for eight years. At the same time, restrictions imposed on political parties also apply to entities that are not formally parties but effectively engage in political activity.

The legislative package also tightens administrative liability for private companies if they become involved in public political activity.

Georgia’s Law on Grants

World.title: Police investigate disappearance of 200 cattle from outback station
World.content:
Police are investigating the disappearance of more than 200 head of cattle from a property in outback New South Wales.

Inquiries are in the "early stages" and officers are working to establish whether the cattle strayed or were stolen.

The disappearance of the 212 head from the station on West Wilcannia Road, Wilcannia, was reported on September 6, but police believe they may have gone missing between March and August.

Rural Crime Prevention Team Detective Chief Inspector Cameron Whiteside said the cattle had been on agistment and were not reported missing until after they were returned to their owners north of Broken Hill.

"At this stage we're keeping an open mind," he said.

"In that area of the country … the properties are quite sparse, so it's maybe some time before … they're not checked on daily, they're checked on infrequently.

"There can be a range of explanations for the stock being unaccounted-for."

Detective Chief Inspector Cameron Whiteside says police are open to all possibilities. (ABC Landline)

Police say the landholders had made "significant inquiries" before making the report and investigators are appealing to the public and local landholders for information.

"The rural community is our eyes and ears in respect to these matters," Chief Inspector Whiteside said.

"The people working on adjoining properties, contractors, stock agents or transport operators and people travelling through the district may have seen something that didn't seem significant at the time, but it could be important to our investigation."

Detectives say 155 black Angus cows, eight black Angus bulls, 48 Shorthorn cows and one Shorthorn bull are missing.

The NSW Rural Crime Prevention team regularly attends saleyards across the state. (ABC Landline: Kerry Staight)

According to police, the cattle are branded with a capital "F" over a lazy capital "B", or a "B" on its side, and are also marked with a "V" in each ear and a rectangular notch under each ear.

"Should it be established that they were stolen, it's quite a large number to take," Chief Inspector Whiteside said.

"Especially if it was taken in one hit or over a period of time."

The cattle are valued between $500,000 and $1 million and the owners are reportedly devastated by their disappearance.

"Obviously they want their stock back … it does have a significant impact financially, but also mentally," Chief Inspector Whiteside said.

"We're very mindful of that, so we're seeking information from the public … to help us solve this matter."

World.title: Mary Fowler's Man City score controversial goal with flare burning on pitch
World.content:
Mary Fowler's Manchester City have started their Women's Champions League campaign with a controversial draw against Bayern Munich, scoring a crucial goal with a flare burning among the players.

The reigning English champions came back from 2-0 down to equalise after Fowler's injection in the 63rd minute.

But it was City's first goal from Beth Mead that had Bayern players fuming.

In the final seconds of the first half, Kerstin Casparij broke down the right wing and was pursued by Franziska Kett towards the edge of the 18-yard box, where a flare was sending purple smoke billowing.

Bayern goalkeeper Ena Mahmutovic waved her arms in an apparent attempt to get the attention of officials as the play unfolded, but Casparij seemed unfazed by the nearby flare as she outpaced Kett and whipped a cross into the box, where Bunny Shaw's shot was blocked, and Mead cleaned up the scraps to make it 2-1 heading into the break.

As City celebrated, Mahmutovic and Kett started to complain before their teammates joined in, with referee Olatz Rivera Olmedo immediately removing the projectile from the pitch.

Discussions continued as the ball returned to halfway for the kick-off before VAR confirmed the goal would stand, giving City crucial momentum heading into half-time, leading to an improved second-half performance and ultimately an 86th-minute equaliser by Carlotta Wamser.

Elsewhere on the first matchday of the tournament, Arsenal's trio of Australians — Steph Catley, Kyra Cooney-Cross and Caitlin Foord — all started as the 2025 winners began the quest to regain their continental crown against Danish part-timers HB Køge.

The Gunners won 1-0, but needed an injury-time penalty from Mariona Caldentay that bank worker Alberte Vingum almost saved.

"It was a pretty crazy last five minutes, but that's football," Catley said.

"They defended great; we tried so many avenues to goal.

"Credit to the girls, they kept trying, and Mariona was very calm in that moment."

And in Monza, veteran Matildas defender Aiva Luik played the 90 minutes as Hacken went down 1-0 to Internazionale, becoming the oldest group stage/league phase player at 41, according to UEFA.

Capped 45 times by Australia, Luik is at her 16th club in her 10th country during her 26-year career.

"I still feel young. The secret is coffee and chocolate," she said.

Inter, making its competition debut, scored in the fifth minute through Haley Bugej from a corner but couldn't find a second, with the Swedes more dangerous on the break.
