World.title: Banned Swans to make first public appearance since Pullman Hotel scandal
World.content:
Sydney's five suspended players will make their return to the club this morning and will address the Swans' playing group "at some point".

Swans coach Dean Cox arrived at the club's Moore Park base early today, before Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich briefly spoke to media.

"Look, it's a natural thing that the players will come into the club over the next period," Pavlich said.

"Don't know exactly when that'll be, given that the season's now finished and player exit meetings are occurring.

"And the players at some point will have a chat to the broader group and the club, but yeah, there's no timeline."

Swans coach Dean Cox arrives at the club's headquarters ahead of player exit meetings. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

The five have not been at the club since August after they were stood down for breaching club standards following a post-match party at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne.

Those suspensions are separate from a police investigation into sexual assault allegations, with Victoria Police flagging an update is not expected until late October.

No charges have been laid, and there is no suggestion of any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

Pavlich would not be drawn on the specifics surrounding the five's return.

Asked what he would want the five to say in their address, Pavlich said: "I want them to be themselves.

"I want them to come in and do what we'd normally do at the end of a season, which is, yeah, player exit meetings.

"If they've got something to say to their player group, if they've got something to say to the club, then we'll hear them out then."

World.title: Hacking group purports to have stolen FBI data in cyber attack
World.content:
The digital extortion group known as ShinyHunters says it has stolen data about the majority of the FBI's current and former employees during a cyber attack.

In a statement posted to its dark-web site and during an online chat with Reuters, ShinyHunters said it had targeted the FBI in response to a May 2026 agency announcement that detailed the hacking group's methods and advised its targets not to pay it.

The FBI has suffered from past data breaches that have also compromised the privacy of its staff. (AP Photo: Charlie Neibergall)

ShinyHunters wrote that it had stolen data "on almost ALL FBI Agents, and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job".

As proof, the group offered what it said was a screenshot of a vandalised FBI job site and what it described as a small sample of its stolen data.

The FBI released a statement saying the agency was "aware of claims regarding unauthorised activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is ​currently investigating".

Job site disrupted

Reuters could not verify the authenticity of the screenshot, but the job site did appear to have experienced recent disruption.

A message posted to the site on Tuesday, local time, said both it and the FBI Special Agent Applicant Portal were "currently unavailable".

The data sample appeared to contain information about FBI agents' names, home addresses, social security numbers, their assignments and, in some cases, the names of their family members.

What we know about the 'remarkably devious' ShinyHunters hackers An international syndicate that uses a Pokémon avatar often claims to be behind major cyber attacks. This is what we know about them.

Reuters was able to partially verify the authenticity of the information by running the details, including the social security numbers, against credit bureau records and previously breached data preserved by the dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs.

In at least 10 instances, including in the case of FBI director Kash Patel, Reuters found details that appeared to match.

A person familiar with the matter said the job descriptions in the data also matched in at least some cases.

However, the news agency could not establish where the data came from, or whether it had been stolen from the FBI's internal systems as the hackers said.

Attempts to reach the people whose details were in the sample data were unsuccessful.

Such breaches 'incredibly harmful'

Cynthia Kaiser, a former FBI official, said breaches like the ones claimed by ShinyHunters were "incredibly harmful" because they could be used by criminals to expose and put pressure on the people investigating them.

Ms Kaiser, who is now senior vice-president at cybersecurity firm Halcyon, noted that an old leak dating back to 2016 was still occasionally used today to harass FBI agents.

"Once that information is stolen, it is used forever," she said.

ShinyHunters is one of the world's most notorious hacking groups.

Canvas data breach sees student details compromised Education institutions around the country are scrambling to respond to a global data breach that has affected Australian universities, TAFE and schools.

Its recent break-ins include the purported theft of millions of business records from video game developer Rockstar Games, the maker of Grand Theft Auto, and a May intrusion centred on education tool Canvas, which caused widespread disruption across schools and universities.

Earlier this month, AI company Anthropic said it caught ShinyHunters-linked hackers trying to use its tools.

On Sunday, the group told Reuters it had gone to war against another notorious cybercrime group, cl0p, in a rare bout of public score-settling.

Reuters

World.title: Children in 'birthplace' of Mary Poppins mark coming-of-age ritual
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Each spring, children in the NSW Southern Highlands take part in an aging ritual that preserves their town's unique connection with one of the world's most beloved literary characters.

Australia-born author Helen Lyndon Goff, also known as PL Travers, spent her formative years in the town of Bowral.

Her experiences as a child, as well as the town's local characters, became the inspiration she would later draw on when creating the magical nanny Mary Poppins.

On Bowral Street, in Glebe Park, stands a 5-metre bronze statue of Mary Poppins, erected in 2012.

On the equinox, when the day is as long as the night, year 6 students turn the statue 180 degrees, the coming-of-age ritual reflecting their transition into high school.

Allana Winn and her daughter Piper both participated in the coming-of-age ritual. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Allana Winn, president of the Southern Highlands Youth Art Council, conducted the ceremony.

"Our year 6 students are here today and have been invited to the spring equinox turning to mark not just the changing of a season, but the new phase in their lives," she said.

Ms Winn reminded the children that everything changes with the wind, including visits from Mary Poppins, and that waiting periods and change are two of the hardest things for us to understand.

"Transitions are difficult, but change is exciting and inevitable. Embrace this rite of passage and be brave just like PL Travers and follow your dreams," she said.

'Birthplace' statue honours author

Paul McShane, with his daughter Melissa, initiated the concept of honouring the author's connection to Bowral with a "birthplace statue" and he continues to be involved in the change-of-season ceremonies.

Paul McShane and his daughter Melissa enjoy dressing as characters from the Mary Poppins books. (Supplied: John Swainston)

"In March we're talking about the coming winter, but in spring we're talking about the coming summer, which is when the Mary Poppins stories are set," he said.

"This park was opened in 1908, a year after they moved here, this was probably one of their very first experiences of a park, which is a central motif in the Mary Poppins stories."

An about-face for equinox

With eight books in the series, the nanny flies in on the east wind and out on the west wind, a feature the statue-turning ceremony replicates.

School captains in the Bowral district were invited to participate in the ritual. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

A fundraising activity in 2011 included a human mosaic with 2115 raised umbrellas — a world record. (Supplied: Mary Poppins.com.au)

At the start of spring, year 6 children preparing for high school assist by turning the statue about face, using the built-in turntable.

"We invite children and leaders from the school to turn the statue around to celebrate, not just the coming summer but them going from primary school to high school," Mr McShane said.

"They all think it's pretty special."

Annalese Morris and her daughter are looking forward to Madeline attending high school next year. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Annalese Morris has five daughters and as one gets ready for university next year her middle child is preparing for high school, so changes are flying in all directions.

"I feel like when Mary Poppins says I'll go when the wind turns, it doesn't mean that life is predictable, it means you have to go with whatever comes," 12-year-old Maddie said.

"It's something special we get to do, it's a once-in-a-lifetime thing but there's always something new that will happen."

The Neleus Guild

Mary Poppins in the Park, staged in Bristol's Hippodrome theatre, includes statues that magically move. (Sourced: Phillip Giandiletti)

Inspired by a moving statue included in the fourth book, Mary Poppins in the Park (1952), Mr McShane and friends spent five years causing a little mystery and hubbub of their own on the equinox.

"We don't know how exactly, but that statue got up and moved around the park," he said.

"We called ourselves the Neleus Guild, and we would come out here in the middle of the night and turn the statue.

"In fact, the deputy mayor, Gary Turland, phoned me one day and said, 'We're infuriated about this at upper council.

"'We're going to get to the bottom of this. We want these vandals caught'.

"And I had to explain, in a roundabout way, there was nothing to worry about," Mr McShane laughed.

A personalised turntable was installed for the Bowral statue a decade ago. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

By 2016, a turntable was erected in the park and the location of the statue changed again.

"She went on a jolly holiday and when she returned, there was this beautiful turntable built that she now sits on," Mr McShane said.

From one park to another

Loading...

Australian sculptor Tanya Bartlett created the statue from a sketch proposed and modelled for by Travers herself.

"She wanted to see a statue of Mary Poppins in Central Park New York, but it never happened," Mr McShane said.

"In 1966, she talked to sculptor Sean Crampton in England, who sketched her holding the umbrella."

Mr McShane tracked down the sculptor's widow, who "remembered it all like it was yesterday".

"We got permission from her to use that design for our statue," he said.

"So, we built the statue that New York should have but never did."

World.title: Tones And I reveals why she turned down NRL grand final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Tones And I has broken her silence after the NRL declared it will forego a grand final tradition of pre-match entertainment.

On Tuesday, Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'landys told ABC Sport the NRL's plans to have Tones And I perform before next month's showpiece event would be cancelled.

The NRL will use the money set aside for pre-match entertainment to contribute to children playing rugby league.

But Tones And I's management said no deal had been signed or confirmed in writing.

Via a statement sent to ABC Sport, her management representative Regan Lethbridge said "prior commitments" were a sticking point.

"Tones was recently approached to perform the pre-show at the NRL grand final," the statement read.

"An offer was presented to Tones via management on September 5.

NRL grand final loses pre-match act The NRL grand final is set to go ahead without pre-match entertainment after negotiations with Australian artist Tones and I collapsed.

"Tones had a prior commitment with Macklemore in America and explored all avenues to make it work.

"Nothing was signed or confirmed in writing.

"Due to the last-minute nature and prior commitments by Tones, we were unable to accept the offer.

"We wish the NRL nothing but the very best for their event."

The Sydney Morning Herald reported the issue centred the NRL's insistence Tones And I perform the song Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.

But neither Tones And I nor V'Landys has cited the set list as the issue at play.

Tones And I has previously said she loathed the hit song, which enjoyed significant commercial success when released in 2019.

Macklemore found himself at the centre of his own live upheaval after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's The Loop Tour, over pro-Palestinian comments.

'A different direction'

V'landys said he wished Tones And I well.

"I'm a fan of Tones And I," he told ABC Sport on Tuesday.

"She is a great performer, no doubt about that, and she's got some great songs, but as I said, we both decided to go to a different direction."

V'landys said the cost of putting on any artist for a grand final performance was about a million dollars.

"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend a million dollars on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.

Peter V’landys said money set aside for pre-match entertainment would be invested in junior rugby league. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

To have no pre-game show would be a stunning break from tradition.

The grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop star Teddy Swims last year.

Billy Idol and Tina Turner are among other acts to have taken the stage for the event.

V'landys was unconcerned as to whether the event could be underwhelming without pre-match entertainment.

"Our game sells itself," he said.

"People come to watch rugby league. They don't come to watch a pop concert."

V'landys did not provide details on the record of why or how the negotiations with Tones And I broke down.

"You spend money to get outcomes, and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to … play rugby league," he said.

" We consider a lot of artists over a period of time, but as I said, I've been toying with this idea for a couple of years now, about giving the money to kids to play rugby league rather than a musical act. "

State governments across the country are bidding for the grand final hosting rights.

New South Wales holds the rights, but it is unclear whether the state minister for sport, Steve Kamper, or Premier Chris Minns were consulted.

Neither provided comment in response to questions.

New South Wales Rugby League chief executive David Trodden said he had "a short conversation" with V'landys about the prospect of funds being directed towards grassroots footy.

"I applaud his decision to use the funds to support grassroots rugby league, and particularly those children who may have financial constraints on their ability to participate in such a wonderful community sport," Trodden said.

"Rugby league has a unique ability to provide community support to those who need it the most."

World.title: Record sheep prices see farmers turn crop paddocks over to stock
World.content:
Graeme Golder has been farming "for a day or three" and his instinct to lean further towards sheep has delivered a record payday this season.

The Riverina farmer and his son, Chris, sold first-cross ewes for what is understood to be an Australian saleyard record of $620 a head at West Wyalong.

They sold 600 ewes for an average of $607 a head.

Mr Golder said the sale price made it a no-brainer to turn some of their traditional cropping land over to run more sheep at their Temora property.

"Our boys, especially Chris, he knows which side his bread's buttered on," Mr Golder laughed.

" He knows while ever I stand upright, there'll be sheep at home. "

While the Golder family's prospects are aligning, elsewhere in New South Wales, farmers are struggling with dry conditions.

Commodity forecaster ABARES says NSW winter crop production will fall 30 per cent to 13.1 million tonnes in 2026–27, with stronger conditions in central and southern regions partly offsetting poor prospects in the north.

Strong livestock prices are also being underpinned by a shrinking national sheep flock, forecast at 67.1 million head, down 21 per cent from 85.7 million two decades ago.

Fields of thriving green and gold canola pictured in the Riverina are not representative of the uneven season across all parts of NSW, where some farmers have planted no crop this year due to low rainfall. (ABC Riverina: Rosie King)

Rain turns Riverina season around

Strong lamb, mutton and wool prices are encouraging farmers to prioritise livestock over crops.

"We did find that a few farmers were retaining some of their sheep, and probably just easing back on that cropping side of things a bit," West Wyalong livestock agent Paul Quade said.

" They are not chasing the money, but just sort of leaning that way and just keeping their sheep numbers right up. "

After a dry start to the year, timely autumn rain also improved the Golder family's grain yield.

"We had dams going empty at the end of February. I even got halfway through [cleaning one], and two days later it was a metre from being full," Chris Golder said.

"We fluked good rain at the start of March and then at the end of March, and that set us up for the winter with feed."

The family's crops are now among the best they have grown.

"We're just waiting for the wheels to fall off the season because they look exceptional," Chris Golder said.

Graeme Golder said it was unusual to have strong livestock and grain prospects coincide.

"We have had good grain years in the past, but they haven't necessarily lined up with very good livestock years," he said.

Competition is strong for ewes this spring. (ABC News: Cara Jeffery)

Uneven season across NSW

But not every farm is as lucky.

About 45 per cent of NSW is under varying degrees of drought, according to NSW Drought coordinator Ray Willis.

"It's been just a real mixed bag right around the state, whether you've got the rain or not," Mr Willis said.

He said the Northern Tablelands and North West remained particularly dry after missing significant winter rainfall, with areas around Ashford, Glen Innes and Tenterfield doing it tough.

About 45 per cent of NSW is in drought. (Supplied: DPIRD)

Mr Willis said the effect on cropping was particularly stark around Moree, traditionally a "wall-to-wall cropping district", where he had heard only about 10 per cent of the local government area had been planted to crops this season.

Among those growers to forgo a crop was Mungindi's Sam Heagney.

"We actually don't have any winter crops in at all, which may be a first for us going back through the history books," he said.

"It was extremely dry through April and May, and we had no chance of planting anything."

Late May storms brought up to 100 millimetres to some nearby properties, but Mr Heagney only received about 20mm.

A previous bumper crop on Sam Heagney's Mungindi property, in contrast to this year with dry conditions forcing him to sit out the winter cropping season. (ABC News: Jennifer Ingall)

The lack of profitability ultimately convinced him not to plant.

"The numbers very clearly said not to plant," he said.

"It was really easy on paper; going out in the paddock and actually deciding not to plant was a much harder decision."

After several productive seasons, including record wheat yields in 2025, Mr Heagney described this year as "almost the miss we had to have".

"I just hope it's only the one," he said.

Tough calls on the South Coast

Conditions are also proving difficult on the South Coast, where Bega cattle producer Brett Rogers said hopes of a spring turnaround were fading.

"You get a bit of hope up and then the clouds just blow over the top of you and you put another bale of hay out," he said.

Brett Rogers says prices of $6.70 a kilogram for light steers at the Bega cattle sale made it easier for drought-affected producers to sell cattle rather than continue feeding them. (ABC News: Joshua Becker)

Mr Rogers said producers were considering reducing stock numbers, with strong cattle prices providing an opportunity to lighten off.

"Every load of cattle that goes out of our place is one less bale of hay you've got to feed out," he said.

The Aussie Hay Runners have delivered 26 semi-trailer loads carrying 736 bales of hay, along with calf meal, to dairy farmers in the Bega Valley and South Coast.

Founder Linda Widdup said farmers recovering from natural disasters increasingly needed help.

Aussie Hay Runners delivered more than 1,000 bales to farmers in Bingara in northern NSW earlier in the year. Last weekend, they delivered more than 700 hay bales to farmers in the Bega Valley. (ABC New England: Peter Sanders)

"We try to support them with recovery so that they're not left unprepared, because Mother Nature's certainly throwing some curveballs at everybody at the moment," she said.

Drought coordinator Ray Willis, who was preparing to visit the South Coast, said the region was "going backwards at a rate of knots".

Mr Willis warned things could get worse across the state, with the department's drought forecast predicting about 35 per cent of NSW could remain in a drought category at the end of November.

He urged farmers to plan according to current conditions rather than rely on the forecast.

"It's been quite a dry start to spring and temperatures are really starting to warm up," he said.

World.title: Fremantle fans go to great lengths to see their team play at the MCG
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Thousands of people who are dubbed "the purple army" are making the more than 3,000-kilometre march across the Nullarbor for Saturday's AFL grand final in Melbourne.

After Fremantle booked their spot in the big dance on Friday night, airlines have increased the number of flights to Melbourne, but have also increased the cost.

The price of fuel has not deterred the fans who decided not to fly but drive, with a litre of diesel at Eucla fetching $3.22 a litre on Tuesday, according to the government-run FuelWatch, which compared to Perth's cheapest diesel at $2.59 a litre.

Bus driver Phil Robbins is behind the wheel of a purple bus emblazoned with "GO FREO" on the side. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Nullarbor turns purple

About a dozen fans travelling on a separate large purple bus calling itself "The Longmuir Coach" left Perth on Monday night.

Among the group was former Fremantle livewire Hayden Ballantyne, who played in Fremantle's only previous grand final in 2013.

"I've never driven the Nullarbor before, so this is a great way to do it," Ballantyne said during a stopover in Balladonia.

Hayden Ballantyne is hitching a ride interstate on a purple bus. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"This grand final will definitely be a different experience as a supporter, and hopefully they can get the win.

"It means so much to so many people ... you see a tough-as-nails guy like Shaun McManus [who will present the premiership cup if Fremantle wins] reduced to tears this week and that's what it means."

Dockers diehards on the road

For many long-suffering supporters, Saturday's grand final represents a chance to witness history, with Fremantle chasing the club's first AFL premiership since joining the competition in 1995.

Retired Wheatbelt farmer Noel Stone is a Fremantle diehard who is making an emotional pilgrimage to Melbourne, carrying some ashes of his late nephew with him to the game.

Shauna and Noel Stone with Vincent and Christine Hadlow on the Nullarbor en route to Saturday's AFL grand final. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"My nephew Cameron passed away in a car accident in 2015. He played football for Corrigin and had a run with West Perth," he said.

"He he was a mad keen Fremantle supporter. In fact, his nickname was Docker.

"I've got in my possession some of his ashes that his mother has asked me to take to the game.

"At least he's with us for something he would have loved … to see the Dockers playing in a grand final on the MCG."

Travelling with Mr Stone is Quairading farmer Vincent Hadlow, who is a St Kilda supporter but is adopting Fremantle as his team for the occasion.

"I'm just along for the ride, and maybe I'll see Fremantle win one before my mob St Kilda," he said.

St Kilda's flag drought extends to 1966, and if the Nullarbor traffic is any indication, Fremantle fans are desperate to witness theirs to end after 32 years.

Balladonia Roadhouse employee Eleanor Trinh pins up signs around the Nullarbor truck stop to welcome Fremantle Dockers fans. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

No tickets to the game

Natasha Cornish, her husband Troy and their 17-year-old son, Jayden, are driving from their Canning Vale home to Melbourne, despite not getting a ticket to the MCG.

The Cornish family is yet to secure grand final tickets. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

They plan to make a last-ditch effort to obtain tickets on Saturday.

"People think we're a little crazy, but even if we can't get tickets we'll be in Federation Square outside of the MCG to soak up the atmosphere," Ms Cornish said.

"We're mad Fremantle supporters … we have followed them since inception … it was her idea [travelling without tickets]," Mr Cornish said.

Fremantle supporters Val Downing (left) and Choco Crombie leaving Balladonia on the way across the Nullarbor. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Choco Crombie and his wife, Shelley, from Corrigin in WA's Wheatbelt are travelling with close friends.

"It's expensive, but you can't take it [money] with you [when you die], and I wouldn't want to miss this," he said.

"We've filled up the tank for about $3 a litre at Norseman, and hopefully that will get us across the Nullarbor."

Shelley Crombie (left), Choco Crombie, Graeme Downing and Val Downing are making the long journey from Corrigin in the Wheatbelt to Melbourne. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Val Downing, also from Corrigin said her favourite Fremantle player was Patrick Voss but "I love them all".

"We've been members for 20 years, and we go to all the home games," she said.

"We were there in 2013, and we weren't going to miss this one."

Police out in force

With the expected increase in traffic, additional police are patrolling the 710km stretch of Eyre Highway between Norseman and Eucla near the West Australian border.

Norseman Police Station's officer-in-charge, Sergeant Travis Taylor, said speed and fatigue were the two biggest factors in regional road crashes.

Sergeant Tristan Taylor says officers are urging motorists to drive safely on the cross-country journey. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"WA Police literally just want you to get to where you're going, to the football, safely and return safely," he said.

"Take your time, take it steady, there's no rush, plan your trip."

World.title: Big Build royal commission LIVE: Opening hearing to lay foundations for probe into alleged corruption on government building sites
World.content:
Premier Ben Carroll revealed last month that former South Australian chief justice Chris Kourakis would lead today’s royal commission into the building industry.

Kourakis served as SA’s chief justice from 2012 until his retirement from the bench earlier this year. He was previously the state’s solicitor-general from 2003 to 2008.

Former South Australian chief justice Chris Kourakis will head the royal commission into corruption on Victorian Big Build worksites.

Two Victorian barristers, Chris Young and Christopher Carr, have been appointed as counsel assisting the commission.

Young, KC, practises in public and commercial law and has appeared in proceedings involving building and construction projects. Carr, SC, is chair of the Victorian Criminal Bar Association, and practises across criminal and administrative law.

There is no list of witnesses who may appear before the commission yet, but the powers handed to Kourakis extend into the executive government, allowing him to call politicians and advisers alongside public servants, union leaders and building firms.

This could include Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews, as well as senior advisers who sought to warn Allan in writing about lawless CFMEU tactics, cost blowouts and the reported infiltration of organised crime on taxpayer-funded projects.

World.title: Tones and I offered NRL grand final show only three weeks ago
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Tones and I offered NRL grand final show only three weeks ago Chris Barrett September 23, 2026 — 9:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian artist Tones and I was offered the NRL grand final gig on the eve of the finals series and turned it down because of prior commitments in the United States, according to her management. This masthead revealed on Tuesday that the grand final will go ahead on October 4 without a headline pre-game entertainment act after the NRL was unable to come to a last-minute deal with the ARIA award winner. Tones and I broke her silence on the NRL grand final hours after news of negotiations for her to headline the sporting event had fallen through. Getty Images On Wednesday, the star’s management revealed she had been approached with an offer by the NRL less than three weeks ago. “Tones was recently approached to perform the pre-show at the NRL grand final. An offer was presented to Tones via management on September 5th,” her management told this masthead.



“Tones had a prior commitment with Macklemore in America and explored all avenues to make it work. Nothing was signed or confirmed in writing.



“Due to the last-minute nature and prior commitments by Tones, we were unable to accept the offer. We wish the NRL nothing but the very best for their event.” Sources closely linked to the matter but not authorised to comment publicly say the parties had also been unable to come to an agreement over what songs Tones and I would perform at Accor Stadium and that she had not committed to playing her global smash hit Dance Monkey. Teddy Swims performs before the 2025 NRL grand final between the Melbourne Storm and Brisbane Broncos at Accor Stadium. Getty Images However, the timing of the approach to Tones and I has raised questions about why the NRL left it so late to try and lock in a big-name artist for the grand final. By contrast, the AFL secured Kylie Minogue for its grand final five months ago.



Related Article Exclusive

NRL grand final Fallout with star leaves NRL with no pre-game entertainment for grand final Speaking on Nine’s Today show on Wednesday, Australian Rugby League Commission chairman Peter V’landys said: “We love Tones and I. She’s a great performer, great Australian artist. We had artistic differences, and those artistic differences couldn’t be resolved. “That’s when we decided to go with the concept that we wanted to do over the last few years and donate the money to the underprivileged kids that can’t play the game of rugby league. Because rugby league is a game for all.” The NRL’s failure to land grand final entertainment comes less than three months after it announced a record seven-year $5.3 billion broadcast rights deal with Foxtel and Nine, the owner of this masthead. The NRL is already obligated to fund junior rugby league development but V’landys said the money set aside to pay for a grand final act would be better spent in that area.



One of the biggest events on the sporting calendar, the NRL decider has traditionally booked top Australian and international acts for its pre-game show. But after talks with Tones and I proved unsuccessful, the NRL opted not to scramble together a back-up option and has said it will instead donate $1 million to junior rugby league. V’landys said he had been considering scrapping costly pre-game entertainment before negotiations with Tones and I collapsed and believes the money is better spent on the grassroots game. He argues the game itself is the entertainment but the absence of an audience-drawing pre-game act threatens to take the gloss off Sunday week’s grand final as an event.

World.title: Qantas announces when Sydney-New York non-stop flights will start
World.content:
New York: Qantas has announced its direct flights to New York will begin from Sydney in mid-2028, connecting Australia and the east coast of the US with non-stop air travel for the first time. A specially configured Airbus A350-1000 ultra-long range aircraft will be used for the flights. They will be fitted with an additional 20,000-litre fuel tank that will enable the plane to fly more than 16,000 kilometres and up to 22 hours non-stop. A specially configured Airbus A350-1000 ultra-long range aircraft will be used. Chris Zappone Qantas said the direct flight would shave three hours off the typical journey from Sydney to New York. Tickets will go on sale in August next year. The airline made the announcement at a cocktail reception in New York on Tuesday evening (US time).



Related Article Aviation Alan Joyce: Qantas survived COVID because of my decisions “Conquering the tyranny of distance has been part of who Qantas is from the very beginning,” said Qantas chief executive Vanessa Hudson. “Reaching New York non-stop completes a vision we set out many years ago, and it’s a moment of enormous pride for the thousands of our people who have been working hard to make Project Sunrise a reality.” Qantas expects to take delivery of 12 of the A350-1000ULR aircraft, each configured with 238 seats across four cabins. The New York route will follow the start of direct flights between Sydney and London in October 2027.



The choice of New York as the second destination after London for the ultra-long haul flights is a bet by the airline that jet lag-phobic Americans on the East Coast will be willing to pay to fly to Sydney directly, bypassing Los Angeles and other major hubs. One source close to Qantas told this masthead in June that “the north-east of the US is a sleeping giant” for premium travel to Australia, which can be met with the help of Project Sunrise flights. The Project Sunrise plane’s lighting system and cabin service is designed to minimise the impact of jet lag. It will also have a special wellness zone where passengers can stretch their legs in mid-flight. The new Qantas first-class suite planned for its A350 ultra-long range flights. The plane will have 40 premium economy seats, 140 economy seats, 52 business suites, and six first class suites – the latter two designed by David Caon, the mind behind some of Qantas’ Australian coloured-hued cabin interiors.



The specially fitted Airbus, still in its primary paint colours, completed a milestone in July on its road to certification by authorities after completing what appeared to be a record-breaking 24-hour-24-second non-stop flight from Melbourne to Toulouse, France. Related Article Updated

Aviation Millions tune in as Qantas jet completes 24-hour non-stop flight Qantas said the first aircraft was expected to be delivered to the airline by April 2027. Qantas is counting on continued demand for premium travel for the success of Project Sunrise. The airline noted that since 2018, almost two million passengers have flown on Qantas’ non-stop long-haul services from Perth to London, Rome and Paris. The airline also flies directly between Melbourne and Dallas Fort Worth, where demand has held up despite steep rise in airfares this year following the escalation of hostilities in Iran. World.title: Albanese defends Australia’s social media crackdown from Trump admin’s ‘censorship’ blast
World.content:
New York: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has dismissed the US government’s public criticism of his plans to overhaul social media algorithms and regulate perceived harmful content, putting him at loggerheads with United States President Donald Trump. The Trump administration issued a scathing statement on Tuesday afternoon (AEST), arguing the attempt to tackle social media harm announced earlier this month would likely to result in censorship and would disproportionately hit American companies. Speaking to reporters in Manhattan, Albanese said he would not back away from prosecuting Australia’s interests. “The digital duty of care is something that we’ve foreshadowed for some period of time,” he said. “It’s not about giving government control; it’s about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices, which is why it is framed in that way.”



The US is particularly concerned by “potential mandates that would allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements - such as forced chronological feeds or opt-in recommendation systems”. It requested the Albanese government “withdraw any plans to mandate that platforms algorithmically suppress content based on ambiguous government-defined safety criteria”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the United Nations in New York on Monday. Dominic Lorrimer Issued by the US embassy in Canberra, the American response to the bill’s exposure draft came just as Albanese is in New York to speak at the United Nations, where he spruiked on Australia’s leadership in technology regulation. In his speech to the UN, Trump also rejected what he called a “globalist scheme” to regulate AI – which Australia has joined – and said the US would officially rename artificial intelligence to “super intelligence” in a bid to rehabilitate the concept’s image.



Albanese said there’s a recognition that technology could bring enormous benefits, but the internationally community needed to “make sure that humans are in control.” Albanese did not answer a question on whether he would refer to the technology as “super intelligence” instead of artificial intelligence, a push Trump has made to rehabilitate the concept’s image. On the duty of care, the Trump administration has asked Australia to clarify how it would determine what constituted online harm, warning that vague definitions risked becoming a mechanism for “viewpoint-based censorship”. Platforms were likely to over-moderate speech to avoid penalties of up to $109 million, the US concluded, leading to censorship of controversial views. The Trump administration has taken an aggressive approach to regulations that impact American tech companies. Bloomberg



“Such a framework also risks reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics that platforms may preemptively demote to comply with overbroad safety mandates,” the US government said. It added that if the Australian government compelled platforms to filter content in algorithmic feeds, and that filtering drew in “protected speech”, then the impact would be materially indifferent to the government simply removing such speech from the platform. “The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship,” it said. “The US government has made clear its opposition to foreign measures that result in extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online.” Related Article Social media Labor has started a new war on the internet. Will it backfire?



The US noted the majority of online platforms affected were American-owned and global, and that mandatory design features would likely impact content seen by users outside Australia. If other countries adopted their own duty-of-care mandates, platforms could face incompatible design requirements “that are not technically or commercially scalable”, the US said. The most restrictive policy would likely win, it added. World.title: Six-year-old sets new Rubik’s Cube world record
World.content:
WorldAsiaPuzzles Six-year-old sets new Rubik’s Cube world record Lily Shanagher September 23, 2026 — 8:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A six-year-old girl has set a new world record for the fastest solving of a Rubik’s Cube. Lian Yunzhi, from China, broke the women’s world record for the 3x3x3 Rubik’s Cube twice in three days at competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou provinces. Solving the cube five times, she first averaged a time of 4.52 seconds per cube, and then 4.27 seconds, becoming the only female “cuber” in the world to have an average time under 4.5 seconds. Yunzhi, from Chengdu in Sichuan province, has learnt more than 1300 cube algorithms, spending between two and three hours practising on the cube per day in the past year.



Footage shows the young girl solving the cube at a rapid pace before proudly holding up her trophy. In another, she is surrounded by schoolmates as she solves the cube at speed. Yunzhi was also filmed practising solving the cube at home with her parents, while they also showed her trophies lined up on a shelf to Red Star News. Related Video Victorian teen solves Rubik's Cube in less than two seconds Her mother, Lin Yangxi, told Chinese media that she had been introduced to the Rubik’s Cube after attending an extracurricular class alongside dance and music lessons. According to the World Cube Association, she has taken part in 33 competitions across China and has 569 official solves. Her single record for a 3x3x3 cube is 3.54 seconds, and 2.15 seconds for a 2x2x2 cube.



Lin said she had “gradually realised” that cubing was an “excellent activity for fostering a child’s comprehensive abilities” and had shifted her daughter’s focus towards it. She added: “Solving a Rubik’s Cube improves focus, memory, logical thinking, spatial awareness, and helps develop a healthy mindset toward winning and losing. “It’s not just about blindly memorising formulas, but using logical reasoning to find optimal solutions.” The previous record was held by Qixian Cao, a nine-year-old who set an average time of 5.97 seconds in 2023 at the age of six after learning to use the cube at three years old. She later set a record 4.98-second average at Start of Summer Beijing 2026 in May, becoming seventh in the world overall, according to Speedcuber’s Digest. The Telegraph, London

World.title: Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose weeks after leaving rehab, coroner finds
World.content:
Updated CultureCelebrityVale Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose weeks after leaving rehab, coroner finds Jeffrey Collins Updated September 23, 2026 — 8:43am ,first published 12:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Actor Hayden Panettiere died from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl, and had been in rehab just weeks before, according to a coroner’s report. Panettiere, 36, was found unresponsive in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on August 16. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the home. Hayden Panettiere, pictured at the world premiere of Scream VI in New York in 2023, died last month. AP Photo/Evan Agostini A combination of fentanyl and its chemical byproduct, as well as the anti-anxiety medication alprazolam – a muscle relaxer and a drug used to treat major depression and other serious mental health disorders – was found in Panettiere’s system, according to a statement from the Greenville County Coroner’s Office. A more detailed report released to The Associated Press said a senior deputy coroner who visited the Airbnb apartment to investigate Panettiere’s death found blue pressed pills and a straw on a table that would later test positive for fentanyl. A white powdery substance was found in her suitcase in a sunglasses case, according to the report.



Related Article Vale Hayden Panettiere’s final battles: Mysterious pain and trouble with an ex When the investigator called Panettiere’s father, he said she planned to spend her birthday five days later in Greenville, then head to Ukraine to visit her daughter. The investigator spoke to two men in the apartment with Panettiere. Both names were blocked out, but police have said her boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach were with her. One of the men said he saw Panettiere putting on makeup at 10.30am the day she died. He went back to sleep and woke to a knock at the door. Both men found Panettiere face down in a sitting position on a sofa bed with her legs crossed. He said that wasn’t unusual, but he couldn’t wake her and noticed she was deep purple. He administered two doses of Narcan and then called 911 when she didn’t respond, according to the report.



The investigator wrote in her report that the man told her he didn’t know if Panettiere used any illegal drugs in the past two days, but “she was very good at hiding them”. Asked for comment on the coroner’s initial report, Kasey Kitchen, a publicist for the family, told AP: “The investigation is still ongoing and the case is complex.” Panettiere rose to fame in the TV series Heroes, before landing roles in Nashville, Scream 4 and the Bring It On series. Getty Greenville Police confirmed Tuesday that their investigation into Panettiere’s death is continuing. Paramedics attended Panettiere’s apartment last month after a 911 call, performing CPR and other advanced resuscitation efforts for more than 40 minutes before she was declared dead. The autopsy found no signs of trauma that could have contributed to her death, Greenville County Coroner Mike Ellis said in a statement.



Panettiere soared to fame in the TV shows Heroes and Nashville. In her memoir This Is Me, released in May, Panettiere described lifelong scars from her early fame, acknowledging an alcohol addiction and enduring postpartum depression after the birth of her daughter, Kaya, with Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko in 2014. She also endured family struggles and tragedy. Her parents’ marriage was strained and eventually ended. Her younger brother, Jansen Panettiere, who was also an actor, died of a heart condition in 2023, at age 28. Loading Panettiere also talked about her long relationship with Hickerson and allegations that the aspiring actor physically abused her. He was charged in 2020 with multiple counts of felony abuse, and pleaded no contest to two counts of injuring a spouse or partner. Hickerson served a short time in jail and was sentenced to four years of probation, along with anger management and Alcoholics Anonymous meetings. He completed the terms and recently asked a judge to reduce his conviction to misdemeanours; that request was denied.



In 2015, Panettiere said she was in a horrible cycle of using alcohol and drugs to battle depression and anxiety and had to find a way out of the darkness. She had also entered rehab while filming the show “Nashville.” “I was the one who put myself in the first treatment centre. I was drowning,” she said in a 2023 interview with Women’s Health magazine. As a child, Panettiere acted in commercials and soap operas, including as the ever-troubled Lizzie Spaulding on Guiding Light. In This Is Me, she wrote that the traumas her character endured, from being kidnapped to killing her mother’s boyfriend, led her to associate “catastrophe with adoration”. AP

World.title: Big Build royal commission LIVE: Opening hearing to lay foundations for probe into alleged corruption on government building sites
World.content:
Premier Ben Carroll revealed last month that former South Australian chief justice Chris Kourakis would lead today’s royal commission into the building industry.

Kourakis served as SA’s chief justice from 2012 until his retirement from the bench earlier this year. He was previously the state’s solicitor-general from 2003 to 2008.

Former South Australian chief justice Chris Kourakis will head the royal commission into corruption on Victorian Big Build worksites.

Two Victorian barristers, Chris Young and Christopher Carr, have been appointed as counsel assisting the commission.

Young, KC, practises in public and commercial law and has appeared in proceedings involving building and construction projects. Carr, SC, is chair of the Victorian Criminal Bar Association, and practises across criminal and administrative law.

There is no list of witnesses who may appear before the commission yet, but the powers handed to Kourakis extend into the executive government, allowing him to call politicians and advisers alongside public servants, union leaders and building firms.

This could include Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews, as well as senior advisers who sought to warn Allan in writing about lawless CFMEU tactics, cost blowouts and the reported infiltration of organised crime on taxpayer-funded projects.

World.title: Tones and I offered NRL grand final show only three weeks ago
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Tones and I offered NRL grand final show only three weeks ago Chris Barrett September 23, 2026 — 9:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian artist Tones and I was offered the NRL grand final gig on the eve of the finals series and turned it down because of prior commitments in the United States, according to her management. This masthead revealed on Tuesday that the grand final will go ahead on October 4 without a headline pre-game entertainment act after the NRL was unable to come to a last-minute deal with the ARIA award winner. Tones and I broke her silence on the NRL grand final hours after news of negotiations for her to headline the sporting event had fallen through. Getty Images On Wednesday, the star’s management revealed she had been approached with an offer by the NRL less than three weeks ago. “Tones was recently approached to perform the pre-show at the NRL grand final. An offer was presented to Tones via management on September 5th,” her management told this masthead.



“Tones had a prior commitment with Macklemore in America and explored all avenues to make it work. Nothing was signed or confirmed in writing.



“Due to the last-minute nature and prior commitments by Tones, we were unable to accept the offer. We wish the NRL nothing but the very best for their event.” Sources closely linked to the matter but not authorised to comment publicly say the parties had also been unable to come to an agreement over what songs Tones and I would perform at Accor Stadium and that she had not committed to playing her global smash hit Dance Monkey. Teddy Swims performs before the 2025 NRL grand final between the Melbourne Storm and Brisbane Broncos at Accor Stadium. Getty Images However, the timing of the approach to Tones and I has raised questions about why the NRL left it so late to try and lock in a big-name artist for the grand final. By contrast, the AFL secured Kylie Minogue for its grand final five months ago.



Related Article Exclusive

NRL grand final Fallout with star leaves NRL with no pre-game entertainment for grand final Speaking on Nine’s Today show on Wednesday, Australian Rugby League Commission chairman Peter V’landys said: “We love Tones and I. She’s a great performer, great Australian artist. We had artistic differences, and those artistic differences couldn’t be resolved. “That’s when we decided to go with the concept that we wanted to do over the last few years and donate the money to the underprivileged kids that can’t play the game of rugby league. Because rugby league is a game for all.” The NRL’s failure to land grand final entertainment comes less than three months after it announced a record seven-year $5.3 billion broadcast rights deal with Foxtel and Nine, the owner of this masthead. The NRL is already obligated to fund junior rugby league development but V’landys said the money set aside to pay for a grand final act would be better spent in that area.



One of the biggest events on the sporting calendar, the NRL decider has traditionally booked top Australian and international acts for its pre-game show. But after talks with Tones and I proved unsuccessful, the NRL opted not to scramble together a back-up option and has said it will instead donate $1 million to junior rugby league. V’landys said he had been considering scrapping costly pre-game entertainment before negotiations with Tones and I collapsed and believes the money is better spent on the grassroots game. He argues the game itself is the entertainment but the absence of an audience-drawing pre-game act threatens to take the gloss off Sunday week’s grand final as an event.

World.title: Qantas announces when Sydney-New York non-stop flights will start
World.content:
New York: Qantas has announced its direct flights to New York will begin from Sydney in mid-2028, connecting Australia and the east coast of the US with non-stop air travel for the first time. A specially configured Airbus A350-1000 ultra-long range aircraft will be used for the flights. They will be fitted with an additional 20,000-litre fuel tank that will enable the plane to fly more than 16,000 kilometres and up to 22 hours non-stop. A specially configured Airbus A350-1000 ultra-long range aircraft will be used. Chris Zappone Qantas said the direct flight would shave three hours off the typical journey from Sydney to New York. Tickets will go on sale in August next year. The airline made the announcement at a cocktail reception in New York on Tuesday evening (US time).



Related Article Aviation Alan Joyce: Qantas survived COVID because of my decisions “Conquering the tyranny of distance has been part of who Qantas is from the very beginning,” said Qantas chief executive Vanessa Hudson. “Reaching New York non-stop completes a vision we set out many years ago, and it’s a moment of enormous pride for the thousands of our people who have been working hard to make Project Sunrise a reality.” Qantas expects to take delivery of 12 of the A350-1000ULR aircraft, each configured with 238 seats across four cabins. The New York route will follow the start of direct flights between Sydney and London in October 2027.



The choice of New York as the second destination after London for the ultra-long haul flights is a bet by the airline that jet lag-phobic Americans on the East Coast will be willing to pay to fly to Sydney directly, bypassing Los Angeles and other major hubs. One source close to Qantas told this masthead in June that “the north-east of the US is a sleeping giant” for premium travel to Australia, which can be met with the help of Project Sunrise flights. The Project Sunrise plane’s lighting system and cabin service is designed to minimise the impact of jet lag. It will also have a special wellness zone where passengers can stretch their legs in mid-flight. The new Qantas first-class suite planned for its A350 ultra-long range flights. The plane will have 40 premium economy seats, 140 economy seats, 52 business suites, and six first class suites – the latter two designed by David Caon, the mind behind some of Qantas’ Australian coloured-hued cabin interiors.



The specially fitted Airbus, still in its primary paint colours, completed a milestone in July on its road to certification by authorities after completing what appeared to be a record-breaking 24-hour-24-second non-stop flight from Melbourne to Toulouse, France. Related Article Updated

Aviation Millions tune in as Qantas jet completes 24-hour non-stop flight Qantas said the first aircraft was expected to be delivered to the airline by April 2027. Qantas is counting on continued demand for premium travel for the success of Project Sunrise. The airline noted that since 2018, almost two million passengers have flown on Qantas’ non-stop long-haul services from Perth to London, Rome and Paris. The airline also flies directly between Melbourne and Dallas Fort Worth, where demand has held up despite steep rise in airfares this year following the escalation of hostilities in Iran. World.title: Albanese defends Australia’s social media crackdown from Trump admin’s ‘censorship’ blast
World.content:
New York: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has dismissed the US government’s public criticism of his plans to overhaul social media algorithms and regulate perceived harmful content, putting him at loggerheads with United States President Donald Trump. The Trump administration issued a scathing statement on Tuesday afternoon (AEST), arguing the attempt to tackle social media harm announced earlier this month would likely to result in censorship and would disproportionately hit American companies. Speaking to reporters in Manhattan, Albanese said he would not back away from prosecuting Australia’s interests. “The digital duty of care is something that we’ve foreshadowed for some period of time,” he said. “It’s not about giving government control; it’s about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices, which is why it is framed in that way.”



The US is particularly concerned by “potential mandates that would allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements - such as forced chronological feeds or opt-in recommendation systems”. It requested the Albanese government “withdraw any plans to mandate that platforms algorithmically suppress content based on ambiguous government-defined safety criteria”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the United Nations in New York on Monday. Dominic Lorrimer Issued by the US embassy in Canberra, the American response to the bill’s exposure draft came just as Albanese is in New York to speak at the United Nations, where he spruiked on Australia’s leadership in technology regulation. In his speech to the UN, Trump also rejected what he called a “globalist scheme” to regulate AI – which Australia has joined – and said the US would officially rename artificial intelligence to “super intelligence” in a bid to rehabilitate the concept’s image.



Albanese said there’s a recognition that technology could bring enormous benefits, but the internationally community needed to “make sure that humans are in control.” Albanese did not answer a question on whether he would refer to the technology as “super intelligence” instead of artificial intelligence, a push Trump has made to rehabilitate the concept’s image. On the duty of care, the Trump administration has asked Australia to clarify how it would determine what constituted online harm, warning that vague definitions risked becoming a mechanism for “viewpoint-based censorship”. Platforms were likely to over-moderate speech to avoid penalties of up to $109 million, the US concluded, leading to censorship of controversial views. The Trump administration has taken an aggressive approach to regulations that impact American tech companies. Bloomberg



“Such a framework also risks reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics that platforms may preemptively demote to comply with overbroad safety mandates,” the US government said. It added that if the Australian government compelled platforms to filter content in algorithmic feeds, and that filtering drew in “protected speech”, then the impact would be materially indifferent to the government simply removing such speech from the platform. “The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship,” it said. “The US government has made clear its opposition to foreign measures that result in extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online.” Related Article Social media Labor has started a new war on the internet. Will it backfire?



The US noted the majority of online platforms affected were American-owned and global, and that mandatory design features would likely impact content seen by users outside Australia. If other countries adopted their own duty-of-care mandates, platforms could face incompatible design requirements “that are not technically or commercially scalable”, the US said. The most restrictive policy would likely win, it added. They will be able to opt out of receiving content recommended by an algorithm and only receive content shared by creators they choose to follow. Lin said she had “gradually realised” that cubing was an “excellent activity for fostering a child’s comprehensive abilities” and had shifted her daughter’s focus towards it. She added: “Solving a Rubik’s Cube improves focus, memory, logical thinking, spatial awareness, and helps develop a healthy mindset toward winning and losing. “It’s not just about blindly memorising formulas, but using logical reasoning to find optimal solutions.” The previous record was held by Qixian Cao, a nine-year-old who set an average time of 5.97 seconds in 2023 at the age of six after learning to use the cube at three years old. She later set a record 4.98-second average at Start of Summer Beijing 2026 in May, becoming seventh in the world overall, according to Speedcuber’s Digest. The Telegraph, London

World.title: Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose weeks after leaving rehab, coroner finds
World.content:
Updated CultureCelebrityVale Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose weeks after leaving rehab, coroner finds Jeffrey Collins Updated September 23, 2026 — 8:43am ,first published 12:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Actor Hayden Panettiere died from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl, and had been in rehab just weeks before, according to a coroner’s report. Panettiere, 36, was found unresponsive in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on August 16. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the home. Hayden Panettiere, pictured at the world premiere of Scream VI in New York in 2023, died last month. AP Photo/Evan Agostini A combination of fentanyl and its chemical byproduct, as well as the anti-anxiety medication alprazolam – a muscle relaxer and a drug used to treat major depression and other serious mental health disorders – was found in Panettiere’s system, according to a statement from the Greenville County Coroner’s Office. A more detailed report released to The Associated Press said a senior deputy coroner who visited the Airbnb apartment to investigate Panettiere’s death found blue pressed pills and a straw on a table that would later test positive for fentanyl. A white powdery substance was found in her suitcase in a sunglasses case, according to the report.



Related Article Vale Hayden Panettiere’s final battles: Mysterious pain and trouble with an ex When the investigator called Panettiere’s father, he said she planned to spend her birthday five days later in Greenville, then head to Ukraine to visit her daughter. The investigator spoke to two men in the apartment with Panettiere. Both names were blocked out, but police have said her boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach were with her. One of the men said he saw Panettiere putting on makeup at 10.30am the day she died. He went back to sleep and woke to a knock at the door. Both men found Panettiere face down in a sitting position on a sofa bed with her legs crossed. He said that wasn’t unusual, but he couldn’t wake her and noticed she was deep purple. He administered two doses of Narcan and then called 911 when she didn’t respond, according to the report.



The investigator wrote in her report that the man told her he didn’t know if Panettiere used any illegal drugs in the past two days, but “she was very good at hiding them”. Asked for comment on the coroner’s initial report, Kasey Kitchen, a publicist for the family, told AP: “The investigation is still ongoing and the case is complex.” Panettiere rose to fame in the TV series Heroes, before landing roles in Nashville, Scream 4 and the Bring It On series. Getty Greenville Police confirmed Tuesday that their investigation into Panettiere’s death is continuing. Paramedics attended Panettiere’s apartment last month after a 911 call, performing CPR and other advanced resuscitation efforts for more than 40 minutes before she was declared dead. The autopsy found no signs of trauma that could have contributed to her death, Greenville County Coroner Mike Ellis said in a statement.



Panettiere soared to fame in the TV shows Heroes and Nashville. In her memoir This Is Me, released in May, Panettiere described lifelong scars from her early fame, acknowledging an alcohol addiction and enduring postpartum depression after the birth of her daughter, Kaya, with Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko in 2014. She also endured family struggles and tragedy. Her parents’ marriage was strained and eventually ended. Her younger brother, Jansen Panettiere, who was also an actor, died of a heart condition in 2023, at age 28. Loading Panettiere also talked about her long relationship with Hickerson and allegations that the aspiring actor physically abused her. He was charged in 2020 with multiple counts of felony abuse, and pleaded no contest to two counts of injuring a spouse or partner. Hickerson served a short time in jail and was sentenced to four years of probation, along with anger management and Alcoholics Anonymous meetings. He completed the terms and recently asked a judge to reduce his conviction to misdemeanours; that request was denied.



In 2015, Panettiere said she was in a horrible cycle of using alcohol and drugs to battle depression and anxiety and had to find a way out of the darkness. She had also entered rehab while filming the show “Nashville.” “I was the one who put myself in the first treatment centre. I was drowning,” she said in a 2023 interview with Women’s Health magazine. As a child, Panettiere acted in commercials and soap operas, including as the ever-troubled Lizzie Spaulding on Guiding Light. In This Is Me, she wrote that the traumas her character endured, from being kidnapped to killing her mother’s boyfriend, led her to associate “catastrophe with adoration”. AP

World.title: Privileges Committee decides against investigating who leaked FENZ report
World.content:
Parliament's Privileges Committee has decided investigating a leaked report about Fire and Emergency is not worth its time.

The Post newspaper published details from a report written by members of the Governance and Administration Committee, which had not yet been released publicly.

Under Parliament's standing orders, the draft report of a select committee is strictly confidential to the committee until it reports it to the House.

The privileges report noted it was "essential the confidentiality of select committee proceedings is respected".

The Privileges Committee can recommend punishments for breaking Parliament's rules and says it would take action if it receives information about how The Post obtained the report.

But given a "significant number" of people had access, the MPs on the committee say a fulsome inquiry to find the leaker would not be a good use of their time.

The committee has written to all MPs to remind them of the seriousness of the matter.

The report into Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) was a result of an inquiry by the committee seeking to examine the state of FENZ's fleet, the effectiveness of its asset management and procurement practices, the causes of delays and cost pressures, and whether the organisation has the systems and processes needed to ensure that front-line firefighters have access to safe, reliable, and fit-for-purpose appliances.

The powerful privileges committee was called to an unscheduled meeting last week by its chair to discuss how to handle a complaint about the leaked report.

On Wednesday last week, Speaker Gerry Brownlee told MPs in the House he had received a letter from National MP Tim Costley "raising as a matter of privilege the divulging of a draft report of the Governance and Administration Committee contrary to Standing Orders".

Speaker Gerry Brownlee. VNP/Phil Smith

The complaint was in regards to a story published in The Post titled, "Leaked FENZ inquiry report rips into leadership dysfunction, calls for board replacement".

Brownlee said the publishing of the leaked report was "a serious matter, not merely a technical one".

"The unauthorised release of confidential select committee proceedings has previously been considered a contempt. It is essential that the confidence of proceedings is respected to enable committee members to work together. Furthermore, the House is entitled to be the first recipient of the finding of its committees," Brownlee said.

The matter was referred to the Privileges Committee - Parliament's court equivalent - and with just three sitting days remaining of this parliamentary term it prompted the committee's chair, Chris Bishop, to call a meeting.

Bishop noted one of the options the committee would consider was carrying the issue over to the next term, "because there may not be enough time to deal with the matter".

The Speaker noted in his comments to the House "it is unfortunate that the Parliament has just over two weeks left until dissolution, but the timing of this matter was not a choice made by me or the House".

World.title: Privacy Commissioner puts Manage My Health, Health NZ on notice after data breach
World.content:
The Privacy Commissioner has given Health NZ and patient portal Manage My Health until next year to comply with health privacy rules after a massive data breach last year.

Almost 100,000 individuals had data leaked after the portal was targeted by hackers in December.

About 90 percent of those individuals were based in Northland.

The commissioner had found in May Health NZ and Manage My Health "failed in their responsibilities" to have adequate security controls when hundreds of thousands of medical files were stolen in the cyber attack.

The hackers compromised 403,730 Health NZ documents and 22,609 documents that had been uploaded by patients.

Now, Commissioner Michael Webster has put the two organisations on notice, and set deadlines for them to meet requirements.

The notices were issued for failing to comply at the time of the breach with the security requirements of rule 5 of the Health Information Privacy Code.

The rules required Manage My Health to ensure there were reasonable safeguards to prevent loss, misuse or disclosure of personal information.

Webster noted some changes had already been completed.

Manage My Health had already improved on the effectiveness of multi-factor authentication, as well as restricting user access to information and controlling unauthorised external access, the commissioner's office said.

Webster said he was thinking particularly of Māori in Northland, where 90 percent of the affected patients whose data was stolen live.

"These Compliance Notices will ensure, and confirm to me, that Manage My Health and Health NZ are treating patient data securely and it will give New Zealanders assurance that we take these breaches seriously and that strengthening systems is vitally important," he said.

World.title: 'No claims': Taxpayers' Union 'categorically denies' sexual harassment payout claim in Nicky Hager book
World.content:
The Taxpayers' Union has rejected a claim in Nicky Hager's latest book that it settled an employment dispute involving allegations of sexual harassment against its executive director.

Hager's book Dirty Work, released on Tuesday evening, focuses on the organisation and its influence on New Zealand politics, in what he describes as its attempt to "shift New Zealand to the hard right direction".

In one chapter, Hager writes about the background of the Taxpayers' Union's executive director Jordan Williams, including claims about his behaviour.

"Also mentioned was a colleague who had been paid out in a sexual harassment case brought against Williams, the details of which were secret. It was not sexual abuse but textbook sexual harassment.'"

Hager wrote the Taxpayers' Union board had paid out money "to deal with several employment disputes (male and female) in recent years, sometimes more than one at a time, and at least one sexual harassment case against Williams".

Nicky Hager at the launch of his book Dirty Work. RNZ / Melanie Phipps

On Tuesday evening, Taxpayers Union chair Ruth Richardson said the organisation "categorically denies" Hager's allegation the organisation had ever made any payment to settle a sexual harassment claim against Williams.

"There have been no claims, let alone settlements," Richardson said.

"I have spoken directly with previous chairs and with the organisation's co-founder, who served on the board until 2023. All are unequivocal: the allegation is totally untrue."

Approaching Williams for comment on this, he pointed RNZ to earlier comments he had made.

"This really came from nowhere, the suggestion that there is a settlement of some kind or allegations in relation to that that were settled is totally false."

Williams said Richardson had checked with all previous chairs of the organisation and it was "totally wrong".

He said the book's primary objective was to derail the Taxpayers' Union, and he was "not going to let a far-left activist successfully derail" their plans for the election.

Hager told NZME on Wednesday morning he wouldn't make an allegation like that "without very solid information".

"In this case it was two separate sources who knew about what had happened, they also knew that it had been very carefully hidden - even from members of their own board, because they didn't want the settlement to be known about."

Hager emphasised that the allegation was not sexual assault, but "textbook sexual harassment".

Asked if he had "hard evidence", Hager said yes, "multiple credible sources", and that the woman involved went to a lawyer at the time who was involved in reaching the settlement.

Hager wouldn't say if he'd spoken to the lawyer, but said he wouldn't have printed it if he wasn't confident it was the truth.

RNZ has approached Williams about other allegations raised in Dirty Work regarding his behaviour.

Released at an event in Wellington on Tuesday evening, Hager described the book, subtitled The Taxpayers' Union and New Zealand's Hard Right, as an exposé of the organisation.

Speaking to media afterwards, Hager said there was no suggestion of any criminal behaviour.

He also defended the timing of the book, which like Dirty Politics, has landed before an election.

"I thought, what are people going to say to me if I put out a book a week, a year, or a month or two after an election? They're going to say to me, 'why the hell didn't you tell us what was going on before we voted?'"

An email sent to Taxpayers' Union members following the book's release said Hager had not put his allegations to the organisation, or sought an interview.

World.title: The 'AI confidence trap' many New Zealanders are caught in
World.content:
Audio player for " New survey finds gap between what Kiwis say and do with AI " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/business/1530184%2Fthe-ai-confidence-trap-many-new-zealanders-are-caught-in

New survey finds gap between what Kiwis say and do with AI Nine To Noon Download MP3 13m

New research shows many Kiwis are confident they can spot an AI-generated fake but suggests that confidence may not backed up by their online behaviour.

Cybersecurity company Avast's 2026 Safe Tech Report has found 66 percent of New Zealand adults believe they would recognise an AI fake.

But another 40 percent also admitted to sharing, or considering sharing, sensitive information with an AI tool - with 21 percent having shared or considered sharing a CV and 21 percent sharing or considering sharing a work document.

The report describes that as an "AI confidence trap".

It also says while people might know the classic red flags of a good scam - things like pressure to act quickly or an offer that seems too good to be true - they can talk themselves past them. So what does this say about how we're going with our online safety in the AI era?

Stephen Kho from Avast told Nine to Noon despite the fact people were aware of AI's potential to generate fakes, the AI confidence trap came into play.

"But then we go, because it's so convenient, we are using these AI tools, these publicly hosted AI tools that are potentially hosted overseas mainly America and China and we're uploading our sensitive data ... including medical records, financial records because they're so helpful in helping us plan, identify and do diagnosis."

Uploading documents like this to AI was very similar to uploading them to the internet and they could be used for model training, he said.

People should be very careful and to share less with AI, he said.

"All these tools, in fact if you look at the fine print it would say you know the information you give there can be used and probably eventually owned by these companies."

He advised that if people did want to share something like financial information with AI they should ensure that the information has been made anonymous by removing any private or personal information to ensure it could not be traced back them.

"The idea is that if you're not confident about handing it to someone on the high street, then you shouldn't do it to an AI chatbot as well because they are not your confidante, they're not secret companions or personal experts that have signed legal obligations - these are just in fact AI bots on the internet."

Kho said that insecure configuration of AI platforms means information can be dumped into publicly accessible hacked data which is then traded on the internet and potentially leveraged for scams.

AI tools making it harder to identify scams

Kho said AI has enabled deep fakes which include video or audio.

"We've had a really significant hack recently where a person got called up and middle of the night, you know he'd just done a money transfer for the company and got pulled into a conference call, a zoom call with the CEO and CIO," he said.

They said it was a secret last minute transaction and the person needed to transfer $20 million to an account for what was a secret merger acquisition.

"On all accounts it's the people he's recognised on this board meeting, this zoom call, so he did what he was asked to do but it turned out it was a pretty sophisticated fake video of the CIO and CEO ... asking to transfer this money."

In the past it was easy to identify fake SMS or Facebook messages or emails because they often had incorrect spelling or grammar and the context was often not right, he said.

"These days those are all gone, so the quality, the speed, how real the fake website is that mimics the shop that you like, they're all so real now that it's really really difficult to pick out."
