World.title: Te Pāti Māori promises $200 million to change 'who holds power' for decisions about takatāpui
World.content:
Te Pāti Māori will commit $200 million to setting up an independent Takatāpui Commission tasked with powers and funding to uplift takatāpui, if elected.

The commission is part of the party's broader Mana Takatāpui policy which co-leader Rāwiri Waititi said was built on the principle of "nothing about takatāpui without takatāpui".

A policy document released by the party said the definition of takatāpui includes Māori with diverse genders like whakawāhine, tangata ira tāne, irawhiti, irarere, non-binary, and trans identities.

It also included sexualities like lesbian, gay, bisexual, or queer but the document said no Māori was required to use the word to belong because "everyone holds the right to name their own identity".

The Takatāpui Commission would be governed by takatāpui and have powers to allocate funding to community organisations.

The funding would be distributed by Te Puni Kōkiri annually with no ministerial discretion over the "amount, timing, or whether it occurs". The commission would be subject to public annual reporting and independent audit oversight.

Te Pāti Māori would also guarantee gender-affirming healthcare in the public health system including hormone therapy, primary and specialist care and "pathways" to gender-affirming surgery where "clinically indicated".

"The policy includes protection for intersex takatāpui from non-consensual or medically unnecessary intervention and the prevention gender normalising surgery for intersex tamariki."

The full policy includes:

Setting up a Takatāpui Commission;

Protecting takatāpui from violence and hate;

Growing cultural leadership through te reo Māori and tikanga fluency and participation on marae;

Guaranteed gender-affirming healthcare;

Investment in takatāpui mental health and suicide prevention;

and, investment into takatāpui housing.

Waititi said decisions about takatāpui were being made without them and the policy would change "who holds power".

"We are not creating another advisory group that government can choose to listen to or ignore. We are establishing an independent takatāpui-governed commission with authority and guaranteed, ring fenced funding."

World.title: Post code lottery still alive and well in health sector, latest figures show
World.content:
Patients at the very top and very bottom of the country are still waiting longer than many others for healthcare.

Health NZ has released the March to June results for the five targets which measure how quickly people are treated for cancer, seen in emergency departments, get elective surgery and see a specialist for the first time, as well as how many children are immunised.

Nationally, all five targets had improved on the year before.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405445507112

However, a dig into individual regions shows the post code lottery is alive and well.

When it came to planned care, every district showed at least small improvements in the wait for elective treatment on the previous quarter, and all but Lakes improved on first specialist appointments.

In Wairarapa and Mid Central, 95 percent of patients received their elective treatment within four months.

But in the Northland and Southern districts, more than 40 percent of patients were waiting longer than that.

Those districts also struggled in the first specialist appointment measure, with more than 40 percent of patients not able to see a specialist for the first time in the target of four months.

In South Canterbury, 96 percent of patients were seen and 85 percent in Lakes - hitting the target.

Health Minister Simeon Brown. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

EDs divided

Half of the country's emergency departments showed an improvement in wait times from the last quarter, but half declined.

The figures are from March to June so do not reflect the August and September flu peak where many reported being overwhelmed by patients.

Palmerston North Hospital patients faced the biggest waits in the latest stats, with just 55 percent of patients through the department within six hours, a drop on the last quarter.

Capital and Coast came in second to last with 63 percent, although that was an improvement on the last quarter.

ED patients in West Coast, South Canterbury and Tai Rāwhiti fared best in the latest stats, with 90 percent seen within six hours.

Childhood immunisation

There continued to be large variations in the percentage of children fully immunised by their second birthday. While thirteen districts showed improvements, seven declined.

Children in Tai Rāwhiti and Northland were the least immunised in the country, with about 66 percent meeting the measure.

Capital and Coast were the most immunised at about 90 percent, with Southern Canterbury, Auckland and Counties Manukau just behind in the high 80s.

Health NZ said year on year the national rate had improved 1.7 percent.

Cancer treatment

Results also varied for cancer patients within a month of a decision to treat - but the variations were less than other measures, with cancer often prioritised by hospitals.

Waikato topped the chart, with 96 percent of patients seen in time - well over the government's target of 90 percent.

Wairarapa, Lakes, Taranaki, Tai Rāwhiti, Bay of Plenty and South Canterbury were also in the 90s.

The lowest number was in the West Coast, with about 78 percent meeting the target.

Health Minister Simeon Brown said he was pleased to see the progress made under his government but more needed to be done.

The statistics showed that thousands of people a day were being seen in emergency departments or getting their surgery on time, he said.

"I'm not discounting the things that go wrong or the challenges that do exist but I do think for the vast majority of people, the experience they have is a positive one," he said.

World.title: Why the AFL tribunal upheld Neale's grand final ban
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Finding Lachie Neale guilty was the easy bit for the AFL tribunal.

The hard part was deciding whether to apply the "exceptional and compelling clause".

Neale to miss AFL grand final Brisbane's Lachie Neale has failed in his attempt to overturn a one-game ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan at the AFL tribunal and will miss Saturday's grand final against Fremantle.

As tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC noted at the end of a sensational four-and-a-half-hour hearing last night: "There are matters trending both ways on this issue."

Gleeson and his fellow tribunal members, former AFL players Darren Gaspar and Scott Stevens, decided not to enact the clause.

Neale remains banned from the grand final against Fremantle, although the Lions have until midday today to submit a notice of appeal, which would likely be heard tomorrow.

Why was the suspension upheld?

For many reasons, according to Gleeson.

Neale's evidence was rejected by Gleeson as "inconsistent".

Neale insisted he did not strike Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan during last Saturday night's preliminary final.

"It was more a bump or body-check," the dual Brownlow medallist said.

Neale said Ginnivan "might have taken a bit of a dive to get a free kick".

The tribunal did not buy the argument.

"We have listened carefully to Mr Neale's evidence, but we find it was inconsistent in key respects with what we saw on the video," Gleeson said.

"And to that extent we do not accept it."

Lachie Neale was suspended for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in Saturday's preliminary final. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Robert Cianflone)

Neale maintained his shoulder and chest made contact with Ginnivan, but the tribunal found it was "a forceful blow delivered with a swinging arm and an open hand".

The only video footage of the incident was long-range and, even when enhanced, remained grainy, no matter how many times it was played frame by painstaking frame.

"It is the case that there is no single frame in the vision that shows Neale's hand or lower arm making contact with Ginnivan's abdomen," Gleeson said.

"When played at normal speed, it appears clear to us that this was, to use the common vernacular, a strike to the guts.

"We are mindful of the significant consequences for Neale of this finding of intentional strike. But we find the evidence to be cogent."

'He knew the consequences'

That was the guilty part.

Now, for what Gleeson said was "the more difficult issue".

Was using the exceptional and compelling circumstances clause justified to downgrade Neale's penalty from a ban to a fine?

Introduced this year, the clause had been deployed once: to downgrade a one-match ban for Collingwood legend and AFL games record-holder Scott Pendlebury to a fine.

Neale wanted it applied to him.

But, as Gleeson noted, Pendlebury was charged with rough conduct. Specifically, it was graded as careless conduct, medium impact, and high contact.

Neale was charged with striking. Specifically, it was graded as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact.

Gleeson narrowed in on the difference between conduct gradings: Pendlebury was careless, but Neale was intentional.

Lachie Neale (left) has helped the Lions win the past two flags. (AFL Photos via Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

There was also Neale's record, which his barrister — the AFL's former football operations boss Adrian Anderson — compared to Pendlebury's.

Until March, Pendlebury had never fronted the tribunal or been suspended in his 21-year career.

Neale has not previously been banned in a 15-year career that has included two Brownlow Medals, six club champion awards, and co-captaining the Lions to two premierships.

But as AFL counsel Andrew Woods KC pointed out, Neale had previously been found guilty of offences eight times: three of them for striking the body of opponents.

But he had never been suspended.

"This is not the first occasion on which Neale has been found to have struck his opponent," Gleeson said.

The tribunal chair also noted the purpose of the AFL's so-called gut-punch law, also introduced this year. Nine other players have been banned for the offence this season.

"The purpose of the guideline is to stamp out this very sort of conduct. Neale ignored it, and he knew the consequences," Gleeson said.

"Being of Neale's outstanding record does not render a one-match suspension for that act inappropriate or unreasonable."

AAP

World.title: NRL's hardest job a family affair for Rob Toia
World.content:
Marking Herbie Farnworth is just about the hardest job any centre can have in rugby league, but Roosters flyer Robert Toia will not have to do it alone.

Friday night's preliminary final will be a family affair for the 22-year-old in more ways than one.

As a Redcliffe junior and one of 10 siblings, Toia cannot even begin to count how many friends and family he will have in the stands at a sold-out Lang Park, but he is sure to have some kin close at hand for his battle with Farnworth.

"Me, Salesi Foketi and Siua Wong, we're all related," Toia said.

"We're cousins through our grandparents. Me and Salesi have always known since we were young, but Siua we only found out last year.

"[Redcliffe] is home. It's always felt like home, and every time I play at Lang Park, it's the stadium with the best atmosphere."

Toia and Wong discovered they were related last year. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Wong will line up at second row alongside Toia on the Tricolours right edge, against Farnworth and Toia's State of Origin teammate Max Plath, and both know what to expect from the fires of "The Cauldron".

Toia made his Queensland debut there after just 10 NRL games last year, while Wong is in the midst of his fourth finals campaign in as many years.

Foketi has been a later starter, only securing a place in the run-on side in recent weeks, but the three have been close ever since they lived together in the Roosters academy house as boys.

Around that same time, the trio played in a junior grand final against a Penrith side containing future Dolphins kingpin Isaiya Katoa, who will be a target for Foketi on Friday night.

The miracle wins that made Isaiya Katoa Isaiya Katoa prepares for his NRL semifinal debut as the prince of the game's playmakers and four years ago it was a series of brilliant finals performances that birthed his budding legend.

A bustling run from the 20-year-old knocked Cronulla halfback Nicho Hynes out of last week's semifinal after just 75 seconds and proved why he is a danger man even among a team with as much strike as the Roosters.

"I'm so proud of him. Everything is God's timing, because he was battling and playing Cup in the beginning of the year, but he got an opportunity and took it with both hands," Toia said.

"He's one of the best backrowers in the comp."

But as big a job as the Dolphins face with containing Foketi, Toia has an even more difficult one on his hands as he tries to put a saddle on Farnworth.

The Englishman has proven he is the best centre in the world several times over, if not one of the best players overall.

Farnworth leads the NRL in tackle breaks with 161, a full 44 ahead of the next best centre, and is first among all players for offloads with 75.

Farnworth is the best centre in the world and enters the prelim in terrific form. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

He is first among centres for runs, run metres and post-contact metres and is fresh off a magnificent showing in the Dolphins' 26-16 win over the Warriors that has them one win away from their first-ever grand final.

Toia has the size and athleticism to hold his own in any battle — in that star-making Origin debut last year, he held his own against no less than Latrell Mitchell — but Farnworth still shapes as a challenge that will go a long way towards deciding whether the Roosters can progress to their first grand final since 2019.

"You see the tackle-busting ability he has, but his work rate is underrated. He's always involved, on the offensive side and the defensive side," Toia said.

"I think pressuring him, shutting him down, getting my D movements right and hopefully, I can stop him from doing what he does best."

Toia comes into the match in imperious form of his own. He has scored in both the Roosters' finals matches and, along with Mark Nawaqanitawase, was the club's chief destroyer in last week's win over Cronulla.

The highlight was a massive fend on KL Iro that sent the rugged Sharks centre, who normally defends like someone taught a bicep muscle how to tackle, fully airborne.

It is a measure of how much Toia has continued to improve this season after claiming rookie of the year honours last year and a reminder that the best is yet to come, something the Tongan international believes is just as true for his team.

"I got a bit lucky there," Toia said.

"The boys just put me in the right spots and I was just moving for them.

"It's the best feeling [winning]. It's been frustrating for a lot of the year, we haven't been able to produce our brand of game, so it was good to show a glimpse of that.

"I feel like we still haven't played 80 minutes of Roosters footy."

World.title: Chimney colours unveiled for Norwood SANFL victors amid TV ratings boost
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Norwood Football Club's colours have been unveiled atop the Brickworks chimney to celebrate its SANFL Grand Final win in what was the most-viewed game since a modern rating system began.

The total national television audience on Sunday was up 16 per cent on 2025 numbers to 109,700, which included 93,500 broadcast TV viewers.

It also included 16,100 viewers from broadcaster video on demand (BVOD), which was up 52 per cent.

The VOZ ratings, which started in 2022 and combine both broadcast TV and BVOD, found that 87,500 viewers of broadcast TV viewers were from Adelaide, along with 12,800 of those streaming online.

The Norwood and Sturt colours will stay atop the Hoffman Kiln until the end of season 2027. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"The broadcast ratings were exceptional, broke every record for the last five years," SANFL executive Darren Chandler said.

"And when you compare those to what's happening in Western Australia and Victoria, we've absolutely blown it off the charts."

SANFL kicking TV goals SANFL crowds are continuing to climb each year after COVID-19 restrictions put a dent in numbers

Football commentator Mark Soderstrom said 71 per cent of South Australian televisions switched on were tuned into the decider between Sturt and Norwood, which drew 38,250 spectators to Adelaide Oval.

The WAFL Grand Final, on the other hand, drew 19,210 people to Perth Stadium, continuing a four-year decline in crowds, while the VFL Grand Final drew just 12,941, the first time the league had attracted more than 8,000 fans in seven years.

A time-honoured tradition

The annual winners and runners-up of the SANFL grand final have been displaying their colours atop the 1913 Hoffman-designed kiln at Thebarton since the start of the decade.

The much-loved ceremony of nearly 70 years had to be moved from its previous home chimney at the West End Brewery after the facility was closed by its owners, Lion, in 2021.

Redlegs supporters came out to celebrate their team's 2026 premiership win. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Redlegs coach Jade Sheedy, who was a premiership player for Sturt in 2002 when he won the Magarey Medal with teammate Tim Weatherald, also coached Woodville-West Torrens in back-to-back premierships in 2020-21.

He told the crowd of Redleg supporters at Thebarton that when the siren blew on Sunday and Norwood beat Sturt 87 points to 73 after a final-quarter comeback, he thought he was "still in a dream for 15 minutes".

"I guess it was two years of building something pretty special, and to come together in the last 30 minutes and to believe in that, and to kick five goals three to one point in the last quarter showed how much the group had grown and that's what I'm most proud of," Sheedy said.

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley and coach Jade Sheedy were still celebrating on Tuesday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley said the team had not changed "too much structurally" since they lost the preliminary final by two points in 2025 but had "increased the belief in how we play".

"We just fell short in 2025, but we took a lot of learnings from that and a lot of confidence reviewing how we were playing our footy," he said.

Sturt football manager Geoff Riddle payed tribute to the Redlegs at the chimney ceremony. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Sturt football manager Geoff Riddle attended the ceremony on behalf of the runners-up.

"I think we can all agree that Sunday was a great spectacle, and it was a great  for the competition and the league across the country," he said.

He said Norwood were "deserved winners" as the "most consistent team all year".

World.title: NRL grand final loses headline act for pre-match entertainment
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL says it is prepared to have no pre-match entertainment at its grand final this year after talks broke down with Australian artist Tones And I.

Instead the league is offering to increase funding to grassroots competitions with the money set aside for a pre-game performance.

Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC the money spent on pre-match entertainment could be put to better use.

"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend a million dollars on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.

The move would be a stunning break from tradition — the grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop-star Teddy Swims last year.

Teddy Swims performed at last year's NRL grand final. (Supplied: NRL)

Billy Idol and Tina Turner are among other acts to have taken the stage for the event.

V'Landys said the total cost of such performances ran close to $1 million and that the plan for grassroots funding was one he had been mulling for sometime.

V'Landys was unconcerned as to whether the event could be underwhelming without pre-match entertainment.

"Our game sells itself," he said.

"People come to watch rugby league — they don't come to watch a pop concert."

V'Landys did not provide details on the record of why or how the negotiations with Tones and I broke down.

The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the issue centred the NRL's insistence that Tones and I perform the song Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.

"You spend money to get outcomes and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to play with their mates, gear etc, to play rugby league," V'Landys said.

"I'm a fan of Tones and I. She is a great performer, no doubt about that, and she's got some great songs, but as I said, we both decided to go to a different direction.

"We consider a lot of artists over a period of time, but as I said, I've been toying with this idea for a couple of years now, about giving the money to kids to play rugby league rather than a musical act."

Peter V’landys (right) says the league has decided it would prefer to spend its money elsewhere. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The grand final hosting rights are bid for by state governments across the country. New South Wales holds the rights now, but it is not clear if the minister for sport or the premier were consulted over the matter.

Neither office has replied to requests for comment.

NSWRL chief executive David Trodden said he had "a short conversation" with V'Landys about the prospect of funds being directed towards grassroots footy.

"I applaud his decision to use the funds to support grassroots rugby league, and particularly those children who may have financial constraints on their ability to participate in such a wonderful community sport," Trodden said.

"Rugby league has a unique ability to provide community support to those who need it the most."

World.title: Lachie Neale to miss grand final after AFL tribunal decision
World.content:
Brisbane Lions star Lachie Neale has failed in his attempt to overturn a one-game ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan at the AFL tribunal and will miss Saturday's grand final against the Fremantle Dockers.

Neale's "gut-punch" on Ginnivan means the former Brisbane co-captain has played his last game for the Lions, as the team seeks a second premiership three-peat in club history.

The appeal, held remotely with Neale watching from Queensland, took more than two hours, with deliberations going for close to two and a half hours.

The Lions can still take their case to the AFL Appeals Board in a last-ditch attempt to see Neale cleared.

Neale's counsel, Adrian Anderson, argued that the dual-Brownlow-winner's case was not a strike, rather a bump or body-check. He said that if it was ruled a strike, it was of "negligible impact," and if the tribunal disagreed, there were "exceptional and compelling circumstances" to justify overturning a ban.

Neale gave evidence that he had watched Ginnivan come together with Brisbane's Eric Hipwood, ending up lying on the tall forward and giving him several jumper punches.

He said he went over to "express his disappointment", and collided with him shoulder-first.

But the tribunal did not accept his version of events.

AFL counsel, Andrew Woods KC, told the tribunal that Neale was running away from the direction of the ball to confront Ginnivan.

"Neale is running … he has time to decide what he is going to do," Woods said.

"It's not a football act. It's a forceful arm, you really see this with respect to the vision, that swinging towards the opposition player."

Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC told Anderson the incident was "well off the ball, not in play" and not a strike that happened during a grapple or scuffle.

Anderson argued that Neale's long and honoured career (320 games) without suspension was worthy of making an exception to the ban.

"The primary [argument for exceptional and compelling circumstances] is he is one of the best and one of the fairest to have ever played the game," he says.

However, the tribunal disagreed.

"Having carefully reviewed the evidence and listened to Neale's explanation, we find that this was a forceful blow, delivered with a swinging arm and an open hand," Gleeson said, delivering the verdict.

" When played at normal speed, it appears clear to us that this was, to use the common vernacular, a strike to the guts. We are comfortably satisfied that this is what occurred. "

Gleeson said that after consideration, the panel did not feel there were exceptional circumstances to overturn the ban.

"The purpose of the [gut-punch] guideline is to stamp out this very sort of conduct. Neale ignored it, and he knew the consequences,' he said.

"Even Neale's outstanding record does not render a one-match suspension for that act inappropriate or unreasonable."

Look back at how Tuesday night's proceedings unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Diamonds name Klau for Constellation Cup squad
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Diamonds netballer Sarah Klau has retained her spot in Australia's Constellation Cup squad after pleading guilty to assault.

Klau was included in the 14-player squad named on Tuesday, less than a week after the goalkeeper was sanctioned by Netball Australia (NA).

The 31-year-old was handed a $5,000 fine and a two-match ban — suspended for 12 months — by the sport's national governing body.

Klau fined after unprecedented assault charge Diamonds defender Sarah Klau is handed a $5,000 fine and a suspended two-game ban after pleading guilty to assault and failing to disclose the incident prior to the Commonwealth Games.

Klau had fronted Downing Centre Court earlier this month, facing a common assault charge.

She had allegedly kicked a security guard in the back outside a pub in Sydney's eastern suburbs when she was denied entry due to being too intoxicated.

The NSW Swifts player had reportedly attended a Sydney Swans AFL match a day after an ongoing leg injury ruled her out of the remainder of the Super Netball season.

Klau, who has represented Australia on 67 occasions since her Diamonds debut in 2019, failed to disclose the matter to NA before the Commonwealth Games in July, resulting in the sanctions.

Sophie Dwyer also retained her spot in the Diamonds squad, looking for a chance to find redemption after missing an after-the-siren shot in the Commonwealth Games semifinal loss to Jamaica.

Constellation Cup First Test: October 18 (Auckland)

Second Test: October 21 (Christchurch)

Third Test: October 25 (Sydney)

Fourth Test: October 28 (Melbourne)

Dwyer was left on the bench in Australia's bronze-medal win over England in Glasgow.

The core of coach Stacey Marinkovich's squad remains the same from the Games, with Jo Weston unavailable for selection.

Jessie Grenvold, Amy Parmenter and Donnell Wallam return to the side after travelling to Glasgow as reserves.

Grenvold is yet to make her Diamonds debut after earning her maiden call-up in May following a breakout season in defence for the Melbourne Mavericks.

The Constellation Cup begins on October 18, with the Diamonds travelling to Auckland to take on the Commonwealth Games champions.

Diamonds squad: Kiera Austin, Courtney Bruce, Sophie Dwyer, Sophie Garbin, Matilda Garrett, Jessie Grenvold, Georgie Horjus, Sarah Klau, Cara Koenen, Kate Moloney, Amy Parmenter, Jamie-Lee Price, Donnell Wallam, Liz Watson

AAP

World.title: More votes than three entire clubs: How Nick Daicos won the Brownlow
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Coming into the night, the 2026 Brownlow Medal count held little intrigue about who the winner would be.

Few — if any — in the footballing world thought there was anyone who could seriously challenge Nick Daicos for the award.

But there was still one person who was in shock: Daicos, himself.

"I can't believe I'm the Brownlow medallist to be honest," Daicos said at the award ceremony in Melbourne.

The count was close until about the halfway mark, before Daicos pulled away from the pack as the season progressed.

With his 47 votes last night, Daicos has earned more votes in the last four years than any other player has in any five-year period.

Daicos earned more votes than three entire clubs. He collected 63 per cent of Collingwood's votes for the evening.

He racked up record after record: the most votes in one year, most consecutive games with three votes (six), the most games with three votes (13).

It wasn't just a win, it was domination.

With the win, Daicos joins Tom Mitchell, Gary Ablett Jr and Ben Cousins as father-son selections who have claimed the Brownlow Medal (Jobe Watson's 2012 victory was rescinded).

Daicos time

Plenty has been written about what makes Daicos special.

Coaches and opposition players talk about his elusiveness, vision and ability to make something out of what seems like nothing.

And then there is his competitiveness.

"He hates losing," Magpies great Scott Pendlebury said.

"Especially at table tennis. Whenever we travel on the road, he always tries to get a re-match."

That competitive drive is often what turns good into great, and great into legendary.

But words pale into insignificance compared to watching the best of Daicos in full flight.

Players like Daicos stand out due to the highlights they create.

Teams spend more time trying to get Daicos off balance than any other player in the competition.

It hasn't seemed to have an effect yet.

No matter what teams throw at Daicos, he still has an unerring habit of getting the ball and letting his imagination run wild.

That drive was forged from his early days as a player, often being one of the slightest on the field when he played up in age at both the Greythorn Falcons and the Kew Rovers.

When Daicos moved to Carey Grammar for year 10, he was thrust immediately into the first team to compete in the prestigious APS football competition.

His teammates were no slouches either, with Daicos playing alongside the likes of Noah Anderson and last year's Brownlow medallist, Matt Rowell.

No player in the AFL was more important in getting his team in scoring positions than Daicos was this year.

Daicos thrived at winning the ball when no-one had clear control.

He has an innate ability to track the ball before anyone else, working smarter and not harder.

Daicos also has a scary ability to render his direct opponents as traffic cones.

The Magpies look to get Daicos the ball as much as possible, and he repays them with territory.

Few can match his combination of skill, speed and footy intelligence.

Although Collingwood fell short this year, hopes are higher for 2027 with additional reinforcements.

Family zone

Throughout football's history, geography has shaped the make-up of teams to a great extent.

Teams recruited from specific regions. The fortunes of clubs rose and fell based on the growth of different geographic areas.

Urban expansion fuelled Hawthorn's rise, while weak and depopulating zones condemned other clubs to near extinction.

There was one exception to the geography-based dictation of the footy landscape: the sons of former players.

The father-son rule was introduced in 1949 to ensure players such as Ron Barassi could continue on the legacy of their fathers at their clubs regardless of geography.

These days, the role of geography has inverted and it now dictates where all the father-son selections are.

The family zone for Victorian footy now runs through south-east Melbourne.

This was the former recruiting area for Hawthorn, otherwise known as the Family Club.

The ranks of father-son selections are littered with schools and clubs based in the most desirable parts of Melbourne, often far from the origins of their fathers' careers.

For example, the Silvangi and Daicos offspring played their junior footy at the Greythorn Falcons.

That's only a stone's throw from Collingwood captain Darcy Moore's junior club of Ivanhoe.

Nor is it far from where Mitchell or Watson first honed their craft.

The eastern side of Melbourne has increasingly become a powerhouse in junior footy as well, with Sandringham, Oakleigh and the Eastern Ranges dominating the AFL's Talent League in recent seasons.

Brownlow's changing face

A major change took place to the fabric of the Brownlow Medal this year.

Umpires gained access to a select group of 17 statistics before voting. Daicos excelled in several of these measures.

This may rob part of what made the Brownlow so special.

Umpires have a unique perspective. They're also party to the intangibles, such as on-field demeanour, respect and sportsmanship.

This year's votes aligned more closely to the results of the AFL Coaches Association award than ever before, according to Wheelo Ratings.

Coaches pore over key numbers throughout their games and now umpires can rely on some of the same figures to adjudge best afield as well.

Supplying data may condition umpires to discard insights gleaned in the heat of the action, turning them instead into just another spin on the same cold distant observations.

Defenders are already suffering even more than they traditionally do, while midfielders, who often accumulate high "count" stats, get a larger share of the spoils.

Rucks also outperformed their expected output this year, likely benefiting from the inclusion of hit-outs.

This will likely serve to further intensify a growing trend towards vote concentration in disposal-accumulating midfielders.

The leaderboard for career-long average votes is strewn liberally with current players, with previous leaders Haydn Bunton and Graham Moss only playing the prime vote-earning part of their careers in the VFL.

If this trend continues, Daicos will soon break Patrick Dangerfield and Ablett Jr's record for most career votes, at least until the next star enters the scene.

But all of that is for the future.

All that is important now is that the inevitable ascension of Daicos to the pinnacle of the game has taken place.

World.title: Formula 1 agrees to shorter races in 2027
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Formula 1 has approved a 15 kilometre reduction in official race distances starting next season.

The change means the total distance will be cut from 305 to 290 kilometres.

The Formula 1 Commission finalised the decision in London.

"In line with the refinements to the power unit regulations to be introduced in 2027 on fuel flow, a reduction in the total race distance from 305km to 290km was approved, corresponding to a reduction of two or three laps," a statement read.

Aussie F1 GP loses season-opening honour Melbourne's Australian Grand Prix will not have the privilege of opening the 2027 Formula 1 season, but it will boast two races in its biggest weekend yet.

The power unit regulations favour increased engine power over hybrid electrical output.

To better handle rain delays and red flags, the commission has also abolished the strict three-hour overall event cap.

While the two-hour maximum of active racing time remains, the change gives organisers flexibility to complete full race distances.

Another objective ‌is to give spectators the best possible chance ‌to enjoy a full race when disruptions occur.

Practice sessions will also gain added flexibility to extend following stoppages.

AP/Reuters

Tech.title: Paramount will need to release way more movies to make this merger work
Tech.content:
Now that Paramount has reached a settlement with the 12 states that were suing to block its $110 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), the studio is even closer to becoming one of the world’s biggest production houses. In addition to spending at least $300 million more on film and TV projects produced in the US, Paramount says that it will release a minimum of 30 movies annually after it absorbs WBD. On paper, these goals make it sound like Paramount is trying to ensure that the entertainment industry won’t be harmed by its WBD acquisition. But when you look at the studios’ recent output, it seems very much like Paramount CEO David Ellison is making promises to the public that he might not be able to keep.

In a statement about the settlement, California Attorney General Rob Bonta stressed that the settlement was designed to maintain consistent film output and domestic production while “protecting the livelihoods of workers above and below the line.” (Of course, any redundancies caused by a merger of this scale will likely lead to layoffs, which makes Bonta’s claim that the settlement “protects workers, jobs, and Hollywood” questionable in the first place.) In a statement of their own, Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) president Sean Astin and chief negotiator Duncan Crabtree-Ireland thanked Bonta and noted that the settlement represents “the lowest standards that our employers must meet.”

Though the acquisition — which has not yet officially been finalized — would permanently fuse Paramount and WBD, the settlement only requires the newly merged company to adhere to a few rules for just five years. In the first two years, Paramount/WBD has to either put out 30 films annually or pay $30 million per film into healthcare and retirement funds managed by Hollywood’s biggest unions. During the following three years, the merged studio would need to release 32 films annually, and if it fails to meet any of these requirements during this five-year period, it will be forced to sell off its 49 percent stake in Miramax Studios to one of its competitors.

In terms of overall output, these proposed goals would be a step up for both Paramount and WBD as separate corporate entities. Over the past six years (including projects slated to debut later in 2026), Paramount has released an average of 15 films annually while WBD has averaged 17. Assuming that the newly merged studio will stick to Paramount and WBD’s previously announced release slates for 2027 and 2028, it would need to put more than a few new projects on the board in order to avoid multimillion dollar penalties. But that probably isn’t all that much of a concern to Paramount because the settlement doesn’t require the new company to produce the projects necessary to hit its annual movie quota.

Paramount/WBD could fulfill its obligations by distributing films that it acquires from other production houses. These films would carry the Paramount/WBD branding, but they would be the products of labor carried out by teams with no direct connection to the studio. Paramount/WBD could also flood the zone with completely new, original films it greenlights and finances itself. But many of those movies could feel less ambitious because the settlement only requires that 20 percent of them have production budgets over $50 million.

Paramount appears to have convinced Bonta and his fellow attorneys general that absorbing WBD will give it the ability to basically double its usual output. But that logic presumes every single aspect of both studios’ production pipelines will continue to operate normally once Paramount and WBD become one. Though Paramount/WBD could ramp internal production up, what feels much more likely to happen is the studio doing the bare minimum to abide by the settlement’s terms. Everything about this settlement makes it seem like Ellison is playing a long game, and after those guardrails disappear in five years, Paramount/WBD will be in an even stronger position to shape the broader entertainment landscape.

Tech.title: Rabbit’s new AI agent doesn’t need an R1 to run
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Rabbit, the company behind the underwhelming R1 device, is rolling out a standalone AI agent that you don’t need its hardware to use, as reported earlier by Wired. The startup says its new OS3 “agentic operating system” runs in the cloud but operates locally across Windows, Mac, and Linux devices.

According to Rabbit, you can add up to five devices to one account, along with your preferred AI models. OS3 will automatically determine the devices, files, apps, and AI models it needs to complete a task. You can also access OS3 through its dedicated desktop site, a paired messaging app like Telegram or iMessage, as well as on Rabbit’s R1 device.

Though Rabbit founder Jesse Lyu tells Wired that the startup has stopped manufacturing R1 devices, it isn’t giving up on AI hardware entirely. It’s instead focusing on a new vibe-coding “cyberdeck” that will run OS3 when it launches within “months,” Wired reports.

Rabbit claims its OS3 system won’t store, copy, use, or sell your data. It notes that it will still keep your chats and memories stemming from them on its servers. Other AI providers linked to OS3 will also handle your data under their own privacy rules.

Tech.title: Saudi Arabia’s new Exobot EVs make the Cybertruck look normal
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is mostly known for its global dominance over petroleum production and oil reserves — not necessarily cars and auto manufacturing, and certainly not electric vehicle production. So it was a little surprising on Monday when a Saudi startup called Ceer unveiled a pair of hyper-angular, spaceship-like EVs, with plans to launch an additional five models by 2030.

The Exobot (yes, that’s the real name) sedan and SUV are expected to go on sale in Saudi Arabia starting in 2027. The ultra-futuristic designs scream Tron, Blade Runner, and every other sci-fi movie you’ve seen — and then some. The gullwing doors are ripped straight from the Tesla Model X (which, of course, was ripped straight from the DeLorean and a range of other rare production cars). Wild and wedge-shaped, the Exobots seemed built explicitly to draw attention. Which, in an attention-based economy, is probably the right strategy.

Previous Next

















1 / 10

The sedan Exobot has low-slung, supercar proportions with a steeply raked windshield that flows seamlessly into the hood. The front fascia features a razor-thin, full-width LED light bar nestled under a sharp, forward-jutting nose, giving it a mean, visor-like glare. The two-tone bodywork and ample windshield immediately had me thinking about the Ferrari Luce, the polarizing electric supercar released earlier this year.

The SUV boasts a blocky, military-meets-cyberpunk stance with high ground clearance and aggressive angles. The whole thing looks thick and armor-plated, with a flat roofline and a distinctive, tactical presence. I wouldn’t be surprised to see this thing bouncing along the Moon’s surface someday. Both were designed by Rob Melville, McLaren’s former design director. But according to Autocar, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had final say on the design.

Previous Next













1 / 8

Ceer is hoping to take advantage of all the upheaval in the global car market, driven largely by the flood of Chinese electric vehicle exports in Asia, Europe, and South America. The US appears on its way to becoming an automotive backwater, with its ahistorical embrace of internal combustion engines and steep tariffs designed to keep Chinese EVs at bay. Why not release a pair of bombastic Batmobiles as a way to distract from the originating country’s extreme oil dependency?

Ceer didn’t exactly emerge from nothing. Rather, it’s a joint venture between Saudi Arabia’s PIF sovereign wealth fund and Foxconn, the Taiwanese company most known for manufacturing the iPhone for Apple. The company will be funded by the kingdom’s vast oil wealth, but with the purpose of building a lineup of vehicles that run on electricity.

Even though it’s distinctly a project built to jump-start the kingdom’s auto industry, Ceer needed to venture outside its borders when hiring for its top roles. Jim DeLuca spent 37 at General Motors, ending up as executive VP for global manufacturing, before joining Ceer as CEO.

“We ⁠wanted to make sure the world could see what Saudi Arabia is capable of,” DeLuca told Reuters.

The kingdom has had mixed luck when it comes to automotive projects. There were plans to build a Jaguar-Land Rover factory there over a decade ago, but to no avail. Toyota declined a deal with the Saudis in 2019. The Public Investment Fund owns a controlling stake in California-based Lucid Motors, which is now building a manufacturing facility in King Abdullah Economic City.

Ceer is taking a diversified approach to its vehicle lineup. While the first models will be electric, subsequent vehicles will be hybrid and combustion-engine, depending on market demands.

That said, starting a car company from scratch is daunting. Just ask Fisker, Lordstown, or Arrival — all of which went bankrupt. Even Lucid, with its support from PIF, is still struggling. We’ll have to see whether Ceer can buck that trend.

Tech.title: Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 comes in an Extreme version too
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Qualcomm has announced the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, this year joined by the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 too. The company describes both new phone chips as flagships, and the spec differences are relatively minor, mostly limited to improved AI processing, video capture, and gaming performance on the Extreme model.

Both Gen 6 chips are built on a 2nm process, and share much in common, including their modems, display specs, security features, GPS, and memory and storage support. Qualcomm no longer publishes detailed breakdowns of the cores across its silicon, but the CPU details given are identical, with two big cores at up to 5GHz and six performance cores running at up to 4GHz. Despite that, the Extreme is described as having slightly superior performance across its CPU, GPU, and NPU.

Some differences are more clear-cut. The 8 Elite Extreme is capable of driving superior video capture, including 8K at 60fps, 4K at 240fps, and support for the Advanced Professional Video (APV) codec. A larger shared memory pool for the NPU should drive faster and more efficient AI performance on the Extreme chip too, while AI-dedicated matrix cores in the GPU (plus more memory) should boost gaming performance slightly when using AI features.

Image: Qualcomm

With core performance seemingly similar, the jump up to the Extreme chip is relatively minor, so it will be interesting to see which chips manufacturers use for which phones. Motorola is the first to jump on board, confirming that its newly announced Signature 27 flagship will use the Extreme chip. Qualcomm has announced that the two chips will also be adopted by Vivo, Xiaomi, Oppo, Honor, iQoo, Nubia, OnePlus, Redmi, Redmagic, and ZTE.

The two 8 Elite Gen 6 chips are Qualcomm’s first 2nm silicon, joining Apple’s A20 Pro and MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro in bringing the new silicon scale to smartphones.

Tech.title: Motorola’s wild-looking Signature 27 runs Qualcomm’s new Extreme chipset
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Motorola is the first company to announce a phone running Qualcomm’s top-end Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip. The Signature 27 looks set to be Motorola’s most advanced flagship in some years, though we’re still waiting for the full specs, price, and release date.

Any prospective buyers will first have to get over the design, which seems guaranteed to earn mixed reception. The aluminum phone has a thin body, available in either black (sorry, “Pantone coal smoke”) or green (“Pantone capulet olive”), with a woven tactical texture on one and a “feather-inspired” finish on the other. Either way, it slopes upwards into what Motorola calls a “camera plane,” with four lenses and a flash in an odd arch layout. It’s certainly unique.

Only a handful of the Signature 27’s specs have been confirmed, but they’re more appealing to me than the design. The B&O logo by the cameras gives away that Bang & Olufsen has helped design the audio, though the specifics are still unknown. There’s the promise of seven years of Android updates, still rare for Motorola. The cameras will include a 200-megapixel periscope telephoto and a 50-megapixel main camera — the latter is more exciting for using Sony’s LOFIC-enabled Lytia 910 sensor, also seen in this week’s Vivo X500 Pro Max, where it enables 17 stops of dynamic range. Hopefully Motorola’s phone matches that.

Motorola says more details about the Signature 27 are on the way, with a global launch due before the end of the year. Unlike the first Motorola Signature, from earlier this year, that will include the US.

Tech.title: Apple clarifies that Texture and Grain controls are exclusive to the latest iPhones’ cameras
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple’s new texture and grain controls for stylizing photos will be more limited on older phones than initially expected.

A confusingly worded press release from Apple indicated that the new features, announced alongside the iPhone 18 and 18 Pro earlier this month, would be “available” on older devices like the iPhone 16 and iPhone Air that “support the latest generation of Photographic Styles.”

But it turns out that “available” didn’t mean that older iPhone models would have full access to those new features.

Making texture adjustments to enhance or smooth a subject’s skin and adding film grain will only be an option when those phones are being used to edit shots taken with the latest iPhone models. Apple has since updated recent press releases to state that those controls will only be available for “photos captured on iPhone 18 Pro models and the Ultra Wide, Main, and Center Stage cameras on iPhone Duo.”

The original version of a September 11th release, which was issued the day before the latest versions of the iPhone and Apple Watches became available for preorder, is still available in its original form on other websites with a footnote specifying that the new “texture and grain controls in Photographic Styles will be available on iOS 27 on iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 17, iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo.”

This limited compatibility was corroborated by a Reddit user who was able to make adjustments to texture and grain on their iPhone 16 Pro Max, but only while editing sample photos taken on an iPhone 18 Pro by photographer Austin Mann who made them available for download on his website. I also had access to those new Photographic Styles controls when editing Mann’s samples on my own iPhone 16 Pro running iOS 27, but they were not available on photos I captured myself.

The Verge has reached out to Apple for clarification on how the feature is supposed to work on older phones but did not immediately get a response.
